en: Imperially Commissioned Edition of the Baizhang Qinggui, Volume One.
Compiled by the Imperial Subject Monk Dehui, Abbot of the Dazhi Shousheng Chan Temple,
in accordance with Imperial Edict.

The Abbot of Daxiong Xiangjijing Temple, the Subject-Monk Dasu, respectfully submits this memorial in accordance with the Imperial Decree for Collation. Chapter One: Praying for the Emperor’s Longevity. That which is most precious to a person lies in the illumination of the Way.
Therefore, since ancient times, sagacious rulers have honored the teaching of our Sage of the West.
They did not treat our followers according to worldly etiquette,
for they revered his Way.
We humbly observe that our present dynasty has shown the utmost favor;
it has specifically remitted taxes and corvée labor so that people may dwell in peace,
while expecting them to devote their full efforts to the Way.
The Sage’s grace is vast and boundless, as infinite as heaven and earth.
It must lead one to awaken to and clarify the Buddha-nature so as to return to ultimate goodness,
and to manifest wondrous function so as to transcend the ultimate spirit.
To guide the people through the transformation of non-action and to elevate the world to a realm of benevolence and longevity—
this is how I repay my sovereign.
This is that upon which we, his followers, ought to bestow our whole hearts.
As for its manifestation in daily life,
one must offer prayers morning and evening.
Even after a single meal, he did not forget to maintain the proper standards of conduct.
Regarding the auspicious anniversary of the Sage’s birth, whenever this sacred occasion was encountered,
he would invariably first establish a Vajra-Amitāyus ritual arena.
On the first day of the month, the monks shall not be granted leave, as a sign of respect.
One day prior to the commencement of the ceremony,
the Hall Office (Tangsi) shall prepare the official notice.
Hang [the list] to the right of the three gates and above the hall; the format for the single scroll is as seen below, with all written on yellow paper.
The roster for assigning monks shall follow the order of their precepts.
Each person’s name is written as a pair of characters.
Five days prior [to the event], the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) shall carry paper in his sleeve and lead the hall attendants to the office of the *shuji* (scribe).
He shall notify the scribe, who will come out to receive them.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) performs a single prostration with full-body contact and reports: "Please compose the formal prose for the inauguration of the Imperial Birthday Festival.
If the *shuji* (Record Keeper) is absent, the *shizhuang shizi* (Attendant for Formal Prose) shall act in his stead;
if both are absent, use a pre-existing formal prose.
Upon seeing that the record has been completed at the end,
present the draft first to the Abbot,
who shall personally deliver it to the Hall Office.
He performs a single prostration with physical contact to respond to the prior salutation.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) uses yellow paper to write the formal letter and takes it along with an attendant.
Holding the tray, the cloth, the incense burner, the candles, and the incense case, he proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to request the abbot to sign the draft of the memorial.

He burns incense, performs a prostration with full obeisance (*chuli*), and reports: "I have begun the observance for the Sacred Birthday; I request the Venerable Master to sign the draft. Once the signing is completed, [the procedure concludes].
The practitioner approaches the abbot’s quarters;
at dawn, he enters the hall to begin the ritual chanting of scriptures.
He shall also notify all the monastic lodgings to hang the signboard for the scripture recitation.
The incense-bearer informs the abbot;
by dawn, the abbot ascends the hall, arriving at the fifth watch.
The abbot returns after performing the incense offering.
After the second serving of congee has been finished,
the Abbot ascends the hall and orders the guest master to hang the "Ascending the Hall" plaque.
The Rector then goes to the Sangha Hall.
After the morning gruel has been distributed and the wooden mallet (zhui) has been struck, strike the mallet once more and announce to the assembly:
"The gruel is finished. Upon hearing the sound of the bell, [the meal is concluded].
Each assuming their proper dignified demeanor, they proceed to the Great Jewel Hall of the Buddha.
To solemnly inaugurate the celebration of the Imperial Birthday, this is respectfully announced; once again, the mallet is struck once.
He proceeds to the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects.
Then, starting from the head seat’s platform, he makes one circuit of the hall,
moving from the lower section outside the hall up to the upper section.
Return to the center of the inner hall,
exchange greetings, and depart.
After the gruel meal, pause for a short while.
Once the incense, candles, tea, soup, hand-bell, and hand-incense burner have been arranged in the main hall and all preparations are complete,
the attendants of the Hall Office (Tangsi) shall notify the Guest Master (Ketu) of the Abbot’s quarters to first inform the Abbot.
Next, the attendant is covered [with the ritual].
The board of the Abbot’s quarters is struck three times, followed by the drum.
The hall office acolyte first strikes the board in front of the communal quarters three times.
When the assembly gathers in the hall,
they sit facing inward as is customary during seated meditation;
when the drum sounds, they turn their bodies to face outward.
The Head (shouzuo) first assembles outside the hall and waits for the drum to sound;
he then enters the hall immediately.
The Head Seat (shouzuo) enters after him and takes his seat.
The West Hall attendant, the retired officials, the various dormitory masters, and those from the outer hall sit together;
when the drum first sounds, the abbot emerges from the dormitory hall and takes his seat.
The attendant bows and stands to the east;
the ritual assistant bows and stands to the west.
The drum-turner attendant proceeds to the left side of the Dharma seat and stands there awaiting the assembly.
The head monk descends from his seat,
bows before the Holy Monk, leads the assembly out of the hall,
and proceeds to the Dharma seat.
Arranging themselves in a single row, they inquire after one another's well-being and return to stand in order facing west;
the assembly follows behind in a crane-like formation.
If they do not wait for the head monk to arrive...
First, establish that it is not the proper procedure.
When the drum sounds, the hall monitor shall likewise strike the wooden board three times.
The head attendant shall lead the assembly of practitioners.
They stand in a row facing each other before the Kūtāgāra Hall.
Waiting for the drum to be struck,
when the administrative officers (zhishi) emerge, they pay their respects and follow behind them.
Once those on the west side have returned to their positions,
he shall likewise form a single row and perform a formal inquiry before their seats.
The chief monk takes his place at the rear;
the head administrator leads them back to the eastern wing where they stand in formation,
while the assembly of practitioners lines up behind the *jishi* (attendant).
Standing at a slight distance,
the attendant enters to invite the abbot to come out;
the ritual assistant then offers his greetings.
When the abbot reaches the front of the Dharma seat,
the ritual assistant moves closer and stands behind the attendant.
In winter, the assembly removes their hats and bows in greeting.

the attendant follows him onto the Dharma-seat,
holding up an incense box with its lid closed, filled with incense.
When the abbot has finished offering incense and reciting the verses for long life,
the attendant receives the incense;
with his left hand he places it into the burner, and with his right hand he takes up a single stick of subordinate incense.
Having briefly exchanged greetings, the assembly descends from their seats and returns to their respective positions.
They wait until the abbot has adjusted his robes and is seated in the full lotus posture;
at that point, the attendants (shizhe) take their places at the end of the row.
The [official] leads them past the seat below;
they line up in a single row to exchange greetings.
The incense-burning attendant leads the assembly back to their positions.
Next, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) leads the assembly out,
bows before the rows of seats,

The administrative official (zhishi) moves forward to the front of the row of seats and bows;
the attendants (xingzhe) follow suit and bow.
The West Hall and East Hall masters descend from their seats and bow.
The attendant ascends the seat;

with his left hand offering incense, he turns, takes up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*), and performs a formal inquiry (*wenshen*). This is called "requesting the Dharma on behalf of the assembly. He then withdraws to stand by the side of the seat until the questions and answers are concluded.

The Hall Monks' Office issues certificates;

The government provides official certificates as proof.
Therefore, in addition to the travel equipment and the *dùdié* (ordination certificate),
itinerant monks possess an annual exemption from corvée labor.
In what place did he spend the summer retreat?
There are accounts concerning his encounters with sages;
these have been prepared in order to withstand cross-examination.
Each of these was also practiced with caution;
though they are not employed today,
their existence is preserved to illustrate antiquity.
The Abbot [Name], the Guest Prefect [Name], and the West Hall [Name] respectfully submit this memorial on this day of this month.
The Hall Superintendent [Name] has prepared this formal statement to inaugurate the service.
We humbly observe that the all-encompassing protection of Heaven is impartial and without partiality.
Who can fathom the height and thickness of Heaven and Earth?

one realizes that all attempts at praise and veneration are but labor in vain.
I desire to repay [your kindness] boundlessly;
I entrust myself solely to the molding of your transformative power,
for the duty toward the four debts of gratitude is profound.
Therefore, exhausting my heart of loyal devotion,
I reverently offer the three auspicious prayers.
As the pivot of the Dipper is encircled by lightning, the assembly of the dragon-elephants is opened.
The ten billion mountains and rivers of the celestial net all return to the Sage’s measure;
the three thousand worlds of the Flower Treasury further expand the grand design.
I have exhausted my efforts to contribute even a tiny drop to this vast ocean.

Without idleness, morning and evening, I reverently pray that the *lu* and *long* shall be employed, so that the auspicious star may shine and the Three Steps of Heaven be leveled; that the *qilin* and phoenix may manifest their blessings, and that when the Sage arises, all things shall behold him.

I respectfully submit this memorial: The auspicious appearance of the *utpala* flower fills the world; like the Buddha’s descent into birth, the trees of Jambudvīpa cast a continuous shade, and may [the Emperor] share the same longevity as the heavens.
Thus, he nurtures his naturally perfected and sagacious nature from an early age.

He was able to inherit the great and manifest sagely counsel: "How great is Qian! How ultimate is Qian! He embodied Qian and dwelt in correctness; he harmonized with its pinnacle and returned to its pinnacle, establishing the pinnacle and instituting the center.
Thus, through the great harmony of our Way,
it shall contribute to the supreme governance of this sagely age;
in mountains and forests as well as amidst bells and drums, we shall rejoice in the long unfolding of the days of transformation.
Grasses, trees, and even insects are bathed in the pervasive flow of your gracious bounty; auspicious signs unfold from dawn, and we offer hymns of praise like those of the people of Hua-feng.
We reverently pray that you remain in effortless non-action, presiding with sovereign ease.
Heaven and Earth take their places and all things flourish; the molding and shaping have their forms.

This ocean of inconceivability is difficult to praise fully.

Your Highness, be as the sun’s double wheel and the moon’s double radiance,

the hundred rivers overflow their banks, leaving the people with no place of rest.
This is indeed what is evoked by the collective karma of sentient beings.

He was granted a jade seal and appointed as the Dharma Lord of Central China.
He presided over the Buddhist teachings throughout the realm and was the first to establish the division of duties between the monastic and lay communities.
In the fourth year, he took leave of the Emperor and returned to the West.
Before even a full year had passed, he was summoned and returned.
In the seventh year of the Zhiyuan era, the Gengwu year,
an imperial decree was issued to create the national script for the Great Yuan.
The Master alone executed the design and modeling;
it was completed in less than a day,
deeply satisfying the Imperial will.
An imperial edict was immediately issued for its promulgation;
the court, the provinces, and the prefectures and counties all complied with and adopted it,
so that it ultimately became a standard code for an era.
He was elevated to the title of Imperial Preceptor, the Great Treasure Dharma King (Dishi Daobao Fawang),
and further granted a jade seal;
shortly thereafter, he returned to the West.
In the eleventh year, the Emperor again dispatched a special envoy to summon him;
however, he subsequently declined with great earnestness to return to the mountains.
The Emperor insisted on retaining him, but he would not comply.
On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of the seventeenth year, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor was overcome with profound grief and sorrowful remembrance;
he subsequently constructed a great stūpa in the capital.

The true-body relics of the Treasure Treasury, with their magnificent golden and green glazes, are peerless throughout antiquity and the present; this was recorded on the stele composed by Wang Pan, Hanlin Academician, and others by imperial decree, following the posthumous title "The One Above All Under Heaven."

The Great Dharma King, the Son of Buddha from the Western Heaven, Imperial Preceptor of the Great Yuan, who opens the teachings and proclaims the texts to assist governance, possessing the supreme virtue of a Great Sage, universal enlightenment, true wisdom, and the power to bring blessings to the state as a wish-fulfilling great jewel.
The Chapter on Requital concludes. Chapter Four: Honoring the Ancestors. Each person sacrifices to their own ancestors, for they value the beginning of their physical life.
This physical life begins with love.
However, the physical form eventually undergoes transformation,
and craving eventually comes to an end;
only the numinous spirit of one's nature, which remains unclouded, does not depend upon birth to exist.
One does not perish together with [the body], yet one perishes;
therefore, Buddhism requires that people must first clarify their nature (*xing*).
Yet later scholars have again become mired in the literal words and phrases.
To fail to grasp its essential purpose is like a physician who is well-versed in medical texts yet neglects the actual medicinal herbs and stones;
what benefit can there be?
When our ancestor Bodhidharma arrived and demonstrated the Way of Direct Pointing,
people finally attained a state of vast clarity.
Seeing that the wondrous nature of one's own being is not sought through written words nor dependent upon speech or silence,
but is attained beyond the realm of coughs, laughter, sounds, and forms—
then for us who transmit the ancestral Way and succeed to the ancestral position:
It is like fire, fuel, and the vessel;
there is no distinction between past and present, not even as much as a hair’s breadth.
Is this not more significant than the very beginning of physical form and life?
Later, Chan Master Dazhi of Baizhang further established the *Chiqi* (Rules of Purity) for our followers to abide by,
and thus the Zen forest (Chanlin) began from this point.
Haikai Dugong stated that it would be appropriate to enshrine Bodhidharma in the center with Baizhang accompanying him on the right,
while the founding patriarchs of each respective temple are enshrined as associates;
this is recorded in the "Preface to the Regulations for the Patriarchs' Hall."
On the day preceding the anniversary of the Dharma Master’s passing, the Hall Attendant leads the assembly to prepare offerings with their resources.

They request the composition of a memorial preface and sign it; the preparation of the Dharma Hall follows the ritual procedures as for the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, with everything arranged one night in advance.
The true portrait is hung upon the central seat.
In the center, the sacrificial table is solemnly arranged with an incense burner, a vase, and incense.

In the upper section, a Zen chair, a whisk, a rack for robes, and the dharma robe are set out; it is improper to provide beds or couches here. In the lower section, a chair, a scripture desk, an incense burner, a vase, incense, candles, and scripture scrolls are set out.
The attendant of the Hall Office reports to the assembly.
The plaque for the chanting of scriptures is hung.
That evening, the scriptures shall be chanted; furthermore, each person must prepare their full ceremonial regalia for the half-day vegetarian meal on the following day.
After the *sanji* (evening recitation) of the sutras,
he joins the assembly as the Sangha hall bell tolls;
once the congregation has gathered, they await the arrival of the abbot.
The drum is struck and a special offering of broth is presented.
The abbot burns incense and performs three prostrations without folding his sitting cloth.
After the hot water has been served, withdraw three paces and perform three prostrations, then advance again.
First, inquire after the guest’s well-being and bow for the tea;
then return to your position, perform two prostrations, and fold away your sitting mat.
The drums are struck three times;
the practitioners ring their hand-chimes,
and the Rector steps forward from the ranks.
In my recitation, I think with all earnestness:
as for this direct transmission of the Dharma-lineage,
I have humbly received its nourishment from the lingering waves.
The Way is vast and difficult to name;
I am humbled to join its radiance as a descendant.
I look up to the Great Assembly to recite the ten titles of the Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha, and so forth. Regarding the dedication: may the merit of the above recitations [be dedicated].
On behalf of the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, Great Master of Perfect Enlightenment and Grand Preceptor, this is offered to repay his compassionate protection.

[The names of] all beings of the ten directions and three periods of time are hereby concluded. The Sangha hall bell is struck three times, and the assembly disperses; or, they may be invited to sit for the medicinal meal.
The evening bell tolls;
it tolls a second time, and the Sangha hall bell assembles the community.
The Abbot offers incense.
When the Venerable Karmadāna has finished reciting the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī, he performs the dedication, saying:
"The body of the pure Dharma-realm is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing;
yet through the power of great compassionate vows, it manifests coming and going."
I look up to you with hope that, out of your compassion, you will deign to grant your clear inspection.
On the fifth day of this month,
it coincides with the anniversary of the passing of the Great Master Bodhidharma, the First Patriarch and Great Monk of Perfect Enlightenment.
He led the assembly of bhikṣus to prepare fragrant offerings and food,
thereby extending his worship,
while chanting the Great Buddha-Top Myriad Practices Śūraṅgama Divine Mantra.
Having accumulated these distinguished merits, I offer them in gratitude for Your compassionate protection.
I humbly pray that all sentient beings may find reliance therein.
He propagated the family tradition of Shaoshi;
his wondrous wisdom was inexhaustible,
and he brought to fulfillment the root-capacities for the Mahāyāna.
"Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, all [beings]... and so forth. Next, the head of the assembly leads the practitioners in formation.
They call for the session, prostrate, and chant scriptures.
The attendants then form a line and pay their respects.
The following morning, the abbot offers incense and performs prostrations.
He serves hot soup and congee, sitting at the side of the seat to accompany the meal.
After the congee is finished, the abbot again offers incense and tea.
When the Venerable Master (Weina) has finished reciting the Great Compassion Mantra,
he shall dedicate the merit of the preceding scripture recitation for the sake of the First Patriarch Bodhidharma, the Great Master of Perfect Enlightenment.

To repay the compassionate protection [of the ancestors] throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, at the conclusion of the half-day meal, the *sēngtáng* bell is struck to assemble the community.
They stand in a row facing the patriarch.
The abbot offers incense and performs three prostrations;
without folding his sitting cloth,
he steps forward before the incense burner.
The attendant serving the guest presents the first soup and the first dish.
The attendant burning incense waits by the side of the Patriarch’s seat, receives them, and places them upon the table;
he then withdraws to his own position and performs three prostrations.
He continues forward to burn incense and present the offerings;
having completed these, he performs three prostrations and withdraws his sitting mat.
When the drum sounds for the lecture, tea is served specifically for this occasion according to the ritual for hot water. Upon completion, the abbot offers incense and delivers a formal discourse.
The practitioner strikes the hand-cymbals;
the rector steps out from the assembly and bows to the abbot as he offers incense.
The attendant holds up the incense casket;
next, the two orders from the East Hall and West Hall step forward from the assembly to offer incense,
and the entire congregation performs three prostrations together.
The Venerable Karmadāna announces: "The body of the pure Dharma-realm is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
yet, through the power of great compassionate vows, it manifests coming and going. Having recited the preface, the presiding master kneels before the incense burner.
Next, he intones the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī until its conclusion.
I dedicate the merit of reciting this scripture upward,
in honor of the First Patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma, the Great Upādhyāya of Perfect Enlightenment,
to repay his compassionate protection.
"Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time... and so forth. Next, the practitioner recites the scripture.
From the *Commentary*: "How great! This orthodox transmission continues the lineage of the Buddha-King.
'Vast and empty, there is no sage'—this shatters the chronic malady of scholastic learning."

The hundred rivers reach the sea, forever severing their distinct currents; the bright sun adorns the heavens, leaving no shadow cast askew. Pointing to the human mind, one becomes a Buddha; becoming a Buddha, one’s mind is identical [to the Way]. One accords with the wondrous Dao through the forgetting of words.
Seeing the Way through the forgetting of words,
he has rendered great service to the teachings of the world;
it is fitting that he should widely propagate the spirit of our school, appearing as an *udumbara* flower in this defiled age.
Truly the progenitor, he took those of the Great Vehicle from the Divine Land and brought them all within his sphere of influence;
it coincides precisely with the anniversary of the burial of his sandals.
I hereby emulate the offering of the *cǎifán* (white aquatic plants);

I humbly pray that the Saṃghāṭī robe shall manifest the gravity of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, bearing a thousand-jin weight with effortless ease, so that a single flower may bloom as the spring of heaven and earth.
His fragrance shall be linked with ten thousand generations.
The Patriarch was the third son of King Jñānagupta of South India;
his clan name was Kṣatriya.
His original name was Bodhidhara.
Later, he encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra,
who recognized his secret traces.
He was then tested by being made to debate with his two elder brothers regarding the precious jewel he had bestowed,
thereby elucidating the essential points of the mind.
Subsequently, the Venerable One said to him:
You have already attained direct realization (*pramāṇa*) regarding all phenomena (*dharma*).
Now, "Dharma" carries the meaning of "penetrating the great";
you should therefore be named Dharmatrāta.
Consequently, he changed his name to Bodhidharma.
The Master then addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"Since I have now attained the Dharma..."
"To which country should we go to perform the Buddha-work?
We pray that you will deign to grant us your instruction.
The Venerable One said:
"Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not travel far yet.
Remain in Southern India for now,
until sixty-seven years after my parinirvāṇa."
I shall go to China to administer the great medicine of the Dharma directly to those of superior faculties.
Be careful not to travel too hastily, lest you wither under the sun.
On the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the eighth year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the year of Dingwei, I arrived at Nanhai.
Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, submitted a memorial to inform Emperor Wu.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree to welcome him.
On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived at Jinling and spoke with the Emperor.
The appointment was not fulfilled.
On the nineteenth day of this month, he crossed the Yangtze River to the north.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived at Luoyang.
This was during the tenth year of the Tahe era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty.
Baowu dwelt at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song,
sitting with his face turned toward a wall.
He remained silent all day long;
no one could fathom him,
so he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin."
In the tenth month, on the fifth day of the year of Bingchen, the nineteenth year of the Taihe era, he passed away while sitting upright in meditation.
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of that same year, he was buried at Xiong’er Mountain.
A stupa was erected at Dinglin Monastery;
he was posthumously titled Great Master Yuanjue by the Tang court,
and his stupa was named Kongguan.
On the eve of the anniversary of Baizhang’s passing, the Hall Attendant leads the assembly to prepare offerings.
On the day itself, the Dharma Hall is prepared according to ritual the night before;
the portrait is hung upon the seat.
He solemnly prepared the sacrificial tables for the intermediate rites, arranging the desks and offerings between the upper and lower sections.
That evening he chanted the sutras; on the actual day of dispersing the taboos, he specially offered tea and soup, incense, and read the memorial petitions.
Upon leaving the hall, the assembly offers incense and performs prostrations together with the same ritual as for the anniversary of Bodhidharma’s passing, except that no recitations are performed.
At the end of the first watch of the night, the dedication is made as follows: "The body of the pure Dharma-realm is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing."
Through the power of your great compassionate vows, you manifest coming and going;
we look up to you with reverence, hoping that your compassion will graciously deign to examine us.
The seventeenth day of the first month.
I humbly avail myself of this occasion, the anniversary of the passing of the Great Monk Chan Master Hongzong Miaoxing, the Great Wisdom Awakened Illuminator,
to lead a community of bhikṣus in preparing incense and offerings.
To extend this offering,
I shall recite the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī of Myriad Practices;
may the extraordinary merit thus accumulated be offered upward to repay your compassionate protection.
I humbly pray that the *tāpa* flower may reappear,
once again opening the spring of the blossoms of awakening;
may the sun of grace shine forever bright.
Eternally illuminating the night of the dark alleys;
"All those of the ten directions and three periods," and so forth.

These words from the *Sūtra Commentary* state: "A single word serves as the law for all under heaven; square within the square and round within the circle, for ten thousand generations the Way of the Teacher is known to be honored, possessing both its guiding principles and its regulations."
It may be compared to the flourishing ritual and music of a great monastic forest.

One beholds the multitude of "dragons and elephants" at this Dharma assembly; Chinese and Sanskrit texts are harmonized, as rich as the renowned channels of the Imperial Archives. Sūtras and Vinaya complement one another, as solemn as golden statutes and jade ordinances, possessing the dignified decorum of those who pace with measured steps upon the hall.

It is not the ritual of spreading grass mats in the wild; it is used right here and yet transcends this very use. The words transcend the profound mystery; emerging from the occasion and entering into the occasion, its principle exhausts all wonders.
It is fitting that you be paired with the Patriarchs of Chan to join in the ancestral sacrifices;
why not observe the anniversary of your passing to perform the *zhāi* (fasting) rites?

We humbly pray that you, as the Victorious Banner of Śakra’s diligence, shall subdue all demons and heretics, and that you, like the great cooling tree of the North, shall provide shade throughout Jambudvīpa.
The Master was a native of Changle in Fuzhou and a son of the Wang family.
Having left the secular world at the age of seven,
he became thoroughly proficient in the three branches of Buddhist study.
During Mazu’s flourishing period of teaching in Jiangxi, where the Dharma assemblies were so magnificent that figures such as Dazhu,
Nanquan, and Guizong were hailed as "Dharma elephants," the Master served as their preeminent leader.
When Master Zu passed away at Ledu Pond,
the Master succeeded him;
as the crowds of followers gathered there, there was no space to accommodate them all.
Desiring to take his leave,
he passed through Xinwu on his way and rested beneath the Che-lun Peak. There,
Gan Zhen was enjoying a leisurely stroll.
He requested land for his residence;
subsequently, the assembly arrived once more,
whereupon he established a monastery, which was named Da Tuo Ti.
On the seventeenth day of the first month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era, the Master returned to quiescence.
The forest of Binlin was consumed by fire without being ignited;
the sacred stream of Lingxi dried up even in the midst of spring.
The fourfold assembly, overcome with grief, buried him on Mount Daxiong.
Previously, there was an extraordinary person named the Śramaṇa Sima who selected the burial site, saying:
It adjoins three peaks, yet their wonders remain unexplored.
The Dharma King dwells therein as a teacher and model for all under heaven;
thus the world considers it to be truly so.
In the first year of the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Wisdom Chan Master (Dazhi Chanshi),
and his stupa was named Great Precious Victorious Wheel (Dabaoshenglun).
In the first year of the Daguan era of the Song dynasty, his posthumous title was further augmented to Enlightened Illumination (Juezhao).
The pagoda is named Huìjù (Gathering of Wisdom).
In the third year of the Yuántǒng era of the Great Yuan, he was posthumously honored with the title Chán Master Hóngzōng Miàoxíng (Master of Expansive Doctrine and Wondrous Conduct).
This commemorates the memorial services for the successive patriarchs who founded the mountain, as well as the founder’s own memorial service; his spiritual conduct was held in the highest esteem.
Regarding those whose merit benefits the mountain gate:
the preparations are made in the Dharma Hall the night before;
the ritual consists of one hundred items, or perhaps there is no formal petition.
The administrative office shall prepare the offerings.
If there is no memorial record for the anniversaries of successive generations,
no special tea or soup shall be offered.
At the appointed time, the Hall Office shall notify the Treasury Office in advance to prepare the offerings and request the ancestral tablets.
The seat is prepared with its head facing west.
After the morning gruel, the assembly gathers;
the abbot and the two orders of officials stand in a single row.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) steps forward, bows to the assembly, and after completing the offering of incense, returns to his position.
Together, they perform three prostrations.

When the attendant at the end of the row reaches the point of bowing, the Great Rule states: "In some places, it is considered improper to recite the sutra while seated in the lower food-position of the Patriarchs' Hall. [The assembly] then chants the *Mahākaruṇā-mantra*.
The dedication verse says: The jewel-luminous ocean of emptiness is the profound whirlpool of the waves of birth and death;
it is the gate of great tranquil concentration.
I dissolve the phenomena of past and present, of going and coming.
I look up with hope for your steadfast compassion and pray that you will deign to grant me your clear discernment.
On the [day] of this month, at the mountain gate.
I humbly take this opportunity on the anniversary of the passing of the Chan Master [Name], the [Number]th generation of this mountain, whose posthumous title was [Name].
I have prepared rare delicacies to extend my offerings,
while the assembly of bhikṣus recites the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī.
May the accumulated extraordinary merits further elevate his rank.
We humbly pray that the Sun of Wisdom may shine forth once more with renewed brilliance.
The light of the ancestral hall shines as the seeds of illumination;
the numinous roots sprout anew,
restoring the vernal bloom to the flowers and trees of Shaolin.
Thus it was said; whether by local villagers or those from the rivers and lakes, they chanted the incantations and dedicated the merit, saying:
"By the merit of reciting the sutras as performed above..."
On behalf of the Great Monk [Name], may his rank and status be further exalted.
[Recite] "The Ten Directions and Three Periods of Time," and so forth.
If there are offerings to be distributed, then recite the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī.
The dedication of merit is the same as before.

Regarding the anniversary of the Dharma Master’s passing: the former masters merely used it to vigorously propagate the vehicle of the school and to illuminate their own realization, thereby instructing later students so that they might know there is a transmission of the lineage.
This is to repay his kindness.
For instance, the three turns of speech from Baling were used as a memorial service for Yunmen;
those who came before us held this in deep significance.
Nevertheless, as one honors the teacher and values the Way,
ritual propriety must not be discarded.
Prior to the scheduled date, the abbot shall provide his own funds to the treasury office.
To prepare the offerings for the ritual,
they shall be arranged according to the Dharma in the Dharma Hall one night prior;
the hall attendant (tángsī xíngzhě) shall then notify the assembly.
A plaque for the recitation of sutras was hung.
That evening, the *Śūraṃgama-mantra* was chanted;
the local people and dharma-relatives intoned the *Mahākaruṇā-mantra*.
Next, the practitioners recite the sutras and perform the dedication of merit in the same manner.
Early the next morning, the abbot serves congee;
once the meal is finished, the assembly recites the Great Compassion Mantra.
When local residents or dharma-relatives raise the invocation, the midday meal is concluded with the recitation of scriptures for the memorial service.

The abbot serves the food and offers incense specifically for the tea ceremony on the anniversary of Bodhidharma’s passing; he joins the two ranks of officials in offering incense and the assembly bows together, for it is understood that everyone from the head seat downward is engaged in formal study. At the time of the meal, the abbot enters the hall, burns incense, performs prostrations, and returns to his place.

When the robe-bearer (yiboshi) and attendants distribute alms (xingqin), it is improper for them to do so while the assembly is chanting sutras in the Dharma Hall; rather, the distribution of alms should take place after the meal is concluded. Once the meal is finished, the assembly takes their seats; tea is served, incense is burned, and the attendants perform the formal rites.
If a special *tantui* (special guest) is present for the *zhaikai* (vegetarian meal), after the meal the Abbot and the Guest Master invite the West Hall Master and the two ranks of officers.
In the evening, they eat *tang* (congee) together before the True Image (the Buddha statue).
A seating chart is arranged according to rank and placed to the right of the seat.
The abbot bows and takes his seat.
He burns incense and serves hot water,
followed by serving hot water to his accompanying attendants.
Withdrawing, he burns incense and performs prostrations.
Rising, he inquires after the master’s well-being and thanks him for his companionship.
The drum is struck three times, and the assembly withdraws from their seats.
If there are three or five people at the West Hall,
they shall be divided into two seats;
the first seat at the West Hall will consume the medicinal broth.
The abbot performs the ritual.
The second seat and the two orders partake of the medicinal soup.
The attendant performs the ritual; if there is no West Hall monk, it is omitted. When the recitation of the sutra is finished, the medicinal soup and fruit are prepared.
I request in advance that the officials of the two orders and the veteran elders be invited;
if there are dharma-relatives who are seniors or fellow disciples,
all of them should likewise be invited.
Junior disciples and their grand-disciples must not sit at the same table.
Once everyone is seated, the abbot rises, offers incense, and completes the offering of hot water.

The attendant burns incense and serves tea and fruit; this concludes the "Chapter on Honoring the Patriarchs. **Chapter Five: The Chapter on the Abbot** Four hundred years after Buddhism entered China, Bodhidharma arrived.
Furthermore, the lineage was transmitted through eight generations to Baizhang,
who passed on the Dharma solely through the direct transmission of the Way.
He sometimes dwelt among cliffs or lived in caves.
Previously, some had resided in monasteries following the Vinaya,
yet the title of "abbot" (zhuchi) did not yet exist.
Baizhang, observing that the Chan school was gradually flourishing, [established this office].
From the sovereign, ministers, dukes, and marquises above,
down to the Confucians, Daoists, and the various schools below,
all turned toward his influence to inquire about the Way.
His disciples were truly numerous;
yet, had his position not been exalted, the teacher-disciple relationship would not have been strictly observed.
Consequently, he was first appointed as the abbot to serve his master.
They honor them by calling them "Elders" (zhǎnglǎo),
just as in India one refers to Śāriputra and Subhūti,
because they are both distinguished by their seniority and virtue.
A grand hall was constructed to house the assembly,
and two courtyards were established to divide their duties;
thus, the system of regulations became resplendent.
As for manual labor,
he shared the toil equally with the community,
often saying:
"If one day you do not work, you shall not eat for that day.
How could there be the luxury of granaries overflowing with grain or the security of servants and carriages?
Therefore, he was initially selected by the consensus of the assembly.
Soon thereafter, he was appointed to office;
yet he still declined the summons and did not go,
for subsequently there followed the exorbitant selling and the violent seizure of property.
They regard it as a rare treasure;
yet if the person is not worthy,
the entire monastery will fall into ruin and desolation.
Furthermore, they left behind a remnant of their faction;
after several decades, it had spread so extensively that it could no longer be eradicated,
and its gruesome instances of retribution from the unseen world were frequently reported.
There are those who cannot bear to hear [such things].
Should they not therefore be cautious and fearful?
Regarding the daily duties of the abbot: for every *shangtang* (ascending the hall) on the first and fifteenth days of the month, the attendant must inform the abbot one night in advance.
He said, "Tomorrow morning I shall offer prayers for the Sage Emperor. The following day, he reported this again.
He then instructed the guest-head attendant to hang the "Ascending the Hall" plaque and notify the assembly.
After the morning gruel is finished, the bell for descending from the hall is struck three times.
Once the Dharma seat has been prepared,
the attendant of the Hall Office informs the Head Seat.
Strike the board in front of the various quarters.
Once the assembly is seated in the hall, the attendant of the Abbot reports to the Abbot;
next, he reports to the Chief Attendant and strikes the drum.
The two orders of officers lead the assembly of monks to the front of the seat to pay their respects;
they stand in two rows facing each other, and the attendant invites the abbot to emerge.

Ascending the seat, he holds up incense to offer prayers for longevity, as detailed in the "Chapter on Prayers for Auspiciousness" (Zhuxi Zhang). Once seated cross-legged, he expounds the teachings to inspire and uplift his disciples regarding this Way.
If there are guests present, he shall also address them with a formal introduction and expressions of gratitude.
When there are many [people],
the attendant holds up the staff for the sake of those who might forget it.
In some monasteries, the Abbot, the Preceptor, the Head of the West Hall, and other eminent virtuous elders have seats established to their right.

When officials or guests arrive, seats are set for them opposite these positions; however, those who know propriety and honor the Dharma do not sit. This applies during the five formal inquiries and the morning assembly.
The two orders descend to the foot of the seat and proceed directly to their respective positions in the assembly.
When the abbot ascends the seat, he does not offer incense; otherwise, the procedure is as previously described.
If a venerable elder visits, the abbot may specifically ascend the hall for them, or escort them to the seat to proclaim the Dharma.
When a donor requests the master to ascend the seat, there is no restriction regarding the time.
In ancient times, those who studied did so primarily to resolve doubts;
therefore, there were questions and answers.
From the beginning, they were not hindered by words and language;
recently, those known as "Chan guests" have for the most part been ignorant of cause and effect.
They increase their evil habits by treating them as a spectacle,
clamoring with boisterous laughter;
this is a profound failure of decorum.
How much more so when exalting the Dharma Vehicle and offering sincere prayers for the Emperor’s longevity.
Should any government officials or those of renowned virtue visit, [one should likewise act].
I have briefly set forth this account.
However, it is now customary for monastics to demand excessive praise and formal expressions of gratitude;
this is a significant departure from the established rules and methods.
Regarding the affairs of the Mountain Gate,
when the Abbot convenes a tea assembly for discussion,
one must not speak of trivial matters that would cause the assembly to grow weary of listening.
"Evening Assembly; Evening Assembly. Generally, whenever the assembly is gathered for instruction, it is called a *can* (assembly/inquiry).
In ancient times, masters guided their disciples by having them consult and inquire morning and evening, never failing to stimulate and elevate this Way at all times.
Therefore, the evening *can* (formal assembly) must take place during the *pu* period (the late afternoon).
To this day, in the monastic forests (*conglin*), the morning and evening *can* sessions continue as they were, with the abbot ascending the seat for these five assemblies.

When it is time for the assembly to listen to the Dharma, the great multitude sits in the hall; this is detailed in the "Chapter on Prayers for Blessings" (*zhuxi zhang*). If the abbot does not attend the evening *can*, [the procedure follows accordingly].
Then the attendant of the Hall Office reports the command to the Abbot and informs the Head Seat.
The Sangha Hall bell is struck three times;
this is called the "bell for ending the session."
This is as when an abbot enters the monastery,
or when officials or lay patrons enter the mountain,
or when one accepts a special invitation.
Some say it is for the instruction of the deceased;
others say that at the four seasonal festivals, when the evening bell tolls,
this is shifted to what is called the "Small Session" (xiǎocān).
It is permissible to observe the rites of the secular world;
this is what is meant by "family instruction.
Nevertheless, the *míngfàng* and *cānzhōng* bells are not to be struck.
This refers to what is still called "Small Assembly" (Sān).
Small Assembly, small assembly, small assembly—there is originally no fixed location for it;
one observes whether the number of the assembly is large or small.
Either in the dormitory hall or in the Dharma hall,
they arrive after midday on the appointed day.
The attendant informs the abbot, saying: "Tonight there is a small discourse (xiaocan); please have the guest master and the acolytes notify the assembly.
A small discourse plaque is hung.
That evening, the bell signaling the end of the discourse period is not struck.
When the evening bell tolls, the practitioner covers the abbot;
the drum is struck once,
the assembly gathers, and the two orders take their respective places.

When the abbot ascends the seat, he presents the essential points and offers his expressions of gratitude in the same manner as the "Five Visits" (wǔcān) formal lecture; these are detailed and exhaustive.
Thereafter, he cites ancient precedents.
He concludes the session in the same manner as during the four seasonal festivals.
The announcement regarding the invitation of the head monk,
the master of the whisk, and the lecturer shall omit formal ritual procedures;
these matters should be explained in detail or in brief so that the assembly may fully understand them.
The junior seat attendant (shazuo) and the guest master (ketou xingzhe) call out the invitation, saying:
"The Abbot of the Venerable Hall invites the West Hall Master, the two classes of officials, those in private quarters, the elders, the head attendants of the Monks' Hall, and the Zen guests."
Now, as we proceed to the dormitory hall for the offering of hot water, the Ku-si (Storehouse Office) shall prepare the hot water and fruit and deliver them to the Abbot’s quarters.
Formerly, when Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao resided at the Taizi Yuan in Fenzhou:
Because the region of Bingfen was bitterly cold,
he abolished the night assemblies.
At that time, a strange bhikṣu arrived, shaking his monk’s staff.
He said to the Master,
"There are six great beings (mahāsattvas) in this assembly;
why do you not preach the Dharma?"
Having finished speaking, he ascended into the air and departed.
The Master recorded this in secret with a verse, saying:
"The Hu monk’s golden staff radiates light."
For the sake of the Dharma, he went to Fenyang;
six men became great vessels.
He exhorted them to propagate [the teaching].
At that time, Chuyuan (Chuzhi) was the foremost among the disciples;
Chuyuan was none other than Ciming.
Later, he resided at Shishuang.
After the meal, he was walking through Changshan.
At that time, Master Yangqi Hui was serving as the Chief Steward (Jansi).
Anticipating his departure, [the abbot] struck the drum to assemble the community.
Ciming immediately returned in anger and rebuked him, saying, "Why have you come to ascend the seat at such an hour?
Where did you get this set of rules? Huìxu then replied: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates that the full dialogue continues beyond the provided fragment.*
During the evening *chan* at Fenzhou, [the Master] asked, "Why is this not considered a violation of the rules?
Ciming nodded his head in agreement.
Regarding the ritual of offering incense (*gaoxiang*), it is performed every year before the summer retreat.
One person is selected from among those who have newly returned to the hall for the incense offering to serve as the head of the assembly (sanchō).
The *Rector* (Juna) convenes the group, and they proceed together to the office of the *Attendant* (Jisshi) to report, saying:
The newly ordained brothers wish to request that the Venerable Master grant a general discourse on the incense offering;
they venture to trouble the attendant to submit this request for their consideration.
The response was: "I shall consider this for future reference and will inform you accordingly once the Abbot has granted his approval.
Immediately, the Hall Office was notified to produce the ritual diagram for the incense offering (gaoxiang túshì), as shown below, according to the number of participants.
They are arranged in several rows,
divided into two sides— east and west— and stand facing the Dharma seat,
arrayed according to their precepts.
The assembly shall gather in advance to practice the ritual procedures.
The attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi Xingzhe) shall lead the congregation in collecting funds to purchase three pieces of incense, both large and small, as well as paper.
The expenses for the drawing of the diagram shall be paid to the head attendant (sanda) for collection.
On the appointed day, the attendant shall instruct the guest master (katō) to prepare the bedchamber or the Dharma hall.
Spread out the *fusi* screens and arrange the chairs.
Three incense tables and three pairs of candle stands must be used;
they shall be placed in a row directly in front of the chairs, at intervals marked by the character "當" (*dāng*).
A small ceremonial seat is set up outside;
the attendants of the Hall Office (Tangsi) shall first notify the assembly one by one in advance and hang the announcement plaque for the incense offering.
The attendant prepares and posts a small notice on the pillars of the Dharma Hall, stating: "By the compassionate decree of the Abbot,
the West Hall and Head Seat of renowned virtue are both exempted from the incense offering."
The attendant [Name] respectfully announces: On the day of the ceremony, after the morning gruel has been consumed, each of the quarters shall strike the wooden board three times.
The assembly shall gather and stand according to their assigned positions in the diagram, each person preparing a small incense case and a sitting mat.
The head of the assembly, together with the *karmadāna* and the attendant,
enters to invite the abbot to come forth; once the abbot has emerged,
the head of the assembly returns to his position.
The assembly together asks after his well-being; he steps forward and says, "Please, Preceptor, sit cross-legged. The Abbot takes his seat.

The Vice-Head of the Monks (Fu-can) hands over a large piece of incense, which he and the Head of the Assembly (Can-tou), along with the rest of the congregation, offer by bowing and inserting the incense.
The head of the assembly performs three prostrations before each of the high-ranking officials.
He then withdraws his sitting mat (zuoju) and again exchanges formal greetings with them.
The head of the assembly then proceeds to the side of the chair.
Inquiring after his well-being, they submitted this request: "We, [Name] and others, recognize that the matter of birth and death is of great importance and that impermanence is swift.
We humbly beseech the Venerable Master’s compassion to provide instruction on the causes and conditions regarding three cases of kōans presented by the Abbot."
Following the words spoken below,
return to your position to offer greetings;
insert a single stick of incense, and then resume your place together with the assembly.
They stand with palms joined.
Three persons from each side, east and west, step forward from their ranks.
The first and second persons from the east pass before the eastern incense burner.
The third person stands before the central incense burner.
The first and second persons pass to the west of the western incense burner.
The third person passes to the front of the central incense burner.
In pairs, they offer incense and exchange greetings;
thereafter, the three from the east pass to the east,
and the three from the west pass to the west.
Proceeding in order as before, they advance with slow steps, each taking their place at the tail of the line.
In groups of three, they join their palms at the chest, exit the line, and with palms joined, return to their positions.
Once everyone has finished offering incense, they advance in succession to their original stations.
The assembly performs three prostrations without folding their sitting cloths. The head of the assembly steps forward and says:
"We, such-and-such persons, have received the compassionate permission of the Master;

our humble hearts are filled with the utmost gratitude. They return to their positions and perform three prostrations together with the assembly. He steps forward again and says: "At this very time, we respectfully observe the season; we humbly reflect upon it all together."
The Abbot of the Hall respectfully inquires after your health and well-being; [the assembly] returns to their positions and performs three prostrations with sitting cloths folded.
The attendant strikes the drum five times.
The two orders turn around and stand in line before the seat.
The head of the assembly stands below the West Order.
The person who announces the incense turns eastward and westward, standing opposite his position according to rank.
The retired elders (kinko) who have already been announced by the incense-announcement stand behind him.
When the general discourse is concluded,
everyone stands facing the Dharma seat.
The head participant offers incense and, together with the assembly, performs three prostrations.
Upon being granted leave, they perform the *chuli* (prostration with hands touching the ground) and advance, saying:
"We, [Name] and others, have been fortunate throughout our past lives to receive the compassionate instruction of the Venerable Master.
We are moved by a sense of gratitude beyond measure. Having thus inquired after one another’s well-being, they withdraw together.
The head of the assembly leads the group to the lower section of the Dharma Hall;
they perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloths (*chuli*) to thank the rector and the attendant.
Next, the assembly thanks the head of the assembly.
Perform a prostration by touching the ground.
The guest-inviting attendant shall prepare a tea-offering form in advance according to the order of seniority in the precepts.
Prepare the table, incense burner, brush, and inkstone.
After the incense offering is completed,
arrange the seating in the lower section of the Dharma Hall for tea, and have everyone sign their names.
Please invite the Head Seat to accompany you.
After the midday meal, the drum is struck and the assembly returns to their positions and stands.

The two attendants perform the ritual as they would for the special tea service. That evening, the Abbot invites the Head of the Retreat, the Rector, and the Attendants for the medicinal meal (*yàoshí*).
The Head Seat (Shouzuo) accompanies him.
On the following morning, he invites the Head of the Assembly (Cantou) for tea.
At the midday meal, he invites the Head of the Assembly, the Rector (Weina), and the Attendant (Shizhe) for refreshments.
If the entire assembly is invited to incense together,
the head seat (shouzuo) acts as the leader;
he specifically requests the West Hall (xitang) to serve as his companion for the tea reception.
After the abbot has entered the monastery and formalities have been settled,
the administrative office (kusi) prepares incense,
and the head seat (shouzuo) leads the assembly.
I earnestly request that you announce the incense for the assembly.

Then, according to the ancient method of opening the hall, one is not permitted to enter the room for a general discourse (*pūsè*) unless the incense has first been announced by the great assembly to invite it. There are indeed instances where the great assembly announces the incense and requests a general discourse.
They take their seats according to the positions assigned. Among them,
some are specially invited by lay donors (*dānapati*),
while others are the presiding masters who provide instruction for the assembly.
Then he ascends the Dharma seat.
Whenever there is a general sermon (*pūsē*), the attendant shall instruct the guest-head acolyte to hang up the "General Sermon" plaque to notify the assembly.
The dormitory hall or the Dharma Hall is prepared;
after the morning gruel, the practitioners inform the abbot.
Gently strike the drum five times.
The attendant goes out to await the assembly and requests the abbot to come forth.
Sitting according to protocol and preaching universally is the same as the small formal inquiry (xiaocan).
Regarding "entering the room" (rushu): entering the room, entering the room, entering the room.
This is how a master examines and evaluates a student:
he urges on what has not yet been attained,
crushes what is hollow and overbearing, and attacks whatever is one-sided or biased.
It is like a furnace for smelting gold, wherein lead and mercury do not remain;
it is like a jade carver working with jade, wherein common pebbles are entirely discarded.
It is independent of whether it is dusk or dawn, and makes no selection regarding the location.
It was practiced at all times.
Thus, in the past, monks would always carry a small incense box with them;
they would do so whenever they heard the drum strike three times.
He immediately hastens to enter the room. Nowadays, those who enter the room on the third and eighth days do so as a preparation for this ritual.
When the time arrives for opening the room, before the morning gruel, the attendant instructs the guest-head acolyte.
Plaque boards for entering the room are hung before the various quarters in front of the Sangha Hall.
An image of Bodhidharma is installed in the dormitory hall,
with incense, candles, and prostration mats arranged in front.
Having arranged the interior with candles and incense,
the seats for worship are set out on the left side.
Once the gruel meal is finished, the guest master descends from the hall and strikes the drum three slow beats.
The abbot goes before Bodhidharma, offers incense,
and together with his attendant, performs three prostrations and enters to take his seat in the room.
The attendant bows in greeting and stands to the left of the assembly.
The practitioners inquire after his health and stand to the right of the assembly.
The head official leads the group;
each person before the Dharma-body image burns incense and performs three prostrations.
They proceed in a continuous line to the front of the hall.

Those who arrive later follow in sequence, lighting incense, performing prostrations, and joining the ranks to stand in order; they must advance one after another and are not permitted to cut in ahead of others or disrupt the sequence.
The attendant burns incense and inquires after their well-being.
He goes outside, bows to the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera), and invites him inside;
upon entering, he places his left foot forward first.
Again, using the left hand to offer incense,
step forward to perform a formal greeting (*wenshen*) and stand at the right side of the meditation chair to listen for the presentation of the kōan.
Either responding with a word or not responding with a word,
he passes to the left of the meditation chair as he pleases.
Inquire after their well-being and withdraw.
Perform a prostration by touching the ground once, lift the left foot,
and exit to bow to the next person before re-entering.
One person exits and another enters, exchanging greetings face-to-face in an uninterrupted succession.
If the Head Seat (shouzuo) is a great master (dafang) or a West Hall (xitang) monk,
or one of renowned virtue, he shall enter to offer incense.
When the abbot descends from his seat, he bows and escorts [the guest] out.
When encountering the occasion of ascending the hall to address the assembly, this [escorting] is specifically waived; this too is a ritual custom inherited from recent times.
As for the ancient masters, they acted according to the immediate circumstances.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs did not permit it;
rather, they maintained worldly etiquette, for they considered only how the master of the house [the abbot] should conduct himself. Thus, the Rear Hall (Hou-tang) leads the assembly.
Upon arriving, everyone shall enter the room.
The attendant stands at the rear of the assembly; once everyone has entered the room, they light incense and perform three full prostrations.
The practitioner inserts incense and performs three prostrations.
The abbot then steps forward before Bodhidharma, offers a stick of incense,
performs three full prostrations with the robes spread out, and withdraws.
Regarding the ancient regulations for recitation: the third,
thirteenth,
and twenty-third days of the month.
The eighth,
the eighteenth,
and the twenty-eighth.
For now, one should practice only on the eighth,
the eighteenth,
and the twenty-eighth days.
The Hall Superintendent (Tangsi) shall prepare a diagram according to the order of seniority as shown below; on the designated day, he shall sweep and clean before the Sangha Hall.
In the afternoon, the Hall Superintendent’s attendant shall notify the assembly, and the plaque for recitation shall be hung.
Upon arriving before the shrine,
he inspects the monks' hall and all the other halls to ensure that incense and candles are fully prepared,
and then reports this to the abbot and the two orders of officials.
First, strike the board for the Abbot’s quarters and the board for the Hall of Illumination.
Next, strike the boards while patrolling the corridors; the Abbot shall then emerge.
Slowly strike the large board three times.
The assembly gathers and takes their positions according to the diagram;
those who have arrived briefly stand beneath the shoulders of the attendants,
while the attendants follow the position of the abbot.
Proceed to the Patriarchs' Hall and the Land Deity Hall;
burn incense and prostrate in the Main Hall;
then strike the great bell.
The two orders of officials assemble outside the hall;
as the large board (dàbǎn) sounds, they return to their assigned seats.
The abbot enters the hall, and the offering attendant (gòngtóu) strikes the bell in front of the hall.
Seven prostrations.
Burn incense before the Noble Sangha.
The attendant holds up the incense censer.
The attendant for correspondence returns directly to his position.
The attendant for guest invitations immediately proceeds to the western corridor to inquire after [the guests] and circulates to invite them to the hot tonic.
Next, invite those in the eastern order to return to their respective positions.
The abbot steps outside the hall and stands in the center;
the incense-bearer attendant follows him out and returns to his position.
