May the Buddha-sun increase in brilliance and the Wheel of Dharma turn perpetually.
May the local deities of this monastery protect the Dharma and its practitioners.
May the donors from the ten directions increase in merit and wisdom.
With the above conditions as the object of focus,
one should mindfully contemplate the Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha.
Thus the great assembly silently recites.
At the front of each hall, a light bell is struck once;
upon finishing the recitation, it is struck once more in succession.
The eighth section below states: "He addressed the great assembly, saying:
'Since the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, entered parinirvāṇa until the first year of the Zhìyuán era of the Great Yuán [reign],'"
Two thousand two hundred and eighty-four years have already passed.
As these days elapse, life likewise diminishes accordingly;
like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be in this?
You all should apply yourselves with diligent effort as if your heads were on fire;
contemplate impermanence alone and be careful not to be negligent.
The local deities of Kālaṃba protect the Dharma and protect people.
May the ten directions increase their merit and wisdom through this *dāna*.
For the reasons stated above,
recite the ten titles of the pure *dharmakāya*, and so forth, until the conclusion, then return to your seats.
The abbot enters the hall;
the head seat of the front hall enters next;
the eminent monks of the west hall enter in between.
They return to stand at the head of the platform facing the Honored Sangha;
the chief officers lead the assembly,
with three monks forming each procession.
Inquire after the health of the venerable monks;
turn and inquire after the health of the abbot;
then, with palms joined, circumambulate the hall.
Turning to the left, he proceeds to his position according to the diagram;
the attendant who arrived briefly follows the assembly into the hall,
circumambulating only half the hall until reaching behind the Holy Sangha.
The attendant stands at the rear gate.
The guest arrives and stands before the attendant.
Next, the administrator enters the hall and bows in greeting before the Sacred Monk.
Turning around, he stands before the abbot and bows;
with palms joined, he circumambulates the hall and exits.
If he has arrived temporarily, he follows behind the attendant after receiving him.
The attendant of the Hall Office goes before the Head Seat and announces, "The evening session is concluded. They exit the hall behind the Holy Monk (Śāsanadhipati).
The Head of Offerings strikes the hall bell three times.
The assembly bows together in unison.

Each person exits with their outer robe folded in full and disperses; the Abbot emerges with the two orders of officers, following them out to the front of the hall to express thanks for the medicinal broth.
The abbot stops at the lower section; next, they proceed to the bathhouse.
At the dormitory hall, the board is struck and the attendant burns incense;
the ritual proceedings follow the usual format.
After the meal, the medicinal gruel is served.
According to ancient regulations, there are gruels at both the third and eighth periods;
however, during the upper and middle eight-day periods, the medicinal gruel is omitted.
On that day, one does not attend the formal assembly; instead, one practices seated meditation (zazen) in the evening according to the usual custom.
Regarding the inspection of the quarters (xunliao), this is an ancient regulation for the abbot (zhuchi).
A signboard for the inspection of the quarters is hung before the Sangha Hall to notify the community.
Each quarters shall set out seats and prepare incense, tea, and hot water.
They shall await the arrival of the abbot,
at which point the wooden board shall be struck to assemble the assembly.
Standing in a line outside the door, they inquire after his well-being;
then, following the abbot, they enter the quarters.
There, the master of the quarters burns incense and, together with the assembly, inquires after his well-being before sitting down.
The abbot inquired after the aged and infirm,
inspected the quarters for deficiencies,
and after conversing, rose to depart.
The assembly shall unfold their sitting mats to express gratitude for the visit;
if it is excused, they shall instead offer greetings and see the visitor off.

On the first and fifteenth days of the month, when making a formal inspection of the quarters, one does not hang the name plaque; nowadays, the inspection of the monastic offices is conducted solely as a ritual observance on the four seasonal festivals.
On other days, it is not recited.
Those who are able to restore antiquity should practice this.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says:
For five reasons, the World-Honored One inspected the monks' quarters once every five days:
first, he feared that his disciples might become attached to conditioned activities.
Second, the fear of becoming attached to worldly discourse;
third, the fear of falling into sleep;
fourth, for the sake of tending to the sick monks.
Fifth, it is to cause young bhikṣus to observe the Buddha’s majestic deportment and give rise to joy.
Regarding the solemnizing of the assembly, the *Dazangjing* (Great Canon) records that Yang Yi,
the Hanlin Academician of the Song dynasty, traced back the original intent behind Baizhang’s establishment of the monastic rules.
In brief: there are those who,
under false names or by assuming the identity of others,
mingle with the pure assembly and cause disturbances and disruptions.
The *karmadāna* shall immediately investigate and report the matter;
the offender’s seat shall be removed, his bedding shall be taken down,
and he shall be expelled from the monastery.
"I wish the noble and pure assembly well.
Should any among them commit an offense,
I shall immediately strike them with my staff."
Gathering the assembly to burn the robes, alms bowls,
and ritual implements, and expelling [the offender] through a side gate,
serves as a demonstration of disgrace.
In detail, this one regulation provides four benefits.
First, it prevents the defilement of the pure assembly,
as it engenders reverence.
Second, they do not violate the monastic form,
as they follow the Buddha’s regulations;
third, they do not disturb the public offices.
Fourth, one does not leak [secrets] to the outside, for the purpose of reducing litigation and for the purpose of safeguarding the fundamental principles of the school.
However, Baizhang established the original regulations,
synthesizing the five categories and seven groups of the Buddhist Vinaya to propagate a grand model throughout the three realms.
The Brahmadaṇḍa, the formal exclusion, the invitation for confession,
and the raising of faults were employed to solemnize the community.
Throughout successive reigns, the imperial ancestors have repeatedly issued admonitions to the monastic order.
He strictly adhered to the Buddha's regulations;
with the exception of those cases involving grave offenses subject to criminal law, which were handled by the relevant authorities, all other matters followed these rules.
If members of the Sangha offend one another,
they should be regulated by the pure rules.
If they engage in strife and violate their shared boundaries, [they must be disciplined].
Whether they engage in impure conduct and negligence,
or misappropriate permanent property,
or privately steal money and goods.
One should follow the family precepts and not broadcast external disgrace; indeed,
all [of these matters] are termed "Śākya" (Buddhist).
Treat them according to secular custom as if they were kinsmen;
strictly observe the ancestral regulations and administer reprimands and punishments according to the circumstances.
For serious offenses, assemble the community to subject the offender to flogging and expulsion.
For minor offenses, they shall be fined in money, incense, or oil,
and a public notice shall be posted regarding them;
if the offense involves money or goods, they shall be held accountable with a formal statement and required to reimburse the loss.
May they be treated with impartiality and fairness so that they may repent and reform themselves.
An ancient verse on discipline states: "Stealing property and engaging in strife;
indulgence in wine and lust defiles the monastic order."
"Expel him immediately from the pure assembly;
to tolerate his presence would destroy the community. It is further said: "If one commits a grave offense, burn his robes and bowl;
he should then be assembled before the multitude."
Santō merely displayed his shame by being driven out through a side gate.
When Zen Master Dàhuì resided at Yùwáng Monastery,
he posted a notice for the Hall Administration (Tángsī).
If monks contend over ignorance, they are certainly not good monks;
whether they have reason or are without reason, all shall be expelled from the community.
Or, even if it is debated that they have reason, they shall still be banished.
If one suspects that this is not yet appropriate,
it is because a monk ought to practice patience;
if one insists on being right and engages in contention, [he fails in his duty].
This is because it is ignorance itself.
To expel [ignorance] together is to settle disputes before they have even sprouted.

Regarding the instruction of novice practitioners: every morning and on the fifteenth day of the month, after the assembly has finished ascending to the hall for the five-fold attendance, [the instruction follows].
The senior attendant (santou gyōja) orders the food-calling attendant (kekesu gyōja) to notify each department of their duties.
A notice board is hung in front of the hall to inform the assembly.
The evening bell tolls.
Before the hall, strike the wooden board three times to assemble the practitioners;
first, go to the Buddha Hall.
Next, at the Patriarchs’ Hall and the Sangha Hall,
the various quarters and halls call for the formal visit; those from the upper quarters line up facing the hall.
The head of the assembly enters the abbot’s quarters and requests the abbot to come forth and take his seat.
The head of the assembly steps forward,
offers incense, withdraws, and returns to his position.
With a slow voice, he calls out, "Attend! The assembly responds in low voices, "We do not presume to know [your health]. They perform three prostrations with full ceremony.
Holding their breath and bowing, they listen for his instructions;
once finished, they again perform three prostrations.
The head of the assembly shouts, "Be careful! and the entire congregation responds in low voices.
They perform the ritual of inquiry and withdraw.

If the abbot has other obligations, the food server shouts, "In accordance with the compassionate instructions of the Abbot," and the assembly says, "We do not presume to inquire after your health. Next, a long shout is made, saying, "The evening session is dismissed," and the assembly says, "Be careful! together, performing a mutual inquiry and withdrawing.
For the practitioner, the assembly leader (sanchou) shall first go to the attendants' office (shisishi) to offer incense and prostrate,
then report to the attendant (shizhe),
and finally seek formal authorization from the abbot (zhuchi).
Having granted the request,
the head of the assembly immediately struck the board in front of the hall for practice to gather the congregation,
who then lined up in the dormitory hall.
The head of the assembly (sanchō), accompanied by his attendants,
enters to invite the Abbot to come forth and take his seat.
The head of the assembly, together with the congregation, bows in greeting and steps forward.
Insert the incense sticks, withdraw, and return to your position.
With a slow voice, cry out, "Not well? (Pu-shen), and when the assembly has finished responding in low voices, all together perform nine prostrations.
The head of the assembly stepped forward and said:
"We have long contemplated the Master’s promise to grant us instruction.
We humbly beseech your compassion to reveal the causes and conditions for our transformation. Having thus made their inquiry and paid their respects, they withdrew.
On the following day, the Hall Attendant hangs the sign for the General Discourse (pǔshuō) to notify the assembly.
He prepares the seats, the incense table, and the candle stands.
The Head of the Assembly (cāntóu) notifies the assembly and requests the two orders of officials to stand in formation.
The assistant commander and the assembly of officers welcome the two orders of monks into the hall.
The head of the assembly and the hall master proceed to the attendants' office and, together with them, invite the abbot to descend to the hall.
The assembly welcomed him in and took their seats.
The attendant stood to one side to inquire after his well-being.
After the two orders of monks had finished their inquiries, [the master ascended the seat].
The attendant burns incense and requests the Dharma.
The head of the assembly leads the group in standing in a "wild goose" formation, inserts incense, and calls for the formal inquiry; they perform three prostrations.
They then withdraw and stand in a "wild goose" formation behind the east and west corridors respectively.
When the instruction has been heard in full,
the head of the assembly leads the group in bowing three times as before,
then immediately exits to stand outside to the right.
After bowing and escorting the abbot and the two orders of officials,
he then follows them to the dormitory hall,
where he inserts a large piece of incense.
Having performed nine prostrations, one withdraws.
Next, one proceeds to the Office of Attendants,
inserts incense, and performs three prostrations.
The Head of the Assembly and the Deputy Head of the Assembly stand before the two orders of monks and bow in thanks one by one.
Regarding the receiving of the dharma robe: when a special messenger arrives to deliver the dharma robe.
First, consult the guest prefect to convey the message.
Then, together with the attendants, trouble the office to announce it to the Abbot.
He may receive you immediately or at the following morning.
The attendant gives prior instructions.
When the guest master reports that the two orders have arrived,
the special envoy offers incense according to the standard ritual and is received with due courtesy.
Having finished the offering of tea,
insert incense again, perform two prostrations with the palms opened and three full prostrations;
if these are waived, perform a mere touching of the ground.

The liturgical text says: "The monk so-and-so, using this Dharma robe as a token of faith, respectfully presents it to you, supported upon a tray and cloth. Having thus presented the Dharma robe and the token of faith, he then takes his seat.
The two orders of officers then accompany him.
After the tea, hot water is offered;
after the hot water, the two orders of monks together escort him to his quarters.
The attendant leads the way for the inspection of the dormitories.

On another day, he ascends the Dharma seat. To the left of the seat, a position for the Abbot is prepared. The Special Envoy performs three full prostrations with wide-spread sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*), then carries the robe forward and offers it up.
When the Abbot receives the robe, he delivers a formal discourse (*fayu*).
Donning the robe and ascending the seat; or, if the Dharma Master who succeeded him has already passed away, a spirit table is set up in the right side room of the Dharma Hall.
Descending from the seat, one performs the memorial service and recites the sutras.
As for the etiquette regarding the arrival of a written message, see the section below.
Regarding the reception and attendance of a venerable elder (zunsu): when a venerable elder visits, [one should] receive and attend upon them.
One must first hang up the name plaque of the venerable elder.
Ring the bell to assemble the community and welcome him at the gate.
If he prefers simplicity, he may enter the temple quietly.
The abbot must receive [the guest] in the dormitory hall with incense and candles,
while also ordering the striking of the Sangha Hall bell;
the Guest Master shall then notify the Head Seat.
The leader of the assembly offers incense and performs the ritual greetings; when this is concluded, the assembly withdraws.
The two orders of officials and the retired elders then take seats to accompany the host.
After the incense has been burned and tea has been served, the session ends.
While the attendant (shishō) is inserting incense and prostrating,
the traveling attendants, ritual assistants, servants, palanquin bearers, and followers pay their respects. The officials of the Abbot’s quarters (hōjō),
as well as the head ritual assistant (san-tō) leading the assembly of ritual assistants, servants, palanquin bearers, and guards, likewise pay their respects.
They pay their respects in order.
The attendant again burns incense and prepares hot water;
when the water has been served, the two orders and the retired elders together escort them to the guest quarters.
The guest master orders that a sedan chair be prepared;
the abbot, accompanied by the attendants, tours the quarters to announce his visit,
with the ritual attendant following in attendance.
If it concerns the following mountains, the attendant shall lead the tour of the quarters.
The guest-inviting attendant shall prepare a formal document and proceed to the guest’s seat.
Inserting incense, he bows and requests the special tea service, reporting:
"The Abbot has invited the Master;
this evening, the ceremony shall take place in the Meditation Hall."
A special offering of hot water is presented.

We humbly entreat your compassionate descent to receive this; having finished reading the petition, the formal document follows below. Once concluded, the guest master reports: "Please, Venerable Sir, partake of the hot water and then take your seat for the medicinal meal in the dormitory hall, where the curtains have been hung."
Arrange the mirrors and plaques.
Set up a special position for the Light Companion (Guangban).
Sound the drums and perform the rites.
They bow as they take their seats and bow when offering incense.
After the invitation to tea and the tea service have concluded, the medicinal food is served;
these procedures are identical to the regular rites, with the exception that special honors are observed.

The guest master goes to the guest quarters and invites them, saying: "The Abbot requests the Venerable Master for tea and fruit this evening; he also requests the presence of the two orders of officials as companions.
The attendant reports this.
On the following morning, the Master ascends the hall to express his gratitude.
The following morning, the hot water was requested.
The attendant burned incense, the ritual assistant made inquiries,
and the servants responded with a respectful "shēnyòu."
The abbot remained to accompany him in eating the congee.
After the meal, he was invited for tea.
The attendant then reported once more that it was time for the formal discourse.
A seat is established at the head of the hall;
half-day meals and refreshments are provided.
If the deceased was a Great Venerable (Dazunxu), the Head Seat and the various heads of the community shall report the matter to the Abbot.
Exhort him to expound the essential points of the Dharma for the sake of the assembly.

The Abbot first proceeds to the guest quarters to state his intention; if permission is granted, the Head Seat prepares a formal document, and the two orders of the assembly together proceed to the guest quarters.
Insert incense and perform prostrations to invite [the dignitaries].
Next, request the Abbot to lead the assembly to their seats and announce the event by hanging the placard.
The participants shall stand in rows to the left and right before the Dharma seat.
When the time arrives, the drum is struck.
The abbot and the assembly descend together to stand before their positions in the Dharma Hall.
The abbot first leads the way to his seat.
This is the same as the regular ascending to the hall.
Upon descending from the seat, the two orders of officials go before the venerable elder to inquire after his well-being;
the venerable elder then goes before the abbot to inquire after his well-being.
Upon returning to the center, he inquires after the health of the assembly at large and ascends the seat.
The attendants and the two orders of officers step out of their ranks to inquire after his well-being.
After the abbot has inquired after them and finished preaching the Dharma, he descends from the seat.
The abbot first inquires after his well-being;
then he inquires with the entire assembly.
The abbot, the two orders of officials, and the assembly then proceed together to the guest quarters.
Inserting incense, he bows in thanks.
The guest-inviting attendant prepares a formal document to request that special hospitality be provided.
The Sanyuan (Mountain Gate) prepares the meal and the offering for the assembly;
the Changfang (Abbot’s Quarters) prepares the supplementary offering.
The performance of the ritual is the same as usual, with only specific distinctions.
If the various monasteries are of equal status, it is appropriate to follow the middle course of propriety.
If a venerable elder from a Dharma family arrives,
first perform the formal ceremony for mutual greeting between monasteries.
The guest is escorted to his seat and invited to occupy the central position.
The abbot offers incense and performs prostrations;
the Dharma relatives then perform their rites.
When sitting within the abbot’s quarters, one should yield the central seat.
The etiquette for welcoming and seeing off guests is as previously described;
when offering hot water, one should personally perform the ritual.
The guest declines with courtesy.
The attendant performs the ritual prostrations.
If a successor to the Dharma, an administrator of affairs, or a Dharma brother visits, [the same protocol applies].
When you arrive in person at the abbot’s quarters,
the abbot shall immediately strike the Sangha Hall bell to assemble the community for formal business.
First, invite the abbot to sit in the central seat and perform the ritual of disciples and dharma-relatives.
Next, conduct the ritual greetings for the various mountain monasteries.
The procedures for escorting [the guest] are the same as before;
however, for the special provision of a hot bath, no formal written request is required.
Instead, the attendant who invites the guest shall offer incense and present the invitation.
Furthermore, one should observe the seniority of the practitioners' years of ordination (*varṣāgra*) and,
according to the circumstances, adaptively request the serving of hot water, the serving of pipes,
or the request for the master to ascend the seat.
Each has its own formal protocol,
as seen below.
The resident bhikṣu of this temple, [Name], hereby respectfully prepares and serves hot water in the dormitory this evening specifically for [Name].
I humbly pray that Your Holiness will deign to grant me your esteemed presence.

This memorial is respectfully submitted on this day of the [month] year by the monk [Name], the incumbent of this temple, holding the rank of [Rank]. [Name] hereunder ventures to prepare a simple meal of rice and water at the dormitory hall on the coming day.
I humbly entreat Your Reverence to deign to grant me your esteemed presence.

This memorial is respectfully submitted on this day of the [month] year by the monk [Name], the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) of this temple. I, [Name], venture to invite you for the coming day to proclaim the fundamental tenets and provide instruction for future students.
I humbly entreat Your Reverence’s compassionate favor to graciously grant this request.

This memorial is respectfully submitted on the [day] of the [month] of the [year]. Submitted by the petitioner [Name], holding the rank of [Title]. Respectfully sealed. [The petitioner] requests the Abbot Dhyāna Master of [Location] to ascend the seat; the donor requests the Abbot to ascend the seat for the meal offering. When the donor arrives at the gate...
Upon learning of his arrival, he was received and escorted to the Abbot’s quarters,
where tea and soup were served,
and then sent to his place of lodging.
If the donor is a high-ranking official or a great benefactor,
one should strike the bell to assemble the community and go out to the gate to welcome them,
escorting them to their assigned quarters.
The donor then requested the administrative officials to consult together;
they proceeded to the Abbot’s quarters,
where they lit incense and formally invited him to ascend the seat.
On the appointed day, the Dharma seat is prepared.
A seat for the patron is arranged before it,
and the plaque for the Upper Hall is hung.
The bell is struck to announce the assembly,
and the guest prefect, together with the donor,
goes to the abbot’s quarters to invite the abbot.
One must prepare hand-incense burners, lamps, banners, and *nṛtya* and *ghaṇṭā* cymbals according to the ritual protocol.
Having welcomed [the master] to the front of the seat, he ascends and sits cross-legged upon the throne.
The donor then performs prostrations before the seat.

The guest prefect bows and leads [the visitors] to their seats to listen to the Dharma; however, to merely accept the prostrations while remaining seated would be a slight against the Dharma. Upon descending from the seat, they should bow in thanks.
If there is a meal offering for the monks, one must consult with the administrative officers to determine the provisions and expenses for the feast.
The *karmadāna* shall record the number of monks and their respective conduct;
the offerings shall be distributed equally according to that number.
A seat for the donor (*dānapati*) shall be established within the Sangha hall.
After parting from the abbot once the meal is finished,
the administrative officers (zhishi) shall accompany the donor to stand for a short while before the Sangha Hall.
Wait for the Head Seat (shouzuo) to lead the assembly out of the hall to express thanks.
Next, the Abbot (zhuchi) and the administrative officers (zhishi) go to the guest quarters to offer thanks.
There may also be those who have sent money to provide a meal for the monks.
The abbot shall entrust the administrative affairs to the steward,
who must manage and provide all offerings and stipends in their entirety;
take care not to commingle these funds with other purposes.
One should contemplate how cause and effect are clearly manifest.
The *Ren-tian bao-jian* states:
"At night, while sitting in his quarters at Mount Yungai in Hunan, Master Zhi of the Chan school—"
Suddenly, he heard the smell of burning and the sound of shackles.
Upon looking closely,
he saw someone bearing a flaming cangue.
The fire continued to rise and die out without ceasing;
the yoke and tail were leaning against the threshold of the door.
Startled, the wise man asked:
"Who are you that your suffering has reached such an extreme?
The man bearing the cangue replied,
"I am Shouyong, who formerly resided on this mountain."
"It was improper for you to use the offerings of a donor intended for the Sangha to construct a monastic hall;
therefore, you undergo this suffering. Zhi said:
"What expedient means can be employed to avoid this?
Yong replied,
"I hope you will provide an appraisal for the Sangha Hall and establish offerings for the monks."
"You may be spared.
Zhi then used his own funds to repay the debt exactly as he had been told.
One night, he dreamed that Sengyong thanked him, saying:
Relying on the power of the Master, he was spared from the sufferings of hell and reborn among humans and devas;
after three lifetimes, he again attained the status of a monk.
Even now, the burn marks upon the threshold of the gate still remain.
Nevertheless, Master Yong used the provisions intended for the monks to construct the Sangha Hall,
all of which are for the communal use of the monastics.
They still receive the retribution for such mutual use.
If this is so, then the current monastic communities not only engage in mutual use while denying cause and effect.
What, then, should be done with those who even steal the permanent property of the monastery as their own?
Regarding the inspection and accounting by the successor: if the dharma-heir arrives at the temple, they shall conduct the inspection and accounting.
He shall direct the administrative officer to go to the treasury office to perform an accounting and procure the necessary funds and materials for delivery.
The night before, one should first report the matter to the Attendant (Shisi) for consultation and notification.
Then, proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang) to offer incense and perform prostrations;
if these are waived, perform a mere touching of the ground (chuli) and request, saying: "Tomorrow morning, we shall gather in the Cloud Hall (Yuntang) and briefly prepare a humble offering."

I humbly entreat your compassionate grace to deign to issue instructions for the guest master to invite the members of the two orders and those in the single quarters of all the various halls to hang the signboard for the morning tea service.
On the appointed day, the seat of the abbot in the Sangha Hall shall be solemnly prepared and arranged.
As well as the implements for the *zhuofu* (cloth offerings) and the ceremonial money.
When the fire-board sounds,
the assembly proceeds to the hall.
The person serving the fried delicacies follows the abbot into the hall and bows as they take their seats.
Turning toward the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ), they burn incense and join their palms;
then, proceeding before the abbot, they perform a formal greeting.
After the assembly has turned toward the Holy Sangha,
the Abbot extends his hand to invite the person in charge of tea service to sit;
this seat is located at the head of the Hall of the Guest Master.
The attendant calls out, "I request the assembly to set down their bowls; the food will be served throughout.
The person in charge of the tea service rises, burns incense, distributes the monetary offerings (*śraddhā-deya*) to the abbot, and then distributes the offerings to the assembly.
The kitchen staff strike the *zhai-ban* (meal signal) and proceed to serve the meal.
When the meal is finished, the assembly collects their bowls and withdraw the abbot’s table.
The person serving the snacks burns incense and bows in greeting before the Abbot.
They then exit from behind the Sacred Monk (Sengsheng) and bow in greeting before the incense burner.
The bell is struck, and tea is served throughout the assembly.
He proceeds before the Abbot to offer tea.
Then, he emerges from behind the Holy Monk and advances before the Abbot.
Unfolding the sitting mat, he says: "On this day, your humble servant has committed the great offense of intruding upon you with these trivial offerings;

that you have condescended to honor me with such weighty favor leaves me, in my lowly state, overcome with the utmost gratitude. He performs two prostrations for greetings and one prostration for the ritual of touching the feet.
Escort the abbot out.
The person who prepared the tea returns to the hall to burn incense and exchange greetings with those in both the upper and lower sections to thank them for their companionship.
Again, having exchanged greetings and struck the bell to collect the cups,
he next proceeds to the abbot’s quarters to thank him for his gracious visit.
The abbot, in turn, goes to the guest quarters to offer thanks.
If the various mountains have prepared the offerings for the midday meal,
invite the abbot to go together to the hall;
bow to the abbot and invite him to take his seat.
The abbot shall be exempted from performing formal prostrations;
he shall merely bow to the person serving the tea and snacks, who then returns to his place.
The attendant then distributes the food throughout the assembly.
Incense is lit and one proceeds before the Abbot to offer greetings and present monetary offerings; then,
monetary offerings are distributed to the assembly.
Burn incense for the companions of the fire;
serve food for the companions at their respective stations.
Regarding the tea ceremony and formal lectures, deliberate as appropriate according to the circumstances.

The Deceased Master’s Testament Arrives: A special messenger arrives at the temple bearing the testament; the ceremonial procedures are detailed below in the section on the Testament. The Abbot opens the letter.
The two orders first console the abbot.
An offering is established in the center of the Dharma Hall;
before the seat, incense is offered with a formal discourse.
They raise their voices in lamentation and perform three prostrations.
When the hot water is offered, they again perform three prostrations.
The food is presented, the ritual gifts are distributed, and the drum is struck.
The lecture is conducted with special ritual propriety:
three prostrations are performed, tea is served, and the drum is struck three times.
Then, one withdraws from the seat and folds away the sitting mat.

The Venerable Vinaya Master recites the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī for the dedication of merit; this is performed on the anniversary of the passing of the Dharma-successor Master, as well as for the two ranks of officials, the four dormitories, fellow practitioners from various regions, dharma relatives, junior disciples, and those who have served in administrative affairs—all of whom receive memorial offerings.

The abbot sits to the left of the spirit tablet; if there are abbots from other mountains, or those from under his own seat, or dharma relatives who are his peers, then during the superior offering, the abbot shall respond to their bows along with the special messenger.
Below this, one does not respond with a bow. When the offerings are completed, one recites the Great Compassion Mantra (*Mahākaruṇā-mantra*).
For the dedication of merit, one says:
"By the merit of the sutra recitation performed above, I respectfully dedicate it for the sake of the Great Monk [Name] of [Temple Name], to increase and exalt his spiritual rank."
"All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time...
[and so forth]. The Head Seat leads the assembly to console the Abbot, saying: "It is a misfortune for the Dharma-gate."
Our teacher, the Upādhyāya, has passed away;
we later students have lost our reliance and cannot overcome our profound grief and lamentation.
We nevertheless hope that you will endure this with patience and persevere in this Way.
Imperially Commissioned Baizhang Qinggui, Scroll Two;
Imperially Commissioned Baizhang Qinggui, Scroll Three.
By the Subject-Monk, Abbot of Dazhi Shousheng Chan Monastery.
Dehui, the subject-monk and former abbot of the Great Longxiang Jiqing Monastery, respectfully submits this memorial in accordance with the Imperial Edict.

Having received the Imperial Edict for revision, he requests the appointment of a new abbot. He requests the appointment of a new abbot by dispatching a special envoy. Whenever the position of abbot at any monastery throughout the ten directions becomes vacant...
This must be reported to the relevant authorities.
Once the official decree has been issued,
the treasury office shall convene a tea ceremony for the members of the two orders and the retired elders.

A council was held to dispatch a special envoy; the head administrators (*shoushu*), chief officers (*zhishi*), retired elders (*qinjiu*), and the assembly of monks from the *mengtang* and former positions were commissioned to draft the formal letter. A notice for tea and soup offerings was prepared for the various mountains and the rivers and lakes, signed by the special envoy, and a record keeper was requested to compose it.
If there is a deficiency in the record-keeping,
select those capable of writing and divide [the material] among them.
A notice shall be written on silk or paper.
The special envoy invited, or the chief administrator, or a veteran monk,
or the West Hall Head Seat, shall be appointed for this purpose.
Alternatively, one may appoint a head official in their place.
If a non-administrative official is appointed as the special envoy,
they must also be accompanied by at least one subordinate administrative official to manage the funds and deliberate on affairs.
One volume of the *Jùxūzhī* (Compendium of Essential Knowledge) should be kept;
it details the temple's requisite landholdings and property,
as well as the protocol for receiving guests and their retinues.
Everything was fully prepared.
The monastic community provided hospitality for the special envoy and his entire entourage until the day of their departure.
He visits the various quarters to bid farewell;
the Sangha Hall bell is struck to assemble the community, who see him off at the gate.
Beneath the triple gate, stakes are driven in and canopies are set up.
Arrange seats toward the interior and perform the tea ceremony;
invite the members of the two orders and the retired elders to serve as honored companions.
If the head administrator departs,
the subordinate administrator performs the rites;
if the chief officers or long-standing veterans depart, they do likewise.
Then the presiding officer performs the rites:
he bows for them to be seated, burns incense, bows again as they return to their places,
and they partake of tea together.
Rising again, he burns incense, bows to the incense, and returns to his position.
Accompanied by others, they consume hot tonic and collect the bowls.
The special envoy rises to offer thanks and boards the palanquin.
When the special envoy arrives at that temple to invite the current abbot,
he first meets the guest master (*kōshaku*).
Together they proceed to the administrative office (*kusoshi*) to escort the abbot to his quarters and settle him there.
Next, he visits the head officers and the various administrative offices;
he then goes to the Attendants' Office (Shisi) to report his arrival in detail,
whereupon the Attendant (Shizhe) announces it to the Abbot.
I await your decision on whether this may be permitted.
If you grant your consent,
I shall then instruct the preparation of tables and cloths, and the placement of the memorial documents to notify both orders.
The Abbot enters and takes his seat;
the special envoy enters to inquire after his well-being and requests him to sit in the lotus posture.

The attendant *vinaya-dhara* (weina) announces the proclamation.
Next, the various mountain gateways, mountains, rivers, and lakes submit their petitions;
each is successively presented with a formal discourse (*dharmavāda*) to be distributed and read aloud.
If one sees an appointed official requesting the opening of the hall,
there is a formal letter (shu) which he personally carries forward; there is a dharma discourse (fa-yu) for its proclamation, and once it is finished,
there is a dharma discourse for pointing to the Dharma seat.
Ascending the seat, he held up incense to offer prayers for the Emperor.
Next, he held up incense for the Imperial Preceptor, the officials of the Shengyuan, Tai, Xian, and the various prefectures and counties, as well as the civil and military bureaucracy;
the attendants then offered incense one by one.
The Dharma heir Xiang, the abbot, took it out from his breast pocket and inserted it into the incense burner; then,
he adjusted his robes and sat cross-legged.
The attendant burns incense and descends from the seat to inquire after the assembly.
After the two orders of officers have stepped out of their ranks and completed their inquiries,
the attendant ascends the seat once more to burn incense and inquire after the assembly.
The ritual is the same as that for ascending the hall on the first and fifteenth days of the month.
The abbots of various mountains who have escorted the guest into the monastery shall also come out to exchange greetings.
The abbot should then instruct his attendant to invite the officials to be seated.
The head monk among the assembly strikes the wooden mallet.

With the first strike, he says: "O dragon and elephant assembly at this Dharma banquet, you should contemplate the primary principle as the abbot delivers his discourse, questions, and answers to uphold the essential framework."
In thanking the officials and the various mountains, it is said that the opening of the hall on this day is specifically for the purpose of offering prayers for the Emperor.
I dare not elaborate further; I shall briefly mention the special envoys and the diligent elders of the two orders.
The details have been set forth during the *Xiǎosàn* (Small Private Audience).
At the conclusion of the session, the person who strikes the gavel strikes it once more and announces: "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King;
such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. He then descends from his seat. First, the officials receive congratulations, which are completed.
The administrative official escorts the guests to their seats.
The guest master and his attendants then advance with incense burners and candles,
arranging them in a single row before the seats.
The special envoy has finished inserting incense, performing two prostrations with opened sitting cloths, and three full prostrations.

The attendant of the Hall Office calls out, "Greeting from the various mountains! Next, he calls out, "Greeting from the West Hall! He then calls out, "Greeting from the administrative officers! [The envoy] performs two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full prostrations.

Again, he shouts, "The Head Seat, the assembly, the retired officials, the long-serving elders, the monks of the *Mongtang*, the former residents, and those from all the quarters shall all insert incense together with the assembly.
Having completed two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full bows, they conclude.
The Dharma relatives and local laypeople of Zhuangku’an Pagoda arrived briefly to offer their congratulations;
having finished, they took their seats.
The attendant and junior disciples then inserted incense and performed three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths.
Next, the attendant in charge of ritual implements inserts incense and bows;
next, the head of the assembly leads the practitioners in inserting incense and bowing.
Next, after the sedan-chair attendants, village headmen, laborers, masters, and servants have completed their prostrations,
the abbot proceeds immediately to the guest quarters to offer thanks to the officials and the various mountain monasteries.
They proceeded in order to visit the various quarters.
In each quarter, incense tables, censers, candles, and seating arrangements were laid out,
and all assumed their respective dignified postures.
Waiting outside the quarters for the abbot to arrive,
the head of the quarters first stands at the gate with his head bowed.
He escorts him inside, invites him to sit cross-legged, and offers incense.
The abbot responds with incense,
briefly exchanging greetings regarding the weather and expressing thanks as he escorts him out.
Upon reaching the front of the Dharma Hall, the assembly of resident monks from the various quarters all line up outside the gate, led by the lowest-ranking official.
The same protocol applies for both the welcoming and the seeing off.

The Monastery Gate specifically prepares tea and soup for the newly appointed official. A notice for the tea and soup service shall be posted in advance in both the upper and lower sections of the Sangha Hall.
The administrative office (kūsī) shall prepare a formal invitation document (as shown in the appendix), along with a tray, cloth coverings, an incense burner, and candles.
They shall proceed to the abbot’s quarters (fangwàng) to offer incense and pay respects to extend the invitation.
If the abbot declines, they shall perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloths (chùlǐ) and report: "After the midday meal, we shall serve tea in the Cloud Hall (yúntáng) specifically for you."
I humbly beseech your compassionate descent to receive this formal petition. Immediately thereafter,

the guest master was instructed to invite the dignitaries of the two orders and the veteran assembly members to serve as honored companions for the hanging of the plaque and the serving of tea and soup, as announced to the community.
Within the Sangha Hall, the seat of the Abbot is prepared; when it is near the time for a meal and the long wooden board (chángbǎn) is heard sounding,
the administrative officers enter the hall, offer incense, and perform prostrations.
One circumambulates the hall once to request tea;
however, this is specifically for the purpose of offering congratulations to the abbot.
According to ancient regulations, there was likewise no rite of circumambulating the hall to request tea for the entire assembly.
Upon being excused, he shall observe the fast and retire; then, the drums are struck to assemble the assembly.
The administrative officers bow to the abbot as he enters the hall.
Once they have returned to their positions, they bow for him to be seated, and he burns one incense stick.
The abbot bows before the incense burner,
turns behind the Sacred Monk (Shōsō), returns to the center to inquire after his well-being, and stands.
Tea is served throughout, and the tea pitcher is removed.
Approach the abbot, bow for tea, and withdraw.
Behind the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ), exit to the right, offer incense, perform three prostrations with opened sitting cloths,
and rise to lead the entire assembly.
Upon reaching the presence of the Abbot, he performs two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full prostrations, then escorts him out.
Returning to the hall, he burns incense;
having exchanged greetings between the upper and lower sections, he collects his bowl and withdraws from his seat.
The ceremonies for *tāng* (hot water) and tea are identical;
however, there is no escorting of the abbot out of the hall.
Once the *tāng* ceremony concludes, one takes one's seat for the medicinal food (*yàoshí*).
From the temple storehouse steward, Bhikṣu [Name]. Right here, [Name] respectfully submits this memorial:
following the conclusion of the morning meal, we shall gather in the Cloud Hall this evening to serve tea and soup, thereby extending our formal expressions of congratulation.
Your Holiness’s compassionate grace has been specially bestowed upon me in this formal manner.
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], [Name], holding the rank of [Title],
submits this memorial together with the form for the ritual assembly.

That evening, after the meal, the attendant informed the abbot, saying: "Tonight there is a small *seng* (informal discourse); please have the guest master notify the assembly to hang the small *seng* plaque."
He wrote out the names of the special envoys, the two orders of officials,
the retired elders, the monks of the Mengtang,
and those from the various quarters of former resources.
The Hall of the Patriarch’s Reliquary Stupa:
Upon temporarily arriving and entering the monastery,
the attendant and visiting Chan practitioners attend.
If there are visiting officials who accompany [the abbot] and stay overnight at various monasteries, each case shall be listed in detail and submitted in advance for formal notification.
When the evening bell tolls, the attendant reports to the Abbot’s Quarters; after the wooden board is struck, the drum is sounded once.
The assembly gathers and the two orders take their places and stand still.
The abbot emerges and ascends the seat;
having delivered his introductory remarks, engaged in question and answer, and presented the essential outline of the teaching, he concludes with an expression of gratitude.
The practitioner holding the candle and the attendant presenting the *mujishi* (eye-tablet) ensure that the details are exhaustive.

Upon descending from their seats, the *katō* practitioner calls out: "Venerable Abbot, please invite the various mountain masters (*shanzhang heshang*), the two classes of officials, the West Hall, the retired elders (*qinjiu*), the Meditation Hall attendants, and the Zen guests."
Now, regarding the serving of hot water (tō) in the Jūtei-dō: the administrative official (chiji) shall escort the visiting guests to their seats and serve them with hot water and fruit.
For the formal ascent of the seat (jōza) on behalf of the temple’s benefactor (dandaya), the administrative official must notify the abbot (jūji) the evening before.
The following morning, the attendant ordered the guest master to hang the signboard for the "Ascending the Hall" (shàngtáng) to notify the assembly.
The administrative office (kūsī) dispatched personnel to solemnly arrange the ancestral hall.
After the morning gruel offering was completed, [the ceremony proceeded].
Having specifically ascended the hall to announce the purpose of the matter and finished preaching the Dharma,
he descended from his seat.
He then gathered the assembly and proceeded to the ancestral shrine.
Incense sticks are lit and tea and soup are offered as a formal service.
The Rector (Vina) recites the sutra and performs the dedication of merit.
Regarding the hosting of the special envoy, the administrative officers (Zhishi) must first inform the Abbot (Zhu-zhi).
When deliberating on the weight of the offerings for the special envoys who proclaim the memorial and the stationery,
the abbot must prepare these offerings so that they are appropriate and harmonious with the occasion.
On the day of the ceremony, the sleeping hall is prepared by nailing up and arranging the seats;
the elders of the two orders are invited to serve as honored companions,
and a special seat is set aside for them.
The guest attendant shall personally invite [the honored guests],
while for the remaining persons, the head of the guest office at the abbot’s quarters shall submit the request.
The ritual procedures are identical to those used for ordinary occasions.

The two orders of officials are invited to remain; once the two orders have finished attending to the special envoy, they agree to go to the abbot’s quarters for consultation and then withdraw. The abbot must not grant their request immediately.
The attendant instructs the guest-head acolyte to prepare the bath implements, trays, cloths, incense burners, and candles.
The Abbot, accompanied by the attendant, proceeds to the administrative office (kusi) and the various quarters.
He first reports his arrival to the guest master, who then sends word to welcome the Abbot. The guest master earnestly requests that the number of guests be increased.
They entered and sat down separately.
The attendants burned incense and prepared hot water,
offering them every courtesy and urging them to remain.
If your term of office has expired, you must likewise remain patient and tolerant.
Wait until the abbot has some leisure time,
then submit your request once more to take leave and retire.

Regarding expressions of gratitude for arrivals and departures: whenever officials, patrons (*dānapati*), or abbots from various mountains escort one into the monastery, it is proper by ritual to express gratitude.
It is likewise appropriate to pay formal visits to local and prefectural government offices.
If one departs for a distant place in the mountain forests,
one should have the practitioner convey a message to the administrative office (kūsi), the Head Seat (shouzuo), and the Rector (weina) so they may take note.
Once the departure has been long, the administrators should inquire after the expected date of return.
The Hall Monitor shall hang up the "Summoning the Abbot" placard and notify the assembly.
The bell is struck and the gate is opened to welcome him;
however, the Abbot has previously instructed that this formal greeting be waived.
He immediately went to the Buddha Hall and the local deity hall to burn incense.
The Head Seat led the assembly to the Abbot’s quarters to pay their respects.
Once the assembly had withdrawn, he retained the two orders of officials and the veteran monks.
After the hot water has been offered and the assembly has dispersed,
the attendants, the head of the administrative office (fangzhang), and the ritual assistants (xingzhe) insert incense and perform prostrations.
Next, the head of the practitioners (candou) leads the assembly of ritual assistants in their prostrations until completion.
The abbot must inspect the quarters and perform the customary salutations;
however, if he resides within the city walls or the immediate suburbs and enters or exits at irregular times throughout the day and night,
it is not necessary to carry out these practices.
Alternatively, when returning to the Abbot’s quarters,
the members of the two orders and the retired elders should all go to the Abbot’s quarters to inquire after his well-being.
This was the practice during Wuzu Fayan’s tenure at Mount Jing.
He frequently went out on alms rounds;
whenever it was time for the midday meal or morning gruel,
he would return directly to the Sangha Hall.
When the assembly accompanying him has finished eating,
the Chief Cook (fangzhang), the Guest Master (ketou), and the Attendant for the Holy Monk (shengseng shizhe) await the striking of the gavel to descend from the hall.
As the assembly is about to leave their seats, [the procedure continues].
[The Master] shouts, saying: "Assembly, stand in formation! The Abbot of Fangzhang inspects the hall; the Rector burns incense and inspects the hall once, then exits the hall.

Again he shouts, saying: "The Abbot transmits these words to the assembly: there is no need for you to visit the two orders of officials or the retired elders; they too should come to the Abbot’s quarters to pay their respects."
Upon entering the quarters for the handover of the hearth-base and utensils, one must attend the tea ceremony with the two orders of senior monks (*qínjiù*).
Therein, one must inquire in detail regarding the affairs of the mountain gate, as well as the hearth-base, the formal documents, and the utensils.
Each item was inspected and verified for delivery;
wealth and grain were calculated,
ledgers were made clear and distinct, and seals were applied to the currency.
The primary concern must be thorough scrutiny.

Regarding the reception of the two orders of senior and retired officials for the tea service: on the appointed day, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) and the administrative officials (Zhishi), along with the senior and retired officials, proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang).
Inserting incense, he prostrates to invite the abbot;
next, he invites the attendant and the junior disciples.
He then prepares the central seat within the abbot’s private quarters.
The positions of the two orders and the retired elders shall be as usual for the seated assembly.
After the attendants and the junior disciples accompanying them have finished paying their respects to the abbot,
they take their seats at the end of the two orders and the retired elders.
When the time arrives, the Head Seat invites the Abbot to come forth.
They bow to each other as they take their seats;
if the Abbot declines, he simply burns incense, steps forward to inquire after his well-being, and presents the monetary offering.
The head seat (*śrāmaṇera*), the administrative officers (*karmadāna*), and the retired elders (*purāṇa*) lead the way.
Three persons perform their salutations and return to their seats.
When the meal is finished, the head seat rises and burns incense.
If one is exempt from the formal prostrations, one proceeds to sit and drink tea.
The same protocol applies for invitations to the dormitory hall (*shindō*) for tea and refreshments by fellow practitioners from various mountains,
long-standing associates, administrative dharma relatives, or junior disciples.
However, when serving tea and snacks, one must consider the seniority of the seating positions and exercise discretion according to the occasion.
Upon retiring from the abbacy, if the retired abbot is elderly or afflicted by illness, [the following protocol applies].
If the mind becomes weary,
or if conditions are unfavorable, one should know for oneself when to withdraw and remain steadfast with the funds.
It is essential that the ledgers and records be clear and precise.
The inventory of the abbot’s personal effects shall be verified and handed over with two identical copies of the itemized list.
Both the abbot and the members of the two orders of senior monks shall sign and affix their seals.
The temple seal shall be used.
The abbot and the administrative office shall each retain a copy for their records.
A public official shall be appointed to guard the abbot’s quarters.
On the day of departure, the abbot shall ascend the hall to offer words of gratitude, take leave of the assembly, and descend from the seat.
Strike the drum three times and withdraw.
If one remains at the original temple and occupies the East Hall,
thereby severing ties with the abbot, [the following applies].
One must treat them with the utmost courtesy and kindness.
Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty used the vegetable gardens of Lingyin Temple to establish a temple for Empress Yan.
On that very day, Chijue Chong of Zhushan retired from the monastery;
he personally packed his belongings and donned his straw rain-hat to travel to Mount Lu,
but sent a messenger to urge him to stay, to no avail.
Whose lofty character could succeed him through the ages?
As his transformation approached, he manifested illness and felt it grow increasingly grave;
he then requested the two orders and the veteran elders to attend to him for the final rites.
He packed away his robes, bowl, and travel gear,
remained in the abbot’s quarters,
and dispatched the official Jinxing as an attendant to keep watch.
This shall await the auctioneer’s call.
Should there be any items designated for distribution,
they must be allocated with impartiality and fairness.
The mother should ensure that favors and resentments are not unevenly distributed, lest they lead to future disputes.
If the robes and alms-bowl are meager,
one should strive for frugality and simplicity.
The final instructions state that the junior disciples shall not wear hempen garments or wail in mourning.
They are requested to invite the Head Seat Master to preside over the funeral;
all other Buddhist rites are hereby waived.
However, citing the verse on impermanence, it says: "The deceased monk has been sent off;
his mother has exhausted the monastery's permanent assets and exhausted the community."
If a resident monk has served the mountain gate with merit and the monastic community cherishes his enduring kindness,
and his robes and alms bowl are somewhat abundant;
The funeral rites should be conducted according to the prescribed ritual.
Should there be letters from officials, patrons, or dharma-relations from various mountains,
these must be dispatched immediately.
The abbot of [Name] Temple, [Name], has seen his worldly conditions come to an end; like a candle in the wind, life does not endure.
All that remains of him—his robes, bowl, and the offerings and benefits bestowed by lay devotees—[are hereby entrusted].
As this is not a permanent possession,
we request both the Quarters to conduct a census and respectfully invite a certain person to preside over the funeral rites.
Furthermore, whenever he distributed [property] to the assembly of monks for the purpose of reading scriptures,
he would repeatedly entrust his mother with excessive amounts, which she then misappropriated for the use of the monastic community (sanghika).
May you examine this matter.

[Your] humble servant [Name]. It is my earnest hope that [this letter] will reach you in full. [Year], [Month], [Day]. Signed by [Name], resident of [Mountain Name]. Regarding the format for such a letter: [This is addressed to] a Venerable Elder with whom I have had the honor of traveling and associating.
The destiny of Naihe Li was such that, through successive inducements and encouragement, he persevered in these humble circumstances. Now, like dew upon a blade of grass, my life is empty;
like clouds and mountains, the distance grows ever more vast.
I venture to pray for protection so that this culture may endure; my prostrations and prayers never cease.
Though I dwell upon these mountains as a neighbor, I am of no benefit;
I always rely upon the light from your neighboring wall.
The dream-scene is originally empty;
I am fortunate to have escaped the illusions of worldly conditions.
I cannot fulfill my wish for a face-to-face parting, and thus my heart yearns with utmost intensity.
I pray that the Buddha’s radiance may spread ever further,
so that the spirit of our school may flourish all the more.
I humbly beseech you.
Take heed. Fellow Dharma-kinsman, I have received this mountain residence by overstepping my merit;
I am ashamed before my fellow disciples.
Having long been afflicted by illness,
I am resigned to being one who will spend the rest of my life in this state.
I respectfully present these handwritten words to briefly express my parting farewells in person.
To illuminate the sublime virtue of our late master,
the Way lies in the diligent practice of those among us.
Unable to bear [the weight of my feelings], I offer my utmost devotion.
I humbly pray that you will take care of yourself.
[Name] (addressed as appropriate), Bhikṣu [Name] of [Name] Temple, respectfully seals this.
Upon entering the shrine— initially at the time of manifesting parinirvāṇa—
the attendant immediately orders the guest master acolyte to go down to the Sangha Hall to announce to the assembly.
He strikes the wooden mallet once.
Baoyun says to the assembly:
"The wind and fire press upon us so that I cannot reach you in person. He then strikes the mallet once more and subsequently notifies all the quarters.
The attendants of the Hall Office ring the Sangha Hall bell to assemble the community.
After the visit of condolence to the Abbot has concluded,
the Head Seat consults with the two orders of officials and the retired elders.
The format for the notification of death is shown below. Upon receiving the report, one must send letters to various monasteries requesting individuals to preside over the funeral rites.
These individuals must be persons of renowned virtue from neighboring mountains, long-established elders, or senior members of the dharma family.
Alternatively, the head seat (shouzuo) of the temple itself may be appointed;
if there is a final testament, it shall be honored and implemented.
The junior disciples, attendants, and personal followers shall arrange for the ritual bathing.
Having dressed in ceremonial robes and purified their hair, they enter the shrine.
A verse of farewell is posted on the left side of the shrine.
The *vinaya-dhara* leads the junior disciples to offer incense and request the *śrāmaṇera* (head seat) to perform the ritual for entering the shrine.
The dormitory hall is prepared;
an altar with an incense burner, candles, and seating is arranged for offerings.
When the time arrives, the Sangha Hall bell is struck to assemble the community.
Having completed the recitation of the Buddha’s deeds,
the Rector steps forward and proclaims the invocation for the recitation, saying: "Now, with all earnestness..."
His profound power is subtle and mysterious,
manifesting transformative traces for humans and devas;
his innate nature is perfectly luminous.
I reverently contemplate how the Abbot, the Venerable Monk, has grasped the profound pivot of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
his wisdom is as bright as the full moon.
The light gathers the waves of ten thousand acres;
truly, this compassionate heart fully accords with the yearnings of the ten directions.
Beholding his countenance, I find no ground for shame; my aspirations have found their refuge.
For these reasons, this collection is truly intended to extol the holy name.
Thus ends the preface.
Mindfully recollect the Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha.
[Recite] the Great Compassion Mantra as appropriate.
Dedicate the merit of the aforementioned recitations and chanting of scriptures as follows:
On behalf of the Abbot, for the ground of his non-arising recompense, may there be wondrous and ultimate adornment.
[Recite] "The Ten Directions and Three Periods," etc., and once again recite the *Śūraṅgama-mantra*.
The dedication states: "By the merit of chanting this scripture..."
On behalf of the Abbot, may his rank and status be further exalted.
[Recite] "The ten directions and three periods of time... and so forth. That night, assemble the assembly and chant, saying: "I address the great assembly."
The Abbot has already returned to true stillness;
the assembly has lost its reliance.
Simply contemplate impermanence and be careful not to be negligent.
For the aforementioned reasons,
one should bring to mind the pure Dharmakāya Vairocana,
and so forth; the dedication of merit is the same as before.
At the two times [of morning and noon], serve gruel and rice;
at the three times [of morning, noon, and evening], serve tea and soup.
When the assembly recites the sutras, the *karmadāna* (Vina) shall oversee the ritual and perform the dedication of merit as previously described.
In recent times, social customs have become corrupt and degenerate;
monks are unable to find anyone to serve as administrators for the monastic estates,
and some even steal from the permanent property of the Sangha.
The abbot, acting according to public decree, imposed banishment and punishment;
yet the wicked individuals did not reproach themselves for their faults,
but harbored only resentment and hatred.
Upon hearing that he had passed away,
[the king] was as if his heart's desire were fulfilled;
he even went so far as to utter foul words and insults.
They beat upon the coffin and shrine, and by means of spears they seized clothing and belongings, flaunting their cruelty and arrogance.
This included the presiding elders, the venerable monks of various mountains, lay patrons, officials of noble rank, commoners, and fellow students and associates.
You must provide external protection.
Who among men does not face death?
Furthermore, as for the disciples under your guidance, those who offend must certainly be expelled and punished.
If the presiding mourners and officials can beforehand prepare themselves with solemnity and restraint,
causing the deceased to repent and reform early on so that evil is transformed before it has even sprouted,
they will especially preserve the beauty of outward appearance.
The Monk [Name], Director of Funerals at [Name] Temple. Right: It is with great sorrow that the mountain gate has lost its Abbot on the [Day] of the [Month] year [Year].
This memorial statement is submitted by the Monk [Name], Director of Funerals at [Name] Temple.
May it be permitted to leak forth.
Formal Announcement:
To the Abbot Dhyāna Master of [Name] Temple. Respectfully sealed by [Name] of [Rank].
Requested by the Director of Funeral Rites; when the Director of Funeral Rites arrives, strike the great bell.
The assembly gathers to welcome [the guest] at the gate;
upon reaching the front of the shrine, they burn incense, and the Head Seat and the great assembly exchange greetings.
Once the assembly has dispersed, the two orders and the retired elders escort the guest to the guest seat.
Incense is offered and prostrations are performed.
The presiding mourner occupies the principal seat.
The head seat monk takes his place at the side seat and rises respectfully to burn incense.
Returning to their positions, they offer tea.
The junior attendants then line up in front, insert incense,
and perform three full prostrations with the robes fully spread.
The administrative officials of the abbot’s quarters and the head attendant, leading the assembly of attendants,
enter in succession to offer incense and perform prostrations;
thereafter, the abbot’s servants enter to pay their respects, after which the hot water offering is presented.
The two orders are sent out;
the administrative office prepares refreshments.
The two orders escort one another in succession as they tour the various quarters.
Generally, those presiding over a funeral must be elderly and possessed of established virtue.
For example, when Yuanwu presided over the funeral for Master Kaifu Ning,
he received Yue’an Guo as his successor to inherit his Dharma.
This may serve as a standard model.
The officials of the funeral office are requested to take charge; the presiding mourner shall inspect the quarters and conclude the proceedings.
The members of the two orders, the retired elders, and the junior disciples shall follow him to their guest quarters.
Present the robe-and-bowl register, posthumous writings, and other items.

Serve tea and deliberate upon the appointment of the office-holders for the funeral administration: the secretary, the *karmadāna* (vinaya-master), the guest prefect, the attendant to the portrait, and the attendant to the abbot, as well as the sequence for all Buddhist services; these shall be discussed and appointed in order as follows.
With the exception of the two ritual services for lifting the wailing and the small-scale *sǎn* (private sermon), these are performed by the presiding mourner.
The gradations of mourning attire are detailed below; if cloth or silk are unavailable, [the following may be used].
The money should be distributed according to what is appropriate.
The presiding mourner must consult with the head seat regarding the quantity of the deceased’s robes and bowl,
and silently divide them into three parts.
One portion shall be used for expenses related to the mourning rites, such as the cost of ritual garments, the chanting of scriptures, and lamps and candles;
one portion shall be returned to the permanent endowment (sangzhuang) to supplement the offerings.
One portion shall be distributed to the assembly for the purpose of reading scriptures, performing Buddhist rites, and providing board and lodging.
The presiding mourner must maintain impartiality and integrity.
One must not yield to private interests.
Attendant monks are not permitted to interfere in administrative duties.
Each day, they shall recite scriptures, distribute offerings, and present tea and soup.
Regardless of their status within the two orders,
let each group appoint one person from among the diligent seniors to manage the finances;
this will serve to eliminate idle gossip.
The attendant of the Venerable Monk shall take charge of the funeral curtains and the office of the funeral director.
He shall dispatch the storekeeper, the guest master, the tea master,
and their respective staff to manage the affairs of the service.
Please consult with the incumbent *vina* (rector) to deliberate on this matter.
The incumbent *karmadāna* (guest master) shall receive external guests,
while the funeral office shall coordinate with the thousand servants.

The roster is displayed as follows: For the mourner’s attire: - The Director of Rites and the attendant junior disciples wear robes of hempen cloth (*mábù duì*). - The two orders of officials and the presiding mourners and their honored kinsmen wear robes of ramie cloth (*zhǔfù duì*). - The veteran administrators and local lay associates and kinsmen wear robes of raw silk (*shēngbù duì*). - The donors wear turbans and waistbands of raw silk. - The attendants of the Abbot wear turbans and robes of hempen cloth. - The general attendants wear turbans of ramie cloth. - The personal servants of the Abbot, the head laborers, the estate managers, and the various servants wear turbans and shirts of hempen cloth.

Buddhist rites: entering the shrine, moving the shrine, securing the shrine, hanging the portrait in the Dharma Hall, wailing, offering tea and soup, the small *sīmān* (sermon) before the spirit, offering tea and soup, raising the shrine, hanging the portrait at the gatehouse of the mountain monastery, offering tea and soup, raising the shrine, taking up the robes, exhuming the bones for entry into the stupa, entry into the Patriarchs’ Hall, enshrinement of the whole body in the stupa, and the scattering of earth; if the offerings of robes and bowls are abundant, [the rites are performed accordingly].
Every day, tea and soup are offered as libations.
Ritual services such as the shifting of the shrine and the turning of the bones are performed.
The shrine is moved, and after three days of moving it into the coffin, the coffin is closed.
Arrange the upper section of the Dharma Hall by hanging curtains and screens,
setting out beds, seats, and clothing racks,
and displaying all necessary implements and utensils.
Following the ritual procedures for the deceased:
hang the portrait on the Dharma seat in the interim and install the name tablet.
The sacrificial banquet was laid out extensively,
using raw silk for curtains and screens to prepare for the superior sacrifice.
In the lower section, niches are established and draped with curtains of hemp cloth.
In front, tables and stands are arranged, along with incense burners, vases, and plain flowers.
Incense and candles were kept burning without interruption.
At the two designated times, tea, soup, congee, and rice were offered;
while the sutras were chanted as an act of worship, peach-shaped lamps, ritual bells, cymbals, flowers, and banners were also prepared.
The bell of the Sangha Hall is struck;
the assembly gathers for the ritual of moving the coffin.
The ritual of moving the coffin concludes.
The ritual for requesting the locking of the shrine (suikankan) is performed in the lower Dharma Hall.

The true likeness (shōjin) is hung, laments are raised, tea and soup are offered, the true likeness is hung, laments are raised, tea and soup are offered, and the shrine is moved to the Dharma Hall where it is locked.
When the hanging of the portrait of the True Buddha is completed,
if there is a written testament in the Master's own hand,

The person presiding over the funeral reception personally receives the document presented and hands it to the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera).
He incenses it over the incense burner and then hands it to the Rector (Karmadāna) to read aloud.
