Three sounds of wailing were raised,
and the entire assembly wept together;
the junior disciples stood beneath the curtain, sobbing in grief.
The ritual for offering tea and soup to the funeral cakes is performed.
The junior disciples prostrate before the portraits and retire beneath the curtain.
The presiding mourner burns incense and pays homage to the portraits.
The two orders of officials, the retired elders, and the assembly of monks burn incense in succession and pay homage to the portrait [of the deceased].
The junior disciples respond with a bow to the left of the portrait.
The presiding mourners receive condolences from beneath their mourning tent.
The junior attendant follows by performing three prostrations to the presiding mourners.
Next, he consoles the assembly of the two orders, saying: "It is a misfortune for the Dharma gate that the Venerable Abbot has suddenly withdrawn his transformative authority."

"I venture to hope that the assembly will exert its strength to maintain the affairs of the future. The Head Seat replied, "We still rely on the power of the Master to grant his guidance. The two orders and the assembly then comforted the junior monk, saying, "It is an unfortunate misfortune for the mountain gate that the Master has passed away."

On the first day of the month, the fourteenth, and other festival days, one should observe mourning to conclude the major rites; meanwhile, the junior masters shall guard the shrine curtains at night.
The director of funeral affairs shall arrange the order of the offerings, which will be displayed after the main hall and beneath the curtain of the lower section.
All sacrificial texts for mourning rites are composed by the record-keeper (shuji) of the mourning office.
Offerings are made daily, either twice or three times;
there is no fixed restriction regarding the timing of these offerings.
Generally, as donors from various mountains arrive at different times,
if a member of the Dharma family or a disciple comes to offer incense at the gate,
the guest prefect shall receive them and immediately notify the office in charge of funeral affairs.
The mourning garments shall be escorted [to the funeral] accordingly;
thereafter, all offerings and funeral gifts presented at the memorial service shall be used for the remaining expenses,
which must be returned to the permanent endowment of the monastery.
He provided compensation for the expenses of the various mountain-dwelling practitioners.
The funeral director gathered the two orders and the retired elders to deliberate on the matter of copying the inventory of robes and bowls.
In addition to what is left over from the bequest,
the prices of new and old items, as well as their lengths and quality,
shall be appraised so that there may be no confusion or disorder when the robes are auctioned at the last moment.

For the small-scale *xinsan* (private sermon), the offering of tea and soup, the recitation, and the memorial service before the spirit: the *sangsi* (funeral director) and the *weina* (chant master), together with the junior monks, carry incense and proceed to the guest seat to invite the presiding mourner.
For the evening memorial service for the deceased,
prepare the seats for the small formal address (*xiao can*).
Wait for the dusk bell to sound, then strike the drum to assemble the assembly.
The members of the two orders inquire after one another’s well-being according to the usual custom; the chief mourner wears his sash and the attendant burns incense.
If there is no such attendant, the attendant of the Sacred Monk (Śālistamba) acts in his stead. This concludes the informal discourse (hsiao-ts'an).
Upon descending from the seat:
The junior disciples prostrated themselves in succession to offer their thanks.
The Head Seat led the assembly to stand before the shrine, where they offered incense and took their places.
After the ritual for offering tea and soup is completed, the *weina* of the mountain gate recites the following to address the assembly:
"The Head Monk has entered parinirvāṇa.
This day having passed, his life-force has likewise diminished."
Like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be?
You all should exert yourselves with diligence as if your heads or clothing were on fire;
keep only impermanence in mind and be careful not to be negligent.
With reverent decorum, the assembly solemnly proceeded to the curtained shrine;
there they chanted the great names of the myriad virtues,
offering this service to exalt the deceased’s spiritual rank.
We look up with reliance upon the Great Assembly to recite for the Pure Dharma-body Vairocana Buddha...
[and so forth]. Having completed the recitation of the Great Compassion Mantra, the dedication is as follows:
"By the merit of the aforementioned chanting and recitation of the sutras..."
On behalf of the newly deceased Head Monk,
we humbly pray that you do not forget your vow-power to once again manifest as a *tánhuā* (rare flower),
and that you may steer the compassionate vessel across the surging waves of birth and death.
To lead all deluded beings to the other shore of Bodhi,
we again trouble the great assembly to recite the names of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Having finished speaking thus, the guest prefect of the mountain gate recited the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī,
stating that the merit of this chanting of the sutra is offered for the newly deceased Abbot, so that his rank may be further exalted during the great night.

"Throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, all [beings]... and so forth. Next, perform the offerings one by one in sequence; at the conclusion, recite the Great Compassion Mantra and dedicate the merit as performed previously. The attendant bows in prostration, and after the sutra recitation is finished.
The funeral director calls out: "Please, the Head Seat and the assembly take their seats. After the distribution of soup and fruit, the assembly disperses.
The junior disciples, the attendants of the Abbot's quarters, and the servants shall guard the spirit-tablet throughout the night.

Regarding the sequence of offerings: first the administrative officers (*zhishi*), then the heads of departments (*toushou*), the presiding mourner, the West Hall monks, the retired elders (*qinjiu*), those from the *mengtang*, fellow travelers from various regions (*jianghu*), former patrons, senior monks, the various quarters, the office staff, the former attendants, local laypeople, Dharma relatives, those at various hermitages and stupas, the junior disciples, the Abbot’s grandsons, the Abbot himself, the novices, the six departmental novices, the hall attendants, the Abbot’s personal servants, the sedan-chair carriers, the temple laborers (*laolang*), the estate guards, the fire-keepers, the construction bureau, and the various craftsmen.
Regarding the funeral procession, the hanging of the portrait, the offerings, and the serving of tea and soup: these matters pertain to the Storehouse Office (Kūji) and the Funeral Office (Sōji).
They shall supervise the funeral rites, including the incense stand, the portrait pavilion, the ceremonial banners, and the chanting music.
Before the niche are the ceremonial umbrella and chair;
the soup stove and the lamp are lit;
the bamboo rake, the master’s staff, and the whisk are present.
The incense box, Dharma robes,
and other items are followed by the junior disciple behind the coffin;
the great bell and various ritual implements are sounded to escort the funeral procession.
As the coffin was raised for the recitation, it is said:
"The golden coffin rose of its own accord, circling the great city of Kuśinagara;
banners and streamers swayed through the void."
I attend this grand ceremony of cremation;
I rely upon the great assembly to invoke the Great Name with reverence.
I hereby express my contrition and repentance.
May this serve to support the path to enlightenment.
I take refuge in the Vairocana Buddha of the Pure Dharmakāya, and so forth.
If the entire body is to be enshrined in the stupa, it is said:

"This is the magnificent rite of Guanding. The *sangsī* (funeral director) and *weina* (ritual master) advance to offer incense and lead the junior disciples to perform prostrations and make their request.
The rite for raising the shrine begins.
When the shrine reaches the entrance of the mountain gate,
the portrait is invited to the offering pavilion, where the true likeness is hung and tea and soup are offered.
The Buddha-work is performed by all together.
Once the two orders of the assembly have lined up at the gate awaiting the emergence of the reliquary shrine (*kaṅ*),
the *vina* of the mountain gate stands facing inward with palms joined.
Recite the mantra for rebirth in the Pure Land,
or the names of the Four Holy Ones;
let the entire assembly recite them together in unison.
The presiding mourner leads the assembly;
they divide into pairs and disperse to the left and right to scatter snow-white willow branches.
Walk in step together;
do not shoulder-to-shoulder or converse with one another.
Each should harbor a sense of sorrow and reverence.

The *dutsi* (abbatial steward) oversees the funeral procession; the *sōji* (funeral director), *vinaya*, *chikaku* (guest master), *shōsō* (holy monk), and *jissha* (attendant) distribute the funeral offerings (*sōjin*).
When the cremation reaches the *nehan-dai* (Nirvana platform), the *sōji* and *vinaya* wait for the *dutsi* to complete the offering of incense.
Stepping forward to offer incense, he leads the junior monk in performing the ritual for requesting the torch-bearer.
The *vinaya* master of the monastery recites: "On this day, there is one who has newly passed into nirvana."
The Abbot, having completed his rounds for alms, suddenly returned to the state of true permanence.
His sacred coffin was encircled by those from Kuśinagara;
on this very day, the fire of his nature spontaneously consumed him.
I look up in reliance upon the Great Assembly to assist and sustain my awakening spirit.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, who is of great kindness and great compassion.
The ten recitations have been completed with the assembly in harmony.
Thus far, we have invoked the sacred names and respectfully praised the transformative rites,
embodying the principles of the ancient patriarchs.
His sublime faculties were such that not even the Buddhas or patriarchs could contain them;
he employed these to open the way for future students.
Yet his compassionate heart continued to gather in all beings, from humans and devas alike.
Gathering the hundred skeletal members of this illusory transformation,
he enters the samādhi of the fire-light.
As the tea is poured, three libations are offered.
Incense is burned in a censer.
With heads bowed in reverence, one prostrates to the assembly of holy ones and recites the Great Compassion Mantra.
The dedication of merit is made as follows: "By the merit of the aforementioned chanting and recitation of the sutra..."
On behalf of the Abbot, for the purpose of augmenting his spiritual rank through cremation,
the Cloud-Mountain Attendants and Guest Masters of the ten directions and three periods of time recite the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī.
The dedication of merit is the same as before.
Next, a local person recites the sutra,
and when the entire assembly has finished chanting it together, [the ritual concludes].
The Head Seat leads the assembly back to the monastery to attend the midday meal; meanwhile,
the junior monks, fellow countrymen, and Dharma relatives maintain the funeral rites and collect the remains.
After the meal, the Sangha hall bell is struck to assemble the community;
the remains are then escorted with full ceremonial retinue back to the dormitory hall for enshrinement.
Perform the ritual for the enshrinement of the remains;
hang up the portrait for offerings and recite the sutras;
provide gruel and meals twice daily.
Tea and soup are offered three times [daily];
or for ten days or half a month;
this ceases once the assembly has chanted the sutras and the sacred remains have been enshrined in the stupa.
When the entire body has been placed into the burial chamber within the stupa and arrived at the site,
the head monk (du-si) completes the offering of incense and tea; then,
the ritual master (wei-na) of the funeral office proceeds to offer burning incense.
After the ritual for leading the junior monk to pay homage and request entry into the stupa is completed,
the *vinaya-dhara* (Weina) of the mountain gate recites the invocation:
"It is said that the manifestation of the twin lotus feet..."
He followed the legacy of Vulture Peak,
manifesting the Patriarchal Lineage with his single sandal;
he exemplified the teachings of Shaolin, establishing a model for posterity.
The entire mechanism of manifestation and concealment encompasses the beginning and end of the sublime Dharma.
We look up to the great assembly for support to assist our awakening spirit.
*Namo* to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful.
The ten recitations are concluded.
Thus far, we have extolled the ten recitations as an aid for rebirth in the Pure Land.
We only pray:
With a mirror of wisdom that is boundless and clouds of compassion that spread far and wide,
you manifest within the realms of the four modes of birth the cause of neither arising nor ceasing.
Within the paths of the six realms of existence,
the Dharma of no-self and no-person is proclaimed.
Tea is poured for three libations.
Burn a single incense burner.
With palms joined in reverence, pay homage to the assembly of noble ones. The sequence for raising the scripture and chanting it is identical to that of the Nirvāṇa Altar.
However, regarding the dedication of merit, it is said that following the entry into the stupa, once all preparations for the closing of the grave pit are complete,
one then requests the ritual for scattering earth.
The remains are welcomed back to the dormitory hall for offerings.
The presiding mourner offers incense and pays homage to the portrait.
Next, after the assembly of the two orders from all the mountains and the junior disciples have finished paying homage to the portrait,
the junior disciples insert incense and perform three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*).
The Master of Mourning (zhūsāng) receives thanks.
Next, the two orders of the assembly offer words of thanks to the Master of Mourning, saying: "It is a great misfortune for this mountain gate that the late Abbot has passed away.

We are deeply grateful that you have presided over the funeral arrangements. The Master of Mourning replies: "I am humbly grateful for your support, which has ensured that no neglect or failure occurred. The Master of Mourning then joins with the entire staff of the mourning office.
He tours the quarters to express his gratitude.
Next, the junior disciples tour the quarters to pay their respects.
The Monastery’s *weina* escorts the incumbent *shizhe*, the *shizhen shizhe*, and others.
Return to the communal quarters.
Each day, at the three appointed times, tea and soup are served and the assembly gathers to chant scriptures;
this ceases once the ancestral tablets have been welcomed into the Patriarchs' Hall.
Alternatively, one may wait until the new abbot arrives before entering the Patriarchs’ Hall for the ritual proceedings.
Regarding the auctioning of robes: when the appointed time arrives, [the officiant] stands before the Sangha Hall.
Alternatively, seating for the assembly may be arranged on the upper and lower levels of the Dharma Hall;
in the center, facing inward, long tables are set up with brushes,
inkstones, and large sounding-stones placed upon them.
The monastery bell is struck to assemble the community;
the Head Seat and the presiding mourner take their respective places,
and the assembly of the two orders sits down in succession.
The Director of Rites, the *vinaya-dhara*, the Guest Master, the Holy Monk, and the Attendant sit facing the position of the presiding mourner.
The *vinaya-dhara* recites: "Leaving behind garments as a token of faith is the established rule of our successive patriarchs."
Using the Dharma to overcome stinginess,
he followed the inherited models of his predecessors;
now, this auction is held to manifest impermanence.
Relying upon the assembly’s recitation:
"Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha," and so forth.
Having finished, open the cage and take out the robe and bowl.
Arrange the seats according to the designated titles.
Once the ritual for requesting the robe has concluded,
the rector strikes the chime once.
The method for assisting in the chanting of the *kāṣāya* by those in white robes follows established regulations.
One must take care regarding the length of the robe, whether it be new or old.
Once the sound of the *qing* bell has ceased, one may not express regret.
I respectfully submit that if there are many Dharma robes, they should be added to the legacy and left behind.
The robes are then presented in succession.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) shall draw them forth and announce them; it is essential that the funeral administrators and all concerned parties act with a public spirit.
The *vinaya-dhara* strikes the *kṣaṇḍa* gong to announce the fixed prices;
the attendants look before and behind and chant the designated names.
The guest master writes the names on the list;
the attendant issues the tickets according to those names.
Once the distribution of robes is completed:
The tally for the number of mortuary notes shall be settled by the presiding mourner.
When exchanging notes to receive robes, one must not yield to private interests or reduce the price;
the presiding mourner shall take primary responsibility for these matters.
Nowadays, the practice of drawing lots (*jiūniān*) is widely adopted as it greatly suppresses clamor and contention.
Its method is as follows: small slips of paper are used, upon which characters from the *Qianziwen* (Thousand-Character Classic) are written in their sequential order to serve as lot numbers.
Each number shall consist of three sections.
Once written above, they must be sealed with the official seal. The quantity shall be determined according to the size of the assembly.
The funeral director and relevant officials shall seal and secure [the offerings].
When the appointed time arrives, they present them to the presiding mourner.
The head seat of the two orders breaks the seal, and the guest prefect distributes the portions; the hall administrators' attendants hold the trays and follow the serving monks.
The attendant cuts off half of it,
places it in a tray,
and sets the tray down beside the head seat.
Place the water basin below and shake out the ladle.
Once the Rector (Vina) has finished picking up the robe and announcing its price,
the Head Seat (Shouzuo) shall, as the occasion demands, call for a novice monk (Dongxing).
Reaching out his hand, he picked up half a bundle of lots from the tray and handed them to the Head Seat;
the latter opened them to see that the characters on the numbers were clearly legible.
The announcer tells the attendant of the hall office to call out a specific number;
everyone then opens the half-stick of incense they are holding.
If the name is the same, one should respond;
if one does not wish to chant for this [lot] of clothing and requisites, one should not respond.
One should not respond after three chants.
The head seat throws half a handful of incense into the water basin;
he then orders another half-handful to be picked up,
and once again calls for it to be raised.
The attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi) shall go to collect the half-numbered tickets.
Upon arriving at the Head Seat’s (Shouzuo) quarters, he shall verify them against the list and report them to the Rector (Weina), saying: [Insert name].
"Item X is assigned to Person Y.
Ring the chime once.
The Guest Master ascends the register.
The attendant raises the signal flag.
The ritual leader (gòngtóu) passes the items to the one who has been designated by the chant.
The clothing and belongings remain in their baskets as before, and the chanting proceeds in order until it is finished.
The rector strikes the chime once.
For the dedication of merit, he says: "The merit from the chanting and recitation for the distribution of robes is hereby dedicated to increase the rank and station of the late Abbot of the Hall."
The assembly from the ten directions and throughout the three periods of time disperses; each person examines the value, takes the marker, and receives the robe.
After three days, those who have not taken their robes shall be sold at the appraised price, and a ledger shall be prepared.

Single-Form Version. The Venerable Shangtou has passed away; I respectfully present these robes and articles.

The various officers who handled the accounts, the members of the two orders, and the directors of the funeral rites shall each write their names and affix their seals. Regarding the enshrinement of the remains in the stupa: on the eve of the appointed date, the ceremonial processions and equipment must be prepared.
On the appointed day, the bell is struck and the assembly gathers.

How tragic! What hope can I have?

The aforementioned [monks] exit from the front row of the holy monks and stand in line.
They perform three full prostrations.
The Rector leads them on a circuit around the hall once.
Returning to the center, he bows to inquire after the master’s health.
He then steps back across the hall and stands at the head of the western section of the platform.

The attendant of the Hall Office calls out: "The assembly shall offer a collective prostration to congratulate the newly appointed administrative official. Once this single prostration is completed, [the ceremony concludes].
Again, he calls out: "The new administrator bows in thanks to the assembly; all perform a single prostration with the forehead touching the ground. Once this is finished, he calls out again:
"The assembly shall escort the new administrator back to the Kusi (Storehouse Office). The attendant in charge of the storehouse and the practitioners strike the bell for the Sangha Hall.
The abbot escorts [the new official] inside, and they perform one prostration with full prostration (dual-prostration).
The abbot escorts the new official out,
and he takes over the duties from the former incumbent.
Turning toward one another face-to-face,
they perform a single prostration with full-body contact,
then escort the departing person out.
The attendant offers congratulations first.
Next, the head official leads the assembly in their congratulations.

Once this is finished, the ritual assistant shouts, "The assembly shall escort the new Head Seat to his quarters! Then the bell is struck again to conclude the ceremony of sending off the congratulations.
He shouts, "The assembly shall escort the new *vinaya-master* back to the hall! Then, the bell is struck again to signal the conclusion of the congratulations.

He then calls out to each one in turn: "The two classes of officers and the retired elders shall escort the new *first seat* of the rear hall, the *secretary*, the *repository master*, and the *guest prefect* to their respective quarters to offer congratulations. The ritual for the handover of duties is identical to that which preceded.

Again, each person calls out, "The assembly shall escort the former Head Seat and the former Chief Administrator (Dusi) to their quarters," and the bell is struck once more to conclude the congratulations.

Each person calls out again, "The two classes of senior monks shall escort the successive former head officials and administrators to the Former Qualities Hall (Mongtang)," and the ritual for the former patrons is the same as before.
Escort the abbot out.
The head of the quarters (liao-zhu) first receives him;
they turn to face one another.
They prostrate once in greeting,
but do not escort [the guests] out.
Thereafter, when the congratulations have all been completed, both the new and the old members each carry incense in their sleeves.
He immediately proceeds to the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects and offer thanks.
The new monk prepares incense at the administrative office (kusi) to express gratitude;
once this is completed, the new and senior monks together tour the monastic quarters. The abbot then invites them for a midday meal and refreshments.
During the midday meal, he should still invite the West Hall Abbot and the retired elders to accompany him;
once the various duties for the ranked officials have been completed,
he shall visit the Hall Office on another day to announce his retirement.
The selection of personnel for rotation proceeds in successive order.

When hanging the alms bowl, the administrative officer (kaji) is requested to hang it; however, there are instances where the abbot does not first consult with others but silently selects the person and determines the arrangement.
The attendant of the Hall Office (dangsi) shall assign the ritual procedures for the monks' hall:
at the time of hanging the alms bowls after the morning gruel has been finished.
The Master shouts, "Assembly, stand for a moment! I request the newly appointed Karmadāna to enter before the Holy Sangha, burn incense, and circumambulate the hall once.
Upon reaching the position of the Abbot, he shall inquire after his well-being and stand to one side."
The abbot hands over the list of names of those invited;
having received it, he performs a formal greeting face-to-face and then turns behind the Sacred Monk (Sengsheng).
Striking the mallet once, he says: "I inform the assembly.

I have just received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, requesting that such-and-such a person be appointed to serve as the administrative official [for such-and-such a duty]. Having reported each point in full, I now conclude."
The attendant bows and invites the new appointee before the abbot to receive his office;
the ritual is the same as previously described.
It is said: "The Abbot’s quarters serves tea."
Request the head officers to perform their prostrations as before.

The attendants advance and retreat; once the request for the two orders of officials is completed, the former attendants follow the abbot to the Venerable’s Quarters (fangzhang) and report, saying: "We, such-and-such, have long served the Master."
I now wish to request leave to follow the assembly in cultivating the Way.
I humbly beseech your compassion to accept this incense offering and perform three prostrations with full prostration cloths before departing.
The Abbot shall issue an order to the Hall Administration.
Request new attendants.
The *vinaya-dhara* shall instruct the *karmadāna* to issue the official notices for their recruitment;
furthermore, he shall request the head of the quarters (*lao-yuan*) to extend formal invitations.
Together they proceed to the hall; the attendant bows as they enter.
Having finished burning incense and serving tea, they rise and burn incense once more.
Entering, he says: "I have just received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, instructing me to invite Venerable So-and-so to serve as the attendant for such-and-such a period.
Having reported this point by point, he bows to the person being invited.
The officiant steps forward, makes a full prostration touching the ground, and shifts his position.
The *weina* performs the ritual bows, bows to invite [the assembly] to be seated, bows to offer incense, and returns to his seat.
Once the offering of hot water is completed.
He was led to the Abbot’s quarters.
The Abbot came out, and the Rector stepped forward to address him, saying: "I have just received your compassionate instructions."
Having requested a certain person to serve as the attendant for a specific office,
the new attendant now leads the way in offering incense and prostrating before the Abbot, who takes his seat.
Once the new attendant has inserted the incense and performed three full prostrations with wide-spread sitting cloths (*kṣepa*), the ceremony concludes.
The *vinaya-dhara* escorts [the guest] back to his quarters.
[The guest] performs one prostration with unclean hands (*asauca-vandana*).
The attendant (*upasthāyaka*) escorts him out.
The protocol for handing over duties to the former incumbent is the same as the formal greeting; this is recorded in the *Xianchun Gui*.

There is also the practice where the abbot personally escorts the attendant back to his quarters, at which time the attendant should perform a prostration with full prostration (*chuli*) and see him out.
Upon reaching the Great Regulations (Da-gui-zai),
if the person is a man of renown and virtue,
the Abbot shall personally escort him into his quarters.
Perform a single prostration with full contact (touching the ground).
The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) merely offers congratulations.
Do not treat this as a routine matter; the attendants of the Abbot’s quarters shall proceed directly to the hall, and the sedan-chair carriers shall offer their greetings.
The hall attendant (tángsī xíngzhě) leads the new and former attendants together on their tour of the quarters. Once this is completed,
the new attendant again visits the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and pay his respects.
The former attendant shall attend upon the abbot morning and evening, just as a new attendant would,
during the formal inquiries (*wenshen*).
After three days, the abbot issues an order, and the Hall Administration (*tangsi*) shall escort him back to the communal quarters (*zhongliao*).
Exchange a prostration with the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual leader) and escort him out.
Next, after completing the formal salutation with the head of the quarters (*liao-yuan*), [proceed as follows].
He then proceeded to the Abbot’s quarters,
where he lit incense and offered his thanks;
the attendant for the Holy Monk was the Rector (Vina).
He selected harmonious individuals to fill the positions.
Afterwards, they were led to the Abbot’s quarters (shangfang) to pay their respects;
there, they were provided with tea, soup, and refreshments according to custom.
Regarding the handover of furniture and utensils for the quarters: it is not easy for the monastery’s permanent administration to provide and maintain the furnishings for these quarters.
Often, those in office treat them as mere temporary lodgings.
At the time of their departure,
the local residents each moved their belongings away until the place was completely empty,
leaving the newly admitted residents utterly bewildered and at a loss as to what to do.
He could not help but provide a list of items;
however, when he went to the treasury office to request them, they were not forthcoming.
Consequently, the officials, both high and low, were left in a state of unease and conflict.
If it becomes necessary to provide for heavy expenses from the permanent endowment,
the administrative office (kusi) shall maintain a general ledger,
recording in detail all the utensils and equipment belonging to the various quarters.
The abbot and the administrative officers shall collectively determine [the assignments],
and furthermore, small ledgers shall be distributed to each of the quarters so that both sets correspond exactly.
The new and old shall hand over their duties according to established custom.
Damaged items shall be repaired by the public treasury;
missing items shall be compensated for by the resident monks of that hall. This shall serve as the standard for advancement or dismissal.
A few days ago, the Vice Abbot, accompanied by an attendant,
brought the registers to each of the quarters to conduct a preliminary and thorough headcount.
The responsibility lies with the attendants and servants of this residence;
they must not allow [the property] to be lost or stolen.
Any who violate this shall provide compensation.
If there are any additions or increases in the number of items,
they shall immediately be appended to the register so that they may be examined and verified.

The Abbot specially prepares a soup for the new and old members of both orders; the Guest Attendant is then instructed to have the guest-head acolytes prepare trays, cloths, incense burners, and candles.
Go to the head seat’s quarters in the front hall of the new and old sections.
Light incense and perform one prostration with full touching of the ground.

Address him, saying: "The Abbot requests that you attend the pre-meal session; please proceed to the meditation hall to receive the tea offering. Next, go before the new and old administrative officers (dusi) and light incense, but do not prostrate.
The wording is the same as before.
Following the sequence of the new and old orders,
let the guest master (kètóu) issue the invitations.
Furthermore, please invite the veteran attendants to accompany you in hanging the portraits in the dormitory hall and arranging the seating;
the attendants shall then divide their duties.
First, the new head official (śreṣṭhin) emerges;
second, the new administrative officer (vaiyāvṛtyakara) emerges;
third, the former head official emerges.
The four former administrators departed;
the remaining veteran attendants who were invited to join the retinue lined up on both sides of the principal and his companions.
Those from the western corridor sit on the left;
those from the eastern corridor sit on the right.
The incense-burning attendant prepares the name tablets in advance.
When the time arrives, the drum is struck.

The guests assemble, and the attendant for receiving guests performs the rites. The procedures for the small seat, the hot water, and the evening soup and fruit are the same. On the following day, after the morning gruel has been consumed, the new and old members are invited for tea.
The administrative office also invited him for tea,
but he was unable to attend.
He did attend the tea ceremony at the Abbot’s quarters after it had concluded.
He then went to offer his thanks.
He continued to oversee the distribution of the midday meal and refreshments from the storehouse,
and provided three days of rice gruel and meals for those departing.
The Hall Attendant specially prepares tea and soup for the new and former attendants. Once the grass-rice meal is finished, the Rector orders the Hall Attendant’s acolytes.
Request the new and former attendants,
as well as the attendant for the Holy Monk,
to come to the quarters before the morning assembly to offer hot water.
The Hall Attendant prepares the seats and arranges the name tablets;
he invites the Head of the Quarters (Liaoyuan) and his attendants, and strikes the board in front of the quarters.

The procedure for entering and performing the ritual of bowing while seated is the same as that for the administrative office (kusi); it should take place prior to the special soup service for the abbot.
This ensures that the performance of the ritual is not obstructed.
One should wait until the abbot has finished the special tea service for the new head seat (shouzuo).
The Hall Office shall also request the new and old attendants to prepare tea specifically for them;
on the following day, they shall present their thanks in person.

The Kitchen Office shall specially provide soup and medicine for both the new and old orders, and the Stone Storehouse shall specially provide medicinal herbs and rice for the new and old orders. Once these have been concluded, [the ceremony ends].
Instruct the guest master (kakutō) and attendants to prepare trays, cloths, incense burners, and candles.

The senior administrator (shushu chishi) shall proceed to the quarters of the new and former head seats (shuso) and the former chief temple administrator (jūdoshi), offer incense, and speak these words:
"This evening, following the tea service in the Abbot’s quarters (hōjō)," and so forth.
The storehouse office shall specially prepare the hot tonic for this offering.

We humbly request that you grant your presence; the guest master shall follow to invite [the Abbot] to sit after the tonic has been consumed, and to invite both the new and former, great and small officials, to partake of the medicinal food.
He further requested the West Hall and the veteran monks to assist in setting up the seats and arranging the name tablets;
the seating was divided into four sections.
First, the new head official;
second, the former head official;
third, the former administrative officer.
The four exits from the treasury hall are opened;
the newly appointed administrator also takes his seat according to the order of rank,
while the *weina* (rector) alone sits facing the assembly.
The attendants of the Radiance Hall shall follow the order of the seats in the Abbot’s quarters.
Once the Abbot has finished his tea,
the storehouse office shall strike the board.
Each person takes their seat according to the seating chart.
Once the Abbot has completed the circuit of the seats and the ritual bowing,
he burns incense and bows before the incense burner.
Rising from one's seat, one goes out to perform the ritual greeting by circling and bowing.
Returning to the center, one burns incense in a lighted tray and returns to one's seat.
When the soup service is finished, one rises and departs.
Having finished offering thanks for the medicinal broth at the incense burner, he changes his robes and takes his seat for the medicinal meal.

The Hall Attendant (Tangsi) sends the bowls of the former Head Seat and the former Chief Administrator (Du-si) to their respective positions; the Rector (Weina) then proceeds with the two orders of monks for three days after the retreat.
Before the period of silence has ended,
entrust the hall office attendants with the task of leading the laborers to extinguish the lamps.
The former Head Seat and the Chief Administrator are invited to the Hall office to offer hot water;
the Rector receives them inside.
After the incense has been burned and the tea finished, [the abbot] says:
"As your term as Head of the Pure Office (qingzhi) has concluded, it is appropriate for you to pay your respects at the Mountain Gate.
He then escorts him to the position of the alms bowl and leads him to the Sangha Hall.
Entering through the rear gate,
first escort the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) and then escort the Chief Administrator (Karmadāna) back to their respective quarters.
Each person performs a prostration of touching the ground.
On that day, the bowl is hung and one proceeds to the hall.
The Abbot provides hospitality for both the new and old members of the two orders; the Abbot specifically ascends the hall for this occasion, calling each person by name.
Having finished the expressions of gratitude,
the new and old members take their seats and bow in thanks.
The attendant in charge of guests then instructs the guest-head acolytes.
Prepare a tray, a cloth, an incense burner, candles, and an incense case.
Proceed before the new and former head seats and the chief administrative officer (dusi), burn incense, and make the formal request, saying:

"The Abbot of the Vihara requests that you attend the midday reception in the dormitory hall. The guest master shall then invite the successive new and former officials, as well as the long-standing veterans (qinjiu).
The attendant of the light sets up the seats in the sleeping hall and arranges the name tablets.
When the guests have assembled, he reports to the abbot, who goes out to receive them; they each take their seats according to the tablets.
Having taken their seats in formal meditation, the incense is burned.
The attendant and the guest-inviting attendant perform a circuit of bows; once the seating is complete, the incense is offered and the table is advanced.
The assembly of attendants stands before the abbot to perform inquiries of courtesy and takes their places.
After the serving of hot water and the distribution of food are completed,
incense is burned at the time of serving rice.
The attendant leaves his position to burn incense.
After the distribution of offerings and the serving of rice is completed, the lectern is withdrawn.

The drum is struck to signal the tea ceremony; this is identical to the procedure for the special tea service (*tekwei tang*). The drum is struck three times, and the assembly withdraws from their seats.
The new and former officers both perform three prostrations with open hands to express their thanks.
The Abbot specially serves tea for the new Head Seat; having thus provided special hospitality with tea for the new Head Seat, the ceremony concludes.
The following morning, the incense-burning attendant informs the abbot,
who instructs the guest-head acolyte to prepare a tray, a cloth cover, an incense burner, candles, and an incense case.
The invitation-issuing attendant writes out the tea notice (as shown previously), and together with the Head Seat of Renown and Virtue, they proceed to the Head Seat’s quarters.
Light incense, perform one prostration with full prostration, and announce:
"The Abbot has finished his midday meal;
he is now in the Cloud Hall specifically to receive tea."

We humbly request that the guest master be dispatched to announce the assembly and the tea signboard be hung; furthermore, we invite the administrative officers and the great assembly to attend as honored companions.
The attendant shall perform the rites, which are identical to those performed specifically for the four seasonal festivals.
Only the four ends of the board-heads do not hold incense burners.
Once the ritual of circulating the hall to request tea is concluded,
the cups of the Head Seat and the Abbot are collected first.
The Head Seat (Shouzuo) proceeds directly to the abbot and performs a prostration.
Upon the first unfolding of the ceremonial cloth, he says: "On this day, we have been specially honored by your hospitality; your courtesy has been most diligent.
Your subordinate feels a sense of shame and gratitude beyond measure. He unfolds the cloth a second time, and after concluding with inquiries regarding health and well-being, the ceremony ends.
He performs three prostrations with full prostration.
The Head Seat exits from behind the Holy Monk to the right and stands before the hall.
The Abbot escorts him back to his position and takes up the cup.
The attendant burns the incense sticks until they are consumed, then collects the bowls.
The drum is struck three times, and the assembly withdraws from their seats.
The head seat remains in the lower section of the Dharma Hall.
The Abbot waits to offer the tea of thanks.

The new Head Seat specially prepares tea for the assembly of the Rear Hall; if there is no Rear Hall, the successive head officials do so. Once the Abbot has finished personally preparing the tea, [the ceremony concludes].
The following morning, the new Head Seat (shouzuo) went to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) carrying incense.
He prostrated and requested, saying: "After the midday meal, I specially request that you grace the Rear Hall Head Seat and the assembly with tea in the Cloud Hall."

I humbly entreat your compassionate presence; please accept this formal petition as appended below. Having prepared a tray, a cloth, an incense burner, and candles, proceed to the Rear Hall and the Head Seat’s quarters.

Light the incense and prostrate yourself while making this request, saying: "This morning, following the midday meal, we shall serve tea in the Cloud Hall specifically for you; we humbly entreat your honorable descent. Once the petition has been presented and submitted, conclude the rite.
Specifically for individuals, the head tea server of their own quarters shall successively hand over the supply list and affix it to the lower section in front of the Sangha Hall;
the seal flap shall be pasted onto the front of the document.
Next, the attendant of the Hall Office shall notify the assembly to hang the tea-signboard.
The long board gong sounds.
Within the Sangha Hall, the tea is circulated; the drum is struck to assemble the community for the performance of rites, which are identical to those performed during regular or special offerings.
The Head Seat Bhikṣu of the Front Hall, [Name], hereby submits this formal petition: This morning, following the midday meal,
I have come before you to request that a single serving of tea be offered in the Cloud Hall specifically for the Head Seat of the Rear Hall and the assembly,
with a special invitation for all the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) to likewise grace us with their presence.
On this day of this month, [Name], holding the rank of [Title],
respectfully submits this formal petition to the assembly of the Rear Hall and the Head Hall. Sealed respectfully by [Name], holding the rank of [Title].
When the Abbot visits the Head Officers, he serves tea. After the tea and soup ceremony is concluded and the Abbot has finished his midday meal,
he proceeds to the quarters of the various Head Officers to serve tea.
With composure and kindness, he inspects for deficiencies and immediately orders the treasury office to provide for them.
Following this, the tea ceremony for the handover of duties by the two orders is held; after the tea ceremony specifically prepared by the Abbot for the new Head Seat is concluded.
In due order, the newly appointed officials, fully assuming their dignified demeanor,
carry incense and personally approach the respective positions they are to succeed.
They insert the incense and perform one prostration while facing the person whose seat they are replacing.
When the meal has concluded and the formal bows have been performed, request that the Venerable Master deign to visit the quarters for the offering of tea.

Thereafter, instruct the tea master to invite one representative from each of the two orders, one retired senior monk (qinjiu) from the eastern order, and one from the western order to serve as companions for the tea offering in the west.
Thus, one should know that the practice of sitting in separate groups involves requesting one person from among the senior colleagues to sit beside one as a companion.
It is like people on one's shoulders obstructing each other when taking their seats.
When tea is served to the monks of the Eastern Wing,
the head officials sit separately from the rest.
As for the Wei-na residing in the eastern wing:
when tea is being served, he shall send one sub-temple official (fu-si) from his shoulder to the quarters to arrange a special seat facing inward;
the presiding chairperson shall divide the seats for the other officials.
The attendants on the left and right accompany the person to their station.
Upon retiring from the *zhāi* (fasting/meditation), they strike the board in front of the *liáo* (monastic quarters).
They then receive those who have come specifically for this purpose.
Next, receive the attendants accompanying the Light;
they enter their positions and bow as they sit. Burn incense to welcome them, and burn incense for the Light and its attendants.
Once they have taken their seats, serve tea.
When the tea ceremony is finished,
the person acting on behalf of the recipient rises, takes the original incense offered for the invitation, and inserts it into the burner.
Having performed prostrations to express gratitude, they withdraw.
On the following day, the Hall Attendant (tangsi) shall instruct the attendants to prepare the handout refreshments (dianxin).
One person from the "Famous and Victorious" (mingsheng) group shall serve as the companion to the Head Seat (shouzuo) of the Front Hall.
Then, please invite one retired senior monk from the West Hall to serve as an honored companion.
If it is a group from the administrative office (Kusi),
please invite a retired senior monk or a head official (Toushou) from the West Hall to serve as an honored companion.
The administrative office prepares the nail-boards and hangings;
inside, a special seat is established,
with attendant seats arranged to the left and right.
The head official (doushou) parts company with the presiding chairperson (zhuxi).
Those of equal rank follow their respective positions in the assembly.
On the following day, the seating for the light refreshments (dianxin) is the same as before.
In the western corridor, the duties stop with the Guest Master;
in the eastern corridor, they stop with the Rector.
In all cases, the serving attendants shall exchange tea and refreshments.

When requesting the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) to serve as an attendant for arranging seats and performing rituals, all procedures are the same as those for the recent *dianxin* (afternoon refreshment). When inviting guests or fellow villagers, it is improper to do so [during these formal occasions].

Upon entering or leaving the quarters (*liao*), there is tea; upon entering or leaving the quarters, there is tea. Those who enter the *mengtang* (Hall of Enlightenment) must inform the head of the quarters (*liaozhu*).
Hang up the tea signboard (*chápái*).

On a small slip of paper attached to the left of the board, write: "So-and-so respectfully requests the venerable assembly of the entire monastery to retire from the meal and proceed to the *shàngláo* (upper quarters) for the meal. Once the meal in the *shàngláo* has concluded, prepare incense and candles to perform a collective inquiry (*wènxùn*).
The attendant bows to the master of the quarters, who occupies the host’s seat;
the tea server occupies the guest’s seat.
After sitting briefly and rising, they burn incense and perform a formal greeting.
They sit again, serve tea, and withdraw the bowls.

The *Liaozhu* (Head of the Quarters) rises before the incense burner to offer thanks. For those who have been appointed as a *Toushou* (Senior Official) after having served in the *Diantang* (Hall of Transmission), once the tea for the handover of duties has been served:
On another day, the tea master (chátóu) is instructed to inform the head of the quarters (liáozhǔ) to hang the tea service plaque.
After the midday meal, the small board is struck within the quarters.
The tea server stands to the right outside the door, bows to the assembly, and invites them inside.
Inquiring before the incense burner:
the Chief of the Quarters takes his place at the head of the row, while the person serving tea stands at the side of the row.
After sitting briefly, they rise, burn incense, and perform an inquiry.
Once again, having sat down and finished offering tea, the *liàozhǔ* (abbot’s assistant) and the assembly rise before the incense burner to express their thanks.
They escort the person who served the tea out. This applies to those who have emerged from the communal quarters (*zhòngliáo*) to serve as a head official (*tóushǒu*).
Instruct the tea-head to notify the head of the quarters (liaozhu) in advance to hang the tea-signboard.
After the midday meal, strike the board;
the attendant shall first go to the outside of the door of the communal quarters and stand to the right, bowing to the assembly.
Entering the position and establishing meditative concentration;
exchanging greetings, bowing, and taking one's seat;
advancing to the center and inquiring after those above and below while offering incense.
Furthermore, there is mutual inquiry between those in the middle and those above and below;
meanwhile, the central figure inquires after the head of the quarters (*sōen*), who bows to the tea server.
They then sit facing one another in their respective positions.

When the serving of tea is finished, the Head of the Quarters (Liaoyuan) comes before the hearth to express thanks and escorts [the guests] out. The ritual for serving tea to those entering the communal quarters is the same as the tea ceremony for departing from the quarters; however, the Head of the Quarters and the Head of the Hall (Liaozhang) take the positions of host and guest respectively.
The Head Official shall sit in the "Incapable-of-Entering" position.

The Head Official proceeds to the Sangha Hall to serve tea; having attended to the serving and exited the quarters, once the tea service is complete, he prepares the tea notice according to the form shown below and instructs the tea server to post it on the lower section of the front wall of the Sangha Hall.
Having assumed the proper deportment, one requests the Abbot for tea.
The various quarters hang up the tea-serving signboards to announce the invitation.
The attendant in charge of offerings is instructed in advance to heat the water and set out the cups.
The administrative office prepares tea and candles.
Once the meal is finished, the assembly takes their seats.
The head of the tea service enters the hall, burns incense, and serves tea according to the same protocol as the morning and evening services.
My quarters are cramped and humble, and I do not dare to receive you there.
This morning, after the midday meal, I invite you to the Cloud Hall for a single serving of tea.
On this day of this month, I, [Name], of humble station, respectfully request your presence.
The local elders and former disciples offer incense; the assembly of venerable Chan masters and the two orders of officers emerge from their seats to offer incense.
Whenever the two orders of officers emerge from their seats to offer incense or perform the ritual of offering incense, they shall strike the *bō* (small gong).
The rector steps out from before the incense burner and stands slightly to one side facing outward.
He bows to the abbot; the attendant holding the incense box follows, and he then bows to the two orders of officials.
Having exchanged greetings, he departs.

Turning around to inquire after the abbot is called "borrowing incense" (*jiexiang*); only then does one offer incense. On occasions such as the imperial birthday, the anniversaries of Buddhas, patriarchs, lineage masters, or dharma teachers, there is no "borrowing incense" inquiry.
When the Abbot is established in the West Hall,
one should first offer incense;
some say this is because the Head Seat has already attained the position of a world-transcending master.
It is incorrect for one to offer incense first;
this is because one must necessarily exit the assembly together with the *Du-si* (Chief Administrator).
Chapter Seven on the Great Assembly concludes. [Chapter] Seven on the Great Assembly: Like water returning to the void, like trees in the forest of Deng.
"Accumulation" refers to a multitude.
Now, when those of great capacity dwell among hundreds or thousands,
they empty out granaries to cook their rice and burn mountains to provide fuel for their stoves.
It is also that which they gather around;
those coming from the four quarters do so as if returning home,
as if it were something already their own— what indeed could cause this?
For the Buddha [taught that] as people transmigrate through the three realms and emerge from or sink into birth and death,
only by clarifying the Way and awakening to their nature can they transcend to wondrous enlightenment.
Thus, all beings of diverse species rely upon their goodness to instruct their followers,
taking it as a matter of course that they resemble themselves;
consequently, every person regards their own followers as they would their own teacher.
Though they arrived shoulder-to-shoulder and heel-to-heel,

Otherwise, there would be many who dispute over a single foot of land or a peck of grain;
how could it be that he alone is so foolish as to willingly surrender his wealth to expand my residence?
He ceased his own meal to feed us;
we eat here and dwell here—

What is the fruit [of this]?

Insert incense sticks and perform three prostrations.
Select an auspicious day to set up the banners and shave the head according to the Vinaya.

At present, in large halls, one must face toward the Buddha,
or seats may be arranged facing each other.

Now, for the sake of the many in the Sangha hall, we shall provide convenient couches and seats; first, we report this to the Karmadāna for his agreement.

Having extensively expounded the practice of becoming a *brahman* for the sake of sentient beings,

Cloud-pavilions of radiant light pervade the entire Dharma-realm,

The infinite Saṃghas of the ten directions,
through seeing and hearing, are universally perfumed and realize quiescence;

I shall now, having shaved my head this morning and received the precepts, initiate this meritorious deed.

For a tonsured śrāmaṇera, there is no hindrance to cultivation;

The source of the mind is limpid and tranquil; the ocean of Dharma is profound and deep.

To transmit the wondrous Way, there is nothing that surpasses leaving the household life.

and patriarch after patriarch passed on the lineage.

thus, the celestial Māras fold their hands in submission and non-Buddhists turn their hearts toward the truth,

Unable to abandon affectionate love,

"Since you have left the household life, your conduct transcends ordinary custom;

the five precepts are the primary cause for entering the Way."
He emerged as the foremost leader from the three miserable realms;

One shall not sit or lie upon high, wide, or large beds; one shall not wear flower garlands, necklaces, or apply fragrant oils to the body; one shall not engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor go to witness them; one shall not handle gold, silver, money, or precious gems; and one shall not eat at improper times. Diligently contemplate the meaning and review the old to know the new.

Ascending the platform to receive the precepts: all Buddhas of the three periods of time declared that leaving home leads to the realization of the Way.

so too should you enter the maṇḍala and receive the precepts with single-minded concentration;
be careful not to let your attention wander, but maintain the physical form and deportment of the Buddha.
One possesses the Buddha's precepts and attains the Buddha's enjoyments;

If one borrows robes or an alms bowl, even if they ascend the platform to receive the precepts,

The four *pāṭidesanīya* rules,

One must not spread out the sutras extensively—that is, over three sides. One must not support the sutras with one's hands while walking in the cloister.

One must not make noise.

Do not wait for the striking of the meditation board.

Second, properly arranging the kashaya;

Upon opening the ticket, descend from the bed, perform the inquiry, and return to the quarters.

no one shall rise beforehand to serve the meal.

however, one must not exit through the outer triple gate.

"Upon hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions grow light;
wisdom increases and bodhi arises."
Having escaped from hell and emerged from the fiery pit, you vow to attain Buddhahood to deliver sentient beings; you must first return to your place and sit in meditation.

Those who are weary should go to bed;
when sleeping, one must lie on the right side and must not lie on the back.

lying face downward is like the sleep of a madman, wherein many evil dreams occur.
Wrap the *kāṣāya* robe with a towel and place it before the pillow.
Nowadays, many people place their hands behind them, which is inconvenient for the principles of propriety.

upon entering the inner door of the lower chamber, one bows in greeting, returns to an empty spot, and then performs a bow to those on the left and right.
First, hang five-fold hand towels on the bamboo rack,
spread out the bathing cloth,

Without yet removing the *zhiduo*,
first take off the lower skirt and wrap the body with the foot-cloth.

placing them together and tying them with a hand towel.
The ancients said: "When the sound of the three drumbeats enters the hall, one must distinguish between the upper and lower garments for purification.
The garments removed should be placed in a single bundle and covered with a cloth before being turned over; only then may one change into slippers. One must not enter the bath barefoot."
One must wait for one’s turn in the lower section of the empty space to bathe.

One must not occupy the seats of the leaders or the senior elders—referring here to the upper section—and one must not splash water or hot liquid onto another person's body, nor soak one's feet in the bucket.
One must not relieve oneself indoors.
One must not place a wash-tub on a shelf. One must not laugh or speak.
One must not rub one's feet on a wooden trough.
One must not scoop up water.
One must not rise from one's seat and pour water over the body from a bucket.

The foot-cloth must not be separated from the body.
If there are feet that do not enter the bucket,
one must not use an excessive amount of hot water.
There may be sores;
or one may wash and cauterize sores;

one must not preempt others.

then ascends the bed and sits for a short while facing the wall.
First, put on the upper garment and the *zhiduò* (straight robe),

then, put on the lower garment.

As previously compiled,
these matters concerning daily conduct and communal decorum are not intended to be heard by the experienced and mature, but are offered merely to guide the beginner.

Ascending the hall, entering the inner chamber, giving small sermons (*xiao can*), chanting scriptures, reciting mantras, inspecting the quarters, resolving entanglements, attending to human affairs, packing bags, donning hats, escorting the deceased, and distributing robes—all such subtle rules and regulations are already fully recorded in the *Chiqi*.
The venerable masters each have clear records;
I shall not elaborate further here, as it would merely be redundant speech.
*Guijingwen* (Text on the Mirror of the Tortoise), composed by National Master Cijue, Master Zhi.
Now, when two cassia trees cast their shade and a single flower manifests its auspiciousness,
from that moment on, the establishment of monastic groves was essentially for the sake of the Saṃgha.
It is for the purpose of instructing the Saṃgha that there exists the Elder (sthavira).
There is the Head Seat (Śayanāsana) to represent the community of monks;
there is the Steward (Karmadāna) to bear the burdens of the community;
and there is the Rector (Karmadāna) to harmonize the community.
Because of making offerings to the community of monks, there are those who serve as seat-keepers;
because of performing tasks for the community of monks, there are those who serve as year-round administrators;
and because of handling the receipts and disbursements for the community of monks, there are those who serve as storekeepers.
There is a scribe because the monastic community requires the management of calligraphy;
there is a librarian because the monastic community must preserve the holy teachings;
and there is a guest prefect because the monastic community must receive and attend to donors.
There is an attendant to issue invitations for the sake of the community of monks;
there is a dormitory master to guard the robes and bowls for the sake of the community of monks;
and there is a hall master to provide medicinal decoctions and attend to the needs of the community of monks.
To wash the robes for the community of monks, there are bath-masters and water-suppliers;
to protect the community from the cold, there are charcoal-masters and stove-masters;
and to beg for alms on behalf of the community, there are street-wardens and fundraising masters.
Because they perform manual labor for the community of monks, there are gardeners and millers; because they wash and clean for the community of monks, there are cleaners;
and because they serve the community of monks, there are attendants.
Thus, the conditions for practicing the Way are fully provided throughout the ten directions;
the necessities for sustaining the body are spontaneously present in a hundred forms.
Free from anxiety regarding all matters, one directs the single mind toward the Way.
The world honors those who are noble and at leisure beyond worldly affairs;
among these, the pure and unconditioned Sangha is supreme.
This is due to the power of the many who have turned their thoughts [toward them].
How could one not know how to repay kindness?
By attending at dawn and seeking instruction at dusk, never letting even a moment of time pass in vain—
this is how one repays an elder.
Maintaining the proper order between seniors and juniors and conducting oneself with composure is how one repays the Head Seat.
Outwardly, one obeys the laws and regulations; inwardly, one maintains the rules and restraints.
This is how one repays the Karmadāna.
That the six harmonies gather together like water and milk blending is how one repays the Rector (Karmadāna).
One should accept this food for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path;
thus it is to repay the *karmadāna* (steward),
who provides dwellings for the Sangha and protects their belongings.
This is how one repays the *zhisui* (the steward of the year).
Not violating even a single hair’s breadth of the property of the monastery is how one repays the *kutou* (the storekeeper).
Holding no pen in hand, yet acting as if one’s own hair were on fire—
this is how I compose this letter.
By a bright window and a clean desk, let the ancient teachings illuminate the mind.
Thus he repays the Librarian;
by concealing his brilliance and obscuring his traces,
he does not attend to social pursuits, thereby repaying the Guest Master.
In his dwelling he was always consistent, and in requesting instruction he was invariably the first to arrive;
this was how he repaid those who served him.
With a single flask and a single bowl, he dwelt among the multitude like a mountain.
This is how one repays the lodging master (*liaozhu*).
As for the suffering of illness, providing gruel and medicine as appropriate is how one repays the hall master (*tangzhu*).
Moving slowly and remaining silent without losing awareness of the water's source is how one repays the bath master and the water-head attendant. One should maintain silence,
keep the hands folded in reverence, and withdraw from oneself to yield to others.
Thus one repays the charcoal-heads and furnace-heads;
by reflecting upon whether one’s own virtuous conduct is complete or deficient,
one thereby repays the neighborhood alms-collectors and the masters of solicitation.
One calculates the amount of labor expended and measures the distance from which it was brought;
thus one repays the gardeners, the millers, and the stewards.
Drawing water and handling the grain, one comes to know shame and recognize a sense of propriety.
This is how one repays the head of the purification office.
To be broad and easy to follow, and simple and easy to carry out—
this is how one repays the person of the purification office.
Therefore, beneath the forest groves, the path of practice is ever renewed;
those of the highest capacity achieve completion in a single lifetime,
while those of middling capacity nurture the embryo of sagehood.
Even for those who have not yet awakened to the source of the mind,
their time is not spent in vain;
such true jewels among monks serve as fields of merit for the world.
They serve as a bridge for the final age,
ultimately realizing the supreme fruit of the two-fold adornment.
Should the monastic groves not be governed or the wheel of Dharma not be turned, [this purpose would be lost].
It is not for an elder to lead the assembly if his three karmas are not harmonized and his four modes of deportment are not solemn.
It is not for the head seat to lead the assembly if he fails to provide such guidance.
If the capacity to accommodate others is not broad and the heart that loves others is not profound,
one is not fulfilling the role of a karmadāna in protecting the community.
If practitioners find no peace and those who disrupt the group are not expelled, the monastery fails in its purpose.
It is not the duty of the *karmadāna* (Venerable) to seek to please the assembly.
If the six flavors are not refined and the three virtues are not provided,
it is not the duty of the *sthavira* (Dignitary) to serve the assembly.
If dormitories are not repaired and utensils are not provided,
it is not for the sake of settling the community that the *zhisui* (the annual steward) acts in this way;
rather, he amasses permanent property and embezzles the resources of the Sangha.
The storehouse is not for the purpose of providing for the multitude.
If the official correspondence is unskillful and the characters are fragmented,
such correspondence is not for the purpose of adorning the multitude.
The desks and tables were not kept in order, and clamor and distraction did not cease;
this was not how a library director should treat the assembly.
He detested the poor and loved the wealthy, valuing the laity while slighting the monks.
It is not the duty of the guest prefect to offer praise to the assembly;
if one’s etiquette is not respectful, the distinction between the honorable and the humble is lost.
It is not the duty of the attendant to summon the assembly.
If one is not diligent in maintaining order nor careful in guarding the quarters,
this is not what a *liáozhǔ* (lodging master) is meant to do for the community. Furthermore,
if one is unskilled in serving others and causes disturbance to the sick, it is likewise improper.
It is not the duty of the Hall Master (Tangzhu) to provide for the welfare of the assembly.
If hot and cold water are insufficient or the temperature is inappropriate,
it is not the fault of the Bath Master (Yuzhu) or the Water Head (Shoutou) for failing to wash the assembly.
If one is unprepared and fails to attend to the needs of others,
it is not the duty of the head of the hearth or the head of the charcoal pit to direct their efforts toward the assembly.
If one is unjust in handling wealth or fails to exert one's full strength, [one fails in their responsibility].
It is not the duty of the street-almst beggars (*pindapātika*) to provide for the assembly;
there are residual benefits in the land, yet no one possesses complete merit.
It is not the duty of the garden-head, the mill-head, or the estate-manager to act on behalf of the assembly.
If laziness and indolence persist, and various conditions are not fulfilled,
one is unfit to serve as a *śramaṇera* (novice) attending to the community.
If prohibitions do not stop them and commands do not move them, they are unworthy.
It is not because the non-monastics (upāsakas) follow the assembly; rather,
it is because the monks themselves treat their teachers with contempt, disregard the Dharma, and act according to their own whims and circumstances—
this is how they fail to repay their elders.
To sit and lie down in a disordered manner, and to act with such discordant conduct,
is not how one repays the position of the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera).
It reflects a disregard for the royal law and a lack of concern for the monastic community.
This is not the way to repay the Karmadāna.
When those above and below are in disharmony and their strife remains stubborn,
this is not the way to repay the Karmadāna.
To crave fine delicacies while disparaging coarse food is not the way to repay the *karmadāna*.
To dwell in and enjoy one's quarters without considering those who will come after is likewise improper.
This is not how one repays the *zhisui* (the official in charge of annual maintenance).
To be greedily attached to gain and offerings while showing no concern for the monastery's permanent property is not how one repays the *kutou* (the storekeeper).
To devote oneself to holding brush and inkstone and racing through literary compositions is not the way to repay the transmission of sacred writings;
to treat the golden texts with negligence and instead seek out secular classics is likewise improper.
To pursue the company of worldly men and form alliances with the noble is not the way to repay the Abbot.
To do so is not the way to repay the Guest Master.
To forget to summon the assembly of monks for their long-term residence is not the way to repay those who serve you.
To compare oneself with others and to store things carelessly is to invite thieves.
This is not the way to repay the *liaozhu*.
To be prone to anger and lacking in joy, thereby failing to comply with the conditions of illness,
is not the way to repay the *tangzhu*.
To make noise with the bucket or ladle while using water without restraint is not the way to repay the bath master or the water steward.
To have one’s body become uncomfortably warm is an impediment to the rest of the assembly.
This is not the way to repay those who provide charcoal for the hearth;
to neglect cultivation while peacefully accepting offerings is not the way to repay the alms-seekers and fundraisers.
To eat one's fill all day long without applying the mind is not the way to repay the master of the garden and the mill.
To spit and slobber upon the walls and leave the latrine in a state of utter disorder is likewise unworthy.
This is not the way to repay one who purifies the head.
To be solely preoccupied with outward decorum while lacking the foundation of wholesome instruction from the past is not the way to repay one who purifies the person.
For even with a thousand whirlwind turns, there may still be that which is not fully encompassed;
we shall simply set aside our shortcomings and follow what is excellent,
together accomplishing the matter of leaving the household life.
It is my hope that within this lion’s den all shall become lions,
and beneath this sandalwood forest there shall be nothing but sandalwood;
thus may we behold once more the assembly on Vulture Peak during the final five hundred years.
Thus, the flourishing or decline of the Dharma depends upon the monastic community.
The Sangha is a field of merit that should be honored and revered;
when the Sangha is held in high esteem, the Dharma is likewise esteemed.
If the Sangha is held in light esteem, the Dharma will be held in light esteem.
Once internal protection is strict, external protection will necessarily be diligent.
Even if the master who provides the gruel and rice were to exercise his royal transformation for a single period, [the Dharma would not flourish].
When serving as an administrator in a monastic community,
one may occasionally hold authority; yet one should always treat one's fellow practitioners with respect and must never act with reckless arrogance.
If one is arrogant and conceited, treating private matters as public rewards, all things will be impermanent;
how could such a state be maintained for long?
When the day comes to return to the assembly, with what face shall we look upon one another?
The non-differentiation of cause and effect is difficult to avoid.
As a son of the Buddha, the monk’s right to receive offerings is no different;
he is revered by all, both in the heavens and among humans.
The morning gruel and midday meal should, by principle, be refined and abundant;
the four requisites for support must not be allowed to fall short.
For two thousand years, the Buddha’s legacy has provided shade and shelter for his descendants.
The merit from even a single portion of the light of the *ūrṇā-kośa* is inexhaustible in its enjoyment;
one need only know how to serve the assembly and need not worry about poverty.
The Sangha is devoid of ordinary or holy beings, universally gathering from the ten directions.
Since it is called a *caitya* (a monastery for all),
everyone has an equal share;
how can one recklessly give rise to discrimination, treating visiting monks with contempt or aversion?
In the *danguo liao* (overnight guest quarters), they reside for three mornings while receiving offerings with full ritual propriety;
in the *sengtang* (monks' hall), they briefly seek alms,
making offerings with an impartial mind.
Even worldly guests still receive careful attention;
how can members of the Sangha bear to fail to welcome them?
If one lacks a heart of moderation, [one will surely fall into error].
One will naturally possess inexhaustible merit;
the monastic community shall be harmonious, with those above and below sharing a single heart,
mutually concealing each other's shortcomings and virtues as the occasion requires.
Do not allow the ugliness within the household to be heard outside;
although this may cause no harm to the matter at hand,
it will ultimately diminish the respect and admiration of others.
It is like the worms within a lion’s body devouring the flesh of that very lion;
it cannot be destroyed by celestial Māras or non-Buddhist outsiders.
If one wishes for the Way not to fall into ruin, [one must rely on this].
The Buddha-sun shines ever bright,
augmenting the splendor of the ancestral realm and supplementing the sagely transformation of the imperial court.
I pray that you will take these words as a mirror for reflection.

Arrange incense, candles, and Buddha images.
Recite the hymn of praise for the Buddha, saying: "As the autumn moon appears in clear water, may the field of merit be brought forth. Offer earnest prayers.

This morning, for the sake of the sick bhikṣu [Name],...
To release the enmity of many lifetimes and repent for the transgressions of countless kalpas,
