In the year [Year], I registered my residence at [Temple Name].
I have now come here suffering from illness;
fearing that my internal winds and fires may become unstable,
I request that you kindly trouble the public authorities to issue a sealed inventory of all the personal belongings I am carrying with me.
Testamentary Statement for After Death I request that [the deceased] be sent off in accordance with the Pure Regulations of the Forest Monasteries.

On the [day], [month], and [year], the sick monk [Name] speaks these words. [Record of the Deceased Monk’s Robes and Alms Bowl] Regarding the robes and alms bowl of the deceased monk: whenever a monk’s illness becomes critical...
The patient immediately informs the Hall Master (Yantang Zhu) of his illness.
Having received instructions from the Rector (Weina), he requests that his belongings be sealed.
The attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi Xingzhe) then reports this to the Head Seat (Shouzuo), the various Head Officers (Toushou), the Administrative Officers (Zhishi), and the Attendants (Shizhe).
Together they go before the patient to record his oral instructions. Then,
the patient and the attendants together collect the sutra cases,
the storage chests, and the clothing and belongings.
Prepare a detailed inventory of all items. After counting each one, seal them individually from the outside;

however, you must set aside in a separate bundle for preservation the following necessary items: the deceased’s clothing, including outer robes, inner garments, and vestments; prayer beads; incense cases; socks and shoes; bamboo hair-combing mats; clean hair-ties; cotton wicks for wrapping the bones; and so forth. All such items shall be gathered together and secured in one place.
The Hall Master of the Yan-shou Hall shall jointly oversee the care and management of the patient.
If the patient is unable to entrust these matters,
the Rector (Vina) and the Head Seat (Shouzuo) shall take responsibility for their execution.
Even for those without luggage, one must see them off with full courtesy.
The keys to their single tents shall be sealed and deposited with the Head Seat (*shouzuo*).
The luggage shall be sealed, and the Head Seat, Rector (*weina*), Guest Master (*zhike*), Attendant (*shizhe*), and the laborers from the four quarters shall carry it back to the Hall Office.
If the belongings of a retired monk in a single quarters are numerous, they shall be sealed and stored;
only those belonging to his own room shall remain, and the treasury office shall dispatch someone to guard them.
A deceased monk who did not inform the abbot, the two orders of officials, or the retired monks during his lifetime [shall have no such arrangements].
Furthermore, regarding matters where there is no written testament from a close relative and one must not arbitrarily bequeath clothing or goods:
when Dàchuān Wéngshā was residing at Jìngcí Monastery, the Head Seat and the Rector forged a testamentary bequest for a deceased monk.
If one has been expelled like a sick monk closing his eyes,
the Hall Master (Yanshou) shall immediately inform the Rector (Weina),
who shall then instruct the attendants of the Hall Office to notify the Hot Water Attendant.
The Chief Seat (Shouzuo), Guest Master (Zhike), Attendant (Shizhe),
and the Treasury Office (Kusi) shall dispatch personnel to carry the coffin and the bathing boat;
they shall prepare for the ritual bathing of the deceased, and once the bathing is completed, [proceed with the next rites].
Cleanse the hair and wipe the body;
distribute bathing robes and cloths according to need;
provide hand towels to those who have cleansed the hair.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) supervises the dressing of the body and its placement within the shrine.
It is then set within the Hall of Longevity (*yanshou-tang*), where chairs, tables, and a memorial tablet (*wei-pai*) are arranged.
On the tablet is written: "The Awakening Spirit of the newly deceased Elder [Name]."
For the West Hall, one writes: "The Spirit of the Former Abbot of [Name] Temple, Dharma Name [Name], Chan Master [Name].
For other positions, write according to their respective titles, providing incense, lamps, and offerings.
The assembly present shall recite the Great Compassion Mantra and dedicate the merit for the stabilization of the image.
At night, a perpetual lamp shall be lit.
The attendants of the Hall Office shall prepare snow-leaf banners and flower offerings in advance.
The attendants serving the deceased shall daily offer gruel and rice,
and the administrators shall offer tea and soup at the three times of the day.
When the incense burning, the morning meal, the recitation of sutras in the hall,
and the dismissal of the evening session have concluded,
the attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi) immediately strikes the hand-chime to lead the way.
The Head Seat leads the assembly to the front of the shrine;
once the Abbot has finished burning incense,
the Rector recites the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī.

The dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) was as follows: "I now offer the merit from reciting the sutras above for the sake of the newly deceased Elder [Name], to adorn his ground of retribution throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time," and so forth. Next, the local people chanted mantras.
The village head emerges to burn incense;
the three daily services of prostration are the same as before.
Except for the dedication of merit to the public realm, one uses the two-character name.
For the remainder, only the single-word names are recited.
The dedication of merit is the same as before.
If one encounters the first or fifteenth day of the lunar month, or the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday, the chanting of sutras is waived.
The funeral rites may not yet be concluded.
For the performance of Buddhist services, one must request the abbot to preside over the service for holding the torch;
as for other services, such as locking the coffin, raising the coffin, exhuming the bones, and enshrining them in the stupa, these are also required.
The *vinaya-dhara* reports to the *śrāmaṇera-prathama*,
and after deliberation, they follow the order of seniority to take turns inviting a head official (*sthavira*) to perform the duty.
Still using small slips of white paper, write the invitation slip as follows:

"The newly deceased Venerable [Name], native of [Place], [Name] of the Abbot’s Hall and the Monastic Office, bowing and inviting for the incense-lighting ritual. All other ritual services are to be written according to this model. If the deceased was a West Hall monk, a private room resident, or a long-standing veteran whose robes and bowl were relatively abundant, [the procedure remains the same].
Then, for the additional offerings of tea and soup, the turning of the shrine, the turning of the bones, and other such Buddhist rites,
one should invite the West Hall Attendant, the Head Seat, and renowned masters from this mountain and abroad to take turns officiating.
The Rector shall prepare a tray, a cloth, an incense burner, candles, and a piece of incense.
The attendant leads the practitioner to the abbot’s quarters.
He offers incense and performs a prostration with full-body contact (*chu li*), reporting:
"Venerable [Name], the senior monk, passed away on such-and-such a day; his cremation will take place."
Having requested the Abbot to hold the torch, they present the memorial tablet and withdraw.
The procedure for requesting the Head Officers is the same.
The Hall Administration Office shall maintain a record of these ritual services.
To prepare for the formal inspection and invitation,
the *guyi guyi* (clothing appraiser) and the *weina* (rector) shall instruct the hall office acolyte to invite the abbot,
the two orders of officers, and the attendants to the hall office.
Alternatively, he may present the bundles before the assembly in the Zhaotang Hall;
having opened them, he takes out the clothing and items and arranges them upon mats on the floor.
Each item is presented to the *weina* (chant master) for inspection.
The *shouzuo* (head seat), acting as mediator, along with the *zhike* (guest master) and *shizhe* (attendant), appraise its value.
They arrange the seating order according to the recorded prices.
The attendant shall write labels according to the assigned numbers and affix them to the clothing items before placing them in the storage chest; furthermore,
they shall be priced according to those same numbers.
Write out individual long labels for each item separately,
to be used when chanting the distribution of robes.
[These apply to] the Abbot’s quarters, the two orders of officials, and all the various monastic lodgings.
It is not permitted to take away articles under the pretext of public use.
If there are items belonging to the permanent endowment (sangha) that must necessarily be used,
they shall be compensated by deducting their value from the portioned-off fees.
If the deceased monk’s robes and alms bowl are somewhat abundant,
they should be sold at a low price for the benefit of the assembly to dedicate the merit for his posthumous welfare.
One should perform recitations during the "Great Night" (the funeral vigil), and depart for the funeral procession early the following morning.
On the afternoon of the following day, the hall attendant (tángsī xíngzhě) informs the abbot and the two orders (liǎngxù), reports to the assembly,
hangs the sign for recitation (niànsòng pái),
and notifies the administrative office (kùsī) to prepare sacrificial food and dispatch personnel.
The sacrificial banquet is laid out.
Local residents and dharma relatives prepare a memorial text and present money to the treasury office to return the sacrifice.
Three small pieces of incense are prepared.
The superior offering is used for the following:
if the deceased monk was a man of great virtue and renown from a major monastery,
or a West Hall resident, a private room dweller, or a long-standing veteran of the community.
At Gōngshān Monastery,
the abbot and the two orders of officers have a memorial service,
during which the rector reads the memorial text.
When the evening session has concluded,
the Sangha hall bell is struck to assemble the community.
Before the shrine, the ritual master recites the liturgy while first burning incense and offering tea and soup.
The Abbot proceeds to the incense-burning area and stands at the head of the eastern row.
The Rector comes forward to burn incense and request the ritual for locking the coffin.
The person who accepts the request steps out of the ranks to burn incense, then withdraws to perform a formal greeting.
Next, he bows in greeting before the Abbot;
then he turns to bow in greeting before the East Hall;
continuing his circuit, he bows in greeting at the end of the row.
Next, he bows in greeting before the western section;
thereafter, he bows together with the entire assembly.
He then passes by the end of the western section.
If the head officials are present,
each shall pass through their respective positions to an empty space and stand to the right of the shrine niche.
The attendant of the Hall Office shall wait, holding a tray upon which the lock is placed.
Once the Buddhist rites have been concluded,
the practitioner secures the niche with a lock,
and the abbot covers the position.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) steps forward, bows to the left of the abbot and the two orders of officials,
and after the incense has been offered,
he faces the shrine and recites: "Now, it is said..."
Life and death alternate in succession, and cold and heat shift in turn.
Their coming is like a flash of lightning striking the vast sky;
their departing is like the stilling of waves upon the great ocean.
On this day, there was a certain Elder [Name], who had recently passed into parinirvāṇa;
his conditions for birth having come to an end, he has suddenly departed from the great dream,
realizing the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena.
Thus, they attain nirvana as their joy.
With reverence, the great assembly gathered solemnly before the funerary shrine,
chanting the sublime names of the various sages.
I offer this pure spirit to the Pure Land.
I rely upon the Great Assembly to recite the Dharma-body of Vairocana, and so forth, followed by the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī.
As for the dedication of merit: may the merit from the aforementioned chanting and recitation of the sutras...
On behalf of the newly deceased Elder [Name],
we humbly pray that his spirit may transcend to the pure realm and his karmic burdens be shed from the toil of the mundane world.
The lotus has blossomed with flowers of the highest grade;
the Buddha has received the prediction of one more lifetime.
Once again, for the sake of the great assembly, recite the "Ten Directions and Three Periods of All... [verse], etc. The Guest Prefect leads the *Śūraṅgama Mantra* in unison.
The dedication of merit for the recitation of the sutra performed above is offered on behalf of the newly deceased Elder [Name] to adorn his place of retribution.
[Recite] "The ten directions and three periods of time... and so forth. The abbot then returns to stand at the head of the eastern order.
The former associates from the Jianghu, fellow countrymen, and Dharma relatives shall perform the memorial services in succession.
At the conclusion, the Great Compassion Mantra (Dabei Zhou) is recited;
the dedication of merit is the same as that for the Guest Prefect (Zhike).

Regarding the Funeral Procession: When departing for the funeral, the Storehouse Office shall in advance assign the Supervising Craftsman and the Attendants to prepare firewood for the cremation of the deceased and dispatch the servant laborers.
The ritual implements—including hand-bells, cymbals, drums, banners, flowers, incense, and candles—as well as the bier for carrying the shrine and all funeral rites, are fully prepared.
The attendants of the Hall Office notify the Abbot and the two orders the night before;
the memorial tablet for the deceased is then hung.
The following morning, after the rice gruel has been served and the wooden mallet struck for the meal, strike the mallet once more and announce: "Inform the assembly.
Once the gruel is finished, there shall be a general invitation to escort the deceased;
all must attend together, except for those on duty in the quarters or the hall.
Having respectfully announced this, strike the mallet once more and exit to stand before the Sacred Monk (Sengzhong) to perform a greeting.
Next, after completing the greetings before the Abbot,
circumambulate the hall one circuit, beginning from the position of the Head Seat (Shouzuo).
Having gone to the outer hall, return to the inner hall to exchange greetings and depart.
This applies when encountering the Inner Hall during the Imperial Birthday (Śāstṛ-pūjā).
The mallet shall not be struck.
The attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi) shall go directly to inform the Abbot and the two orders.
After the morning gruel is finished, he shall announce to the hall: "I request the Head Seat and the assembly."
Upon hearing the sound of the bell, the monks chant scriptures in the Yanshou Hall; the bell for the Sangha hall is struck and the assembly gathers as the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) recites.
He should recite briefly and with urgency, saying: "I wish now to escort the sacred shrine to the grand ceremony of cremation."
We look up in reliance upon the great assembly to recite the sublime names of the various sages,
thereby manifesting our longing as we part from you and providing supreme support for the path to enlightenment.
Having completed the invocation of the Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha, the presiding master steps forward to stand at the head of the eastern order.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) comes forth to offer incense and request the rite for raising the shrine (*kaṅ*).
Once the ritual proceedings are concluded, the practitioners strike the *ghaṇṭā* (bell) and lift the shrine out to the entrance of the mountain gate.
If tea and soup are offered, the shrine is then turned.
The shrine is arranged facing inward with an incense table set before it.
The Head Seat leads the assembly, standing in two rows.
The Rector burns incense and requests the ritual service.
Wait until the Buddhist rites have been performed before proceeding.
If the shrine is not being moved,
the *vinaya-dhara* goes directly outside the gate and stands facing inward with palms joined.
Recite the mantra for rebirth;
the entire assembly recites it together.
After two rounds, they exit while maintaining continuous palms-joined reverence.
Each holding a snow-branch willow,
the practitioners stand in a row outside the gate,
bowing their heads with palms joined.
When the procession of the assembly has reached its end,
they shall also escort it from behind;
the *vinaya-dhara* follows the reliquary casket.
The Chief Administrator (Dusi) presides over the funeral procession.
Upon reaching the Nirvana Platform for the cremation,
the administrative officials burn incense and offer tea.
Next, the Abbot offers incense, returns to his position,
and the Rector comes forward to offer incense and request the Abbot to perform the ritual of holding the torch.
The Steward bows in greeting and passes the torch to him.
Upon the conclusion of the Buddhist rites,
the Rector (Karmadāna) faces the shrine and recites: "On this day, there has been a newly passed-away Elder named [Name],
who has followed conditions and attained peaceful extinction."
Thereupon, in accordance with the Dharma, he was cremated;
the body that had propagated the Way for a hundred years was consumed by fire like a single path leading to Nirvana.
I look up in reliance upon the venerable assembly to assist my awakening spirit.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One.
(Recite ten times.)
The above has extolled the ten recitations as an aid for rebirth in the Pure Land.
We only pray that the mirror of wisdom may radiate its brilliance and the true wind may disperse its splendor.
Within the Bodhi Garden,
the flowers of the awakening mind bloom;
within the ocean of the Dharma-nature, the defilements of the dusty mind are washed away.
The tea is poured for three libations and incense is burned in a single burner.

We respectfully bid farewell on your journey through the clouds, O Venerable Monk and the assembly of holy ones. The administrative officers wait to recite the verses as the tea is poured and the incense is burned.
To personally go out and offer incense and prostrations is a ritual of the mountain gate;
it is not proper for one to perform this by simply kneeling.
Recite the Great Compassion Mantra.

For the dedication, say: "By the merit of the sutra recitations and chanting performed above, we respectfully dedicate it for the newly deceased Elder [Name], that his place of retribution may be adorned during the cremation."
The Guest Attendant recites the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* for all beings of the ten directions and three periods of time, and so forth.

The dedication is the same as before, except that the two characters "recitation" (niàn-sòng) are omitted. When local laypeople or Dharma relatives chant sutras for the dedication, it is also the same.
After the cremation, the Hall Attendant (Tangsi) and the Ritual Assistant (Xingzhe) inform the Abbot, the two orders of officials, and the attendants.
Once the midday meal has concluded, they chant for the distribution of robes in front of the Sangha Hall;
meanwhile, they notify the assembly by hanging up the "Chanting for Robes" signboard.
Upon the conclusion of the period of fasting, preparations are made in the area before the Sangha Hall.
The Abbot and the Head Seat take their respective positions, with the two orders of monks seated facing one another.
Upon entering the gate, they stand crosswise toward the interior on wooden stools.
The desk is then set with the brush, inkstone, sounding stone, scissors, hanging cords, and other necessary implements.
Once the mats have been spread upon the floor,
the hall attendant (táng-sī xíng-zhě) informs the abbot and the attendants of the two orders, and strikes the bell to assemble the community.
The *vinaya-dhara*, the guest master (*kṣetrapati*), and the attendant (*upasthāyaka*) enter the hall together and take their seats in a row toward the interior.
The hall attendants (*sabhā-karmika*), the food servers (*bhojana-prasthāpaka*), and the various ranks of general attendants line up in a single file.
Having exchanged greetings with the Abbot and the two orders of officials,
he turns to exchange greetings with the Rector, the Guest Master, and the Attendants; once finished,
he carries his bundle and basket before the Abbot and the two orders.
Circulate the sealed envelope.
Request the key from the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) and present it;
upon opening and retrieving the garments, verify them against the inventory numbers.
Arrange the seats in order;
place empty baskets toward the inner side.
The Rector rises and strikes the chime once.
In the recitation it is said: "As drifting clouds disperse, shadows do not remain;
as the waning candle burns out, its light naturally extinguishes.
Now, this auction is employed to manifest impermanence.
Relying upon the great assembly, we respectfully offer this for the sake of the late Elder [Name], to assist his enlightened spirit in rebirth in the Pure Land.

Having recited the ten titles of the Buddha Vairocana of the Pure Dharma Body, and so forth, the gong is struck once, and it is said: "The method of chanting for the distribution of robes is indeed based upon established regulations."
One should naturally attend to the new and the old, the short and the long.
Once the sound of the *qing* has ceased, no regrets or recantations are permitted.
This is respectfully announced; once again, strike the *qing* one more time.
Taking up the ordination certificate (*duòdié*),
one makes a horizontal cut across the deceased monk’s name and says,
"The ordination certificate of the deceased monk, [name], one scroll. While facing the assembly, one cuts it through and strikes the *qing* once.
Hand it over to the attendant,
who presents it to the two orders.
The rector (vinaya-dhara) removes his *kāṣāya* robe and places it inside the *ghaṇṭā*.
Then, the hanging net is exchanged.
The attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi) takes up the articles in order and presents them for handover.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) holds up [the object] and says:
"An item of such-and-such name, one chant for so much;
valued at one *guan*."
Then, beginning with the lead *bǎi* (chant leader),
the attendant of the Hall Office (*táng-sī xíng-zhě*) joins in the chant, and the assembly responds in unison,
chanting sequentially until reaching the "one string" (*yì-guàn*).
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) strikes the chime once and says, "One string. The subsequent calls are all the same.
If several people respond with one voice for a single price, the attendant stops them, saying, "Double break! He then calls out again, and the Venerable strikes the chime to confirm the transaction.
The attendant of the Hall Office asks for the name of the person who has been assigned to meditation.
The guest prefect writes the name on the roster,
and the assistant master issues the identification tag according to that name.
The attendant who distributed the offerings hands them over to the person who received the chant;
the offering-head attendant then collects the robes and places them back into the basket.
At the conclusion of each recitation, strike the chime once.

For the dedication, say: "By the merit of the chanting and recitation of the *yī* (robes) performed above, we respectfully dedicate it for the adornment of the realm of retribution of the late Elder [Name]."
Once again, I trouble the venerable assembly.
Regarding the ten directions and the three periods of time, etc., recently, in order to quell clamor and disorder, we have frequently employed the method of drawing lots (*jiu-nian*).
If the current abbot fails to claim his allotted share of clothing or goods after three days, it shall be forfeited at its appraised value.
Regarding the sale of manufactured boards and curtains,
the *Zenghui ji* states:
"The Buddha established the rule for the distribution of robes with this underlying intent."
He causes those who remain to see that the deceased's belongings are divided and given to the community of monks,
and he reflects: "Since he was thus..."
I am still like this;
because I do not now exercise introspection, I fail to apply the antidote that would stifle my craving and seeking.
To instead engage in clamorous haggling over the price at the time of the robe-offering ceremony is the height of folly.
After the body has been placed in the stupa and cremated, the attendants and local Dharma relatives shall together collect the remains.
Wrap the casket in cotton cloth and shrouds, seal it securely, and bring it back to the Yanshou Hall.
Remove the character "new" from the spirit tablet and recite sutras three times daily.
On the afternoon of the third day, move the platform tent to the front of the Sangha Hall.
He should cause the assembly to be informed if the proceedings do not conform to the proper ritual form or if there is deception.
He may permit a formal announcement (*li-fu*) to rectify matters above and below, provided they are based on reality;
if there is no factual basis, he must not allow disorder or prolixity.
Those who violate this shall be subject to expulsion and punishment.
As for those who serve as abbots or administrators,
they must be public-spirited, upright, impartial, and fair.
It is appropriate for the master to lead by example and set the standard for the assembly.
Once the wooden platform has been dismantled,
the attendants of the Hall Office shall notify the assembly in advance to hang the "Plaque for Sending Away the Ashes."

When the appointed time arrives, the bell is struck to assemble the community for the ritual of "Raising the Bones" (qǐgǔ), which is then conveyed to the stupa site for the ritual of "Requesting Entry into the Stupa.
Once the entry is complete, the administrative officer seals the stupa,
and the *vinaya-dhara* (chamberlain) intones the Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇī.
The dedication of merit from the preceding recitation of the sutra is offered for the deceased Elder [Name], now interred in his stupa, to adorn his realm of retribution.
[Recite] "In the ten directions... and so forth. The Guest Prefect then leads the assembly in the recitation of the *Śūraṅgama-mantra*.
The local people’s recitation of the scriptures and dedication of merit are the same as above.
This concludes Volume Six of the Imperially Commissioned Baizhang Qinggui.
Volume Seven of the Imperially Commissioned Baizhang Qinggui begins.
The monk Dehui, Abbot of Dazhi Shousheng Chan Temple, respectfully presents this;
the monk Dasu, Abbot of Daxiang Jiqing Temple, respectfully presents this.

By Imperial Decree, they have recompiled and corrected the *Ban Zhang Shi* (Format for Ledger Accounts). The current ledger format for the auction of the robes, bowls, and cash of the deceased monk [Name] is detailed below, including all items of income and expenditure.
One receipt for one thousand strings of cash was received as proceeds from the auction of robes;
alternatively, there may be other items listed under the heading of receipts.

A detailed list of disbursements totaling ninety-one strings of cash is provided below: fifteen strings of cash for the coffin platform, three strings of cash for the funeral bier, and [the remainder] for the funeral offerings.
Three *kanmon* for the rice gruel; one *kanmon* for oil for the lamp before the shrine;
ten *kanmon* for brush, paper, ritual tablets, banners, flowers, and *ketsuryō* (willow branches);
two *kanmon* and five hundred *mon* for shaving the hair; five hundred *mon* for moving the shrine and carrying the deceased; [and] bathing water for cremation.
Two *kan* for bathing the deceased; one *kan* for the direct offerings to the spirit; five hundred *mon* for rice and gruel;
five hundred *mon* for the storehouse head and guest master to report the preparation of the altar; five hundred *mon* for nails and hanging materials for the altar mats;
five hundred *mon* for the management and provision of bowls and plates; and five hundred *mon* for the storehouse attendant to provide the materials for preparing the altar.
Wu Bo-wen, supervisor of the kitchen, receives two *wen* for preparing food; Wu Bo-wen, tea-head of the storehouse, receives two *wen* for serving tea and soup;
the head of the attendants (*cantou*) receives two *wen* for dispatching laborers; the attendant of the Hall Office (*tangsi*) receives two *wen* for notifying the assembly;
Wu Bo-wen, supervisor of construction, receives two *wen* for dispatching additional labor; the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) receives two *wen* for calling for the carrying of incense cases.
Ten *kan* for the hall attendant reciting the sutras; one *kan* for the hall supervisor and the corridor board-beater;
two *kan* for the tea master of the four quarters and the attendants; one *kan* for the bier-bearers;
three *kan* for the gong players; and [the same] for the drummers and musicians.
Three *kan* for carrying the incense table and bearing the banners and lamps; six persons at five hundred *mon* each for distributing the snow-branch and willow-branch;
one *kan* for the funeral expenses; three *kan* for the abbot and his attendants to escort the funeral procession;
one *kan* for the laborers of the four quarters to carry the low tables; five hundred *mon* for the attendants of the *Teidō* office to present the vestments.
Five hundred cash for the ritual assistant (*xingzhe*) who chants the distribution of robes; five hundred cash for the attendant (*tie*) who hands over the robe-distribution tally;
five hundred cash for the attendant (*goutou*) who receives the robes; five hundred cash for the ritual assistant (*xingzhe*) who draws lots for the food offering;
one string of cash for the collection of bones; and [one string of cash] for the carrying of the ash casket.

A total of two hundred and seventy *wen* in cash and paper currency shall be disbursed from the general ledger for the One-Guan-Wen-Zhi Pagoda; outside of this disbursement, thirty-seven percent shall be deducted as a share to be returned to the permanent endowment (*changzhu*).

A summary of the aforementioned disbursements and cash payments totaling one hundred thirty-five *guàn* for the funeral rites is set forth below: Twenty *guàn* for the torch-bearing ceremony; Ten *guàn* as a supplement for the torch-bearing ceremony; Forty *guàn* for the locking of the coffin, the raising of the coffin, the removal of the bones, and their enshrinement in the stupa; Twenty *guàn* as a supplement for the four aforementioned ceremonies; Thirty *guàn* for the *vinaya-dhara*’s service at the mountain head; Fifteen *guàn* for the guest prefect (*kṣetrasvāmin*) and the attendant (*upasthāyaka*) handling the accounts; Ten *guàn* as a supplement for the three aforementioned services. In total, fifteen *guàn* in cash and disbursements are provided for the Chief Seat (*śrāmaṇera*) presiding over the funeral.
The Abbot shall provide five strings of cash for the funeral procession;
the Rector shall provide five strings of cash for the sounding of the chime.

According to the above account, the expenditures for the branch temple amount to nine *guan* in cash. The guest prefect, the chanting master, and the incense attendant shall each receive three *guan*.
The attendant of the Sacred Monk shall collect two *guan* from the proceeds of the robe auction.

The *zhisui* (yearly steward) shall provide one *guan* of firewood; in total, the aforementioned expenses amount to fifteen *guan* of cash.
