If they do not go out, they do not sound [the bells].
When the Sangha hall bell and the hall bell are sounded, the great bell is not struck.
Once the assembly has gathered and the recitation of dhāraṇīs is finished.
At the beginning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Verse of Universal Dedication (*pariṇāmanā-gāthā*) is recited;
the entire assembly chants it in unison.
If it coincides with the first or fifteenth day of the lunar month, they offer prayers for the longevity of the Emperor.
The *kai-i* (dedication of merit) by the *vinaya-dhara* continues until the thirteenth day of the seventh month.
The ritual procedures for the concluding distribution are the same as before;
however, at the end of the final chapter of the mantra recited by the head chanter of the *Lengyan*, the *vinaya-dhara* performs the dedication and concludes the service.

The assembly of bhikṣus present before us has recited the *Śūraṅgama Mantra*. We dedicate this merit to the assembly of Dharma-protecting deities, dragons, and heavenly beings, as well as to the local spirits, monastic temples, and all holy ones, so that they may universally create [merit]. May those in the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties be freed from all suffering; may the four debts of gratitude and all beings within the three worlds receive this grace. May the state be peaceful and free from war, may the winds and rains be harmonious, and may the people enjoy health and joy. May this entire assembly cultivate themselves toward further advancement, suddenly leaping to the tenth stage without hindrance. May the mountain monastery remain tranquil and free from all calamity. May donors and believers take refuge [in the Triple Gem], and may the Sangha’s merit and wisdom increase. To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas: Mahāprajñāpāramitā. This commentary on the words of the sutra was initiated with the refinement of gold forged and sharpened; its edge shall never be blunted.
Just as a mirror reflects without distortion when polished and refined,
so too did the former sages manifest the mechanism of suppression and exaltation to shatter the subtle delusions of sentient beings.

Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda, wondrously harmonizing with the hidden power; the World-Honored One Mañjuśrī, uniquely manifesting the patterns of the Dharma. To expound the teachings and contemplations of a single lifetime, there are both contemplation and teaching; to reveal the cultivation and realization of the secret cause, there is neither realization nor cultivation; to clarify true vision, all dust is stilled.
Like flowers in the sky that have no stems, I abide in right concentration to restrain all movement;
like still water that does not ripple,
how could I, a mere descendant, possess any knowledge?
Reciting these final words as a self-exhortation,
I prostrate with the wish that the kalpas of the Ganges River be condensed into a single thought-moment,
so that this long period of uninterrupted time may pass.
The lands of the ten directions are gathered together in one abode;

all have attained perfect enlightenment. Amidst the dispersal of the assembly, this grove and garden appear clearly as the Jetavana Monastery. The ocean-like multitude from former times stands solemnly here, as if at a single gathering on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. The great trichiliocosm is contained within a single mote of dust, and the three periods of time are fused within a single thought-moment.
Coinciding with the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the end of the summer retreat,
there was neither transgression nor observance;
all myriad phenomena were intermingled as one.
Who is ordinary and who is sage?
Every person is wondrously awakened;
in every land is Vairocana. Manifesting a thousand, ten thousand, and ten million bodies, he transcends the fifty-seven stages.
Using a finger to illustrate that a finger is not a finger,
the finger itself also vanishes.
It is like using emptiness to store emptiness and thereby merging with emptiness.
How could Master Kōng not have provided for us? Out of compassion for our youth and special encouragement for our ignorance,
we uphold his bequeathed teachings and rely upon the unimpeded peace of the summer retreat.
I humbly pray that, though Śamatha is fully endowed with the gates of all worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), its great function may flourish extensively as it enters the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Regarding the ordination age plaques: the Hall Office, the Attendant Office, and the various quarters shall prepare them in advance according to the ordination age.
On the afternoon of the fourteenth day,
the tablet of the Hall Administrator (Tangsi) was displayed in the upper section in front of the Sangha Hall,
and the tablet of the Attendant Official (Shisī) was displayed in the lower section of the Dharma Hall.
The plaques for the various quarters are displayed within the quarters.
Each is prepared with an incense table, burner, and candles for offerings.
After the assembly has each lit incense and completed their prostrations, [the ritual continues].
Each person shall then collect their name tablets and hang them up.

Regarding the "Small Seat Soup" (small-seated *tang*) for the Abbot, it is practiced according to four seasonal periods; following ancient tradition, there are three types of seating arrangements for this soup.
The first arrangement is divided into two variations.
Specifically for the East Hall and West Hall, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) is requested;
the Second Seat (Dierzuo) serves as the attendant, and they depart in four groups.
The Head Official (Toushou) constitutes one group.
1. The administrative officer (zhishi) exits from the west corridor; 2. the senior monk (qinjiu) exits; 3.
the senior monk of the east corridor exits; 4.
the attendant (guangban) of the West Hall exits from the third seat.
For the most part, there are six types of activities:
those pertaining to the home mountain (the primary monastery) and those pertaining to various other locations.
Seating is arranged according to the rank of one's office;
those of equal rank sit in order of seniority.
The Head Seat (shouzuo) and his attendants prepare a preliminary seating chart.
Present this to the Abbot for deliberation and determination.
On the appointed day, prepare name-boards according to the list.
In the afternoon, set out tables and ritual offerings.
Prepare one, two, or three seats and arrange them in the lower section of the dormitory hall. The Head Seat (Shouzuo),
the Administrative Head (Dusi), and the Guest-inviting Attendant (Qingke Shizhe) shall take their positions at the front of the East and West Halls.
Each person goes to the abbot’s quarters to prostrate and request, saying:
"We respectfully invite the Abbot, Venerable Master, to partake of hot tonic this evening in the dormitory hall,
specifically for your sake."
The other head officers in charge of affairs, including the Chief of the Guest Quarters and the Attendant, shall invite [the guest] with these words:
"Venerable Abbot, before the morning assembly, we request that you proceed to the sleeping hall for a special offering of hot water."
Having finished hanging the placards in the dormitory hall and lighting the candles and incense,
the attendant in charge of guests informs the chief attendant.
Next, the drum is struck to cover the abbot’s quarters.
The guests for the initial seat assemble, and the attendant bows and leads them forward.
Upon reaching the presence of the abbot, they inquire after his well-being and then enter their positions according to the seating chart, standing firmly in place.
The incense-bearer and the guest-inviting attendant proceed separately to the front of the person being honored specifically for them.
After they have circulated to inquire after their well-being and invited them to be seated,
they return to their positions and stand side by side.
The incense-bearer steps forward to offer incense,
then returns to his position;
simultaneously with the guest-inviting attendant, he turns to distribute himself, performing circumambulatory salutations and bowing to the incense.
Upon hearing the second strike of the wooden board, the hot water is distributed throughout.
After circumambulating and bowing, the serving of the hot water is completed.
The incense-bearer attendant then advances to offer the *shōkō* (light-accompanying) incense.
Upon one strike of the wooden board, the cups are collected; upon five strikes of the drum, the assembly withdraws from their seats.
The ritual procedures for the three seating periods are identical.
In the monastic groves (*sōrin*), the serving of tea and soup constitutes the principal ceremony.
Lately, because of frequent disputes over the relative status of ranks,
[the practice] has been neglected and no longer taught.
The abbot should take the effort to implement it.
Those who are venerable elders of the Jianghu (the world of scholars and officials) should exert their efforts to encourage this.
It is hoped that future generations will have a model to emulate.
Regarding the Chanting at the Temple of the Four Quarters’ Earth Deities on the Four Festivals: whenever a festival occurs...
On the afternoon of the day before, offerings were solemnly prepared at the Local Deity Hall (Jindītáng).
Incense burners, candle stands, censers, and vases were arranged.
The attendants of the hall administration notified the assembly to hang the plaque for the recitation of mantras.
The striking of the wooden board while circumambulating the corridors is the same as on the third and eighth days of the month.
When the assembly has gathered, they stand facing one another in the formation of a goose flight.
The abbot [proceeds] to the Hall of the Founding Ancestors.
Next, offer incense before the Great Hall and perform three prostrations.
Strike the large wooden board three times and ring the great bell.
When the abbot arrives before the assembly, the members bow their heads and join their palms to welcome him;
the attendant follows behind, merely passing by with hands crossed at the chest. After burning incense, they return to their respective positions.
The practitioner strikes the gong, the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) steps forward to bow to the assembly, and after the incense has been offered,
the recitation and dedication follow as seen later.
It is essential to consider:
The fragrant breeze fans the wilds as the God of Fire presides over his quarter;
it is the time when the Dharma King observes the *pāda-pāśa* (the foot-binding retreat), and the day when the sons of Śākya protect living beings.
With reverent solemnity, we assemble the great multitude to proceed in order to this sacred shrine.
We shall recite and uphold the vast and majestic names of the myriad virtues,
dedicating the merit to the true lords presiding over this hall.
I pray that through your protective grace, I may attain peace and dwell securely in the four modes of conduct.
I humbly rely upon the assembly to recite [the mantra] as follows.
It is most earnestly considered that:
The golden wind fans the wilds as the White Emperor presides over the quarter.
This is the occasion when the Buddha-king releases the retreat; it is the day when the year of the Dharma reaches its full cycle.
For ninety days there were no hardships, and the entire assembly remained in peace.
Reciting and upholding the great names of the myriad virtues, we look upward to repay the true lords of this hall;
we rely upon the assembly to recite [the following]... and so forth.
I respectfully consider that as the year draws to a close and the season of the "Cloud-Recording" arrives,
this is the moment when the first yang returns— the beginning from which the myriad phenomena are brought forth.
With reverent solemnity, the great assembly proceeds in order to the spirit shrine.
Reciting and upholding the Great Name of Ten Thousand Virtues,
they dedicate the merit to the True Sovereigns of this hall.
I look up to rely upon the great assembly to recite [the following] at length.
It is essential to consider that as the divine artificer operates in secret, the cycle of the year’s calendar has come to its full term.
All rejoice in the peace of the four seasons and prepare to celebrate the auspiciousness of the returning three yangs.
We respectfully assemble the great multitude and solemnly proceed to the sacred shrine.
Reciting and upholding the great names of the myriad virtues, I dedicate this merit to the true lords of this hall.
I rely upon the assembly to recite [the following]... [etc.]
I now dedicate the merit of the preceding recitations to the local deities of this mountain,
the various ranks of guardian deities of the monastery, and the true sovereigns of the assembly hall.
It is my hope that—
Divine merit and efficacy accorded their support,
manifesting deeds of beneficial service;
the garden of the Dharma flourished in supreme excellence.
May the blessing of impartiality be granted forever.
[The phrase] "Again, for the sake of the honored assembly, we contemplate all beings of the ten directions and the three periods of time," and so forth, is identical for all four seasonal festivals.

At the four seasonal festivals, the Kitchen Office specially prepares a medicinal broth for the Head Seat and the assembly; once the recitation is finished, the Kitchen Office specially prepares a medicinal broth for the Head Seat and the assembly.
Regarding the observance of etiquette in the Sangha Hall:
after the meal has concluded, the Chief Administrator (Dusi) prepares the notice for the hot water bath as detailed below,
and immediately orders the guest master (Kektou) and his attendants to prepare trays, cloths, incense burners, and candles.
Proceed to the front hall before the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera),
insert incense, perform a prostration with full-body contact,
and announce: "This evening, we shall gather in the Cloud Hall."
He specifically prepares the soup for the Head Seat and the assembly.
He humbly requests that, out of compassion, you deign to descend in person to receive the announcement slip from the Head Seat.
He then instructs the tea attendant of his own quarters to deliver it to the offering attendant.
A notice is posted on the lower section of the front wall of the Sangha Hall.

The Guest Master (Kektou) of the Administrative Office (Kusi) follows by announcing: "We respectfully invite you to partake of the medicinal soup; please take your seats. Thereafter, the Abbot (Duzi) carries incense and proceeds to the Abbot’s Quarters (Fangzhang).
Having prostrated once, he requests, saying: "Tonight, in the Cloud Hall, we specially offer hot tonic for the Head Seat and the assembly.
We humbly entreat the Venerable Master’s compassion to deign to honor us with his presence. He then instructs the Guest Master.
Please inform the various quarters of the retired and long-serving monks to each hang a sign for the serving of hot soup;
once this has been done, invite them one by one.
In front of the Sangha Hall, a nameplate is displayed.
The seat for the Head Seat (Shouzuo) is established facing the Abbot (Zhuchi).
Between the upper and lower sections, the seats for the assembly are arranged.
The ritual assistant shall be specially upright and dedicated to others.
Upon the completion of the recitation,
he shall immediately strike the *zhāi* drum once.
The assembly returns to their respective bowl positions.
The group of head officials all return together to the front board.
The administrative head (Du-si) follows them in, bows to the Head Seat (Shou-za), and leaves his position.
He then bows and yields his place to the next head official, who steps forward to lead the procession.
He follows behind the Head Seat as they escort him back to his position,
passing behind the Sacred Monk.
The aforementioned person exits the hall and escorts the abbot into the hall;
the head of offerings then slowly strikes the bell in front of the hall seven times.
Escort the abbot to his seat;
he then proceeds to bow before the head seat and takes his place,
following the same procedure as previously described when exiting from the head seat’s platform.
He rises and circumambulates the hall once.
He visits the upper and lower sections of the outer hall,
returns to the center of the hall, stands, and bows to the seated assembly.
Proceeding forward, burn incense; then, returning from the outer hall of the upper and lower sections, place the incense case back in its original position.
Immediately go before the person specially honored and perform a greeting.
Exit to the right and stand before the abbot to perform a greeting.
He continues to circumambulate and inquire after [the assembly] once more.
Upon reaching the outer hall, he returns to the center of the hall to inquire after them and stands to one side.
Then, the bell in front of the hall is struck twice.
The senior monk first serves the special guest and the abbot with hot water;
next, he serves the hot water for the assembly, passing the pitcher around until it is empty.
He then proceeds to the front of the special guest to perform a formal greeting.
Exit from the right side in front of the Honored Sangha;
perform three full prostrations with the robes fully spread out,
and then circumambulate the hall once.
Having completed the circuit of the outer hall, lead the entire assembly to enter and perform prostrations before the Ritual Master (Juzhi).
For the first unfolding of the curtain, say: "On this day, we offer coarse soup; may you graciously descend with compassion to accept our offerings."

Your humble servant is overcome with the utmost gratitude. Once again, on this very day and at this auspicious hour, I respectfully wish that the Venerable Abbot may enjoy many blessings in his daily life.
Having prostrated three times in accordance with the ritual, I conclude.
Turning around, he leads the attendants to follow behind the Honored Monk;
they exit through the right side of the hall and stand in a row.
The Head Seat follows out and performs a prostration with full contact to express gratitude for the medicinal broth.
Then, from the upper section, one enters the special seat for the guest.
The head monk returns to the center to burn incense and withdraws for the sake of the *yàoshí* (medicinal stone/meal).
The attendant of the Hall Office calls out, "I request the assembly to set down their bowls. The attendant then advances to the table set for the abbot’s special guest.

The assembly spreads their *pātra* bowls, but the bowl-keeper does not descend with the bowls from the storehouse. The steward prepares bowls and plates, and the medicinal food (*yàoshí*) is served. When it is finished, the drum is struck three times, and the assembly withdraws from their seats.

The Abbot has already posted a notice exempting the formal greetings (*rénshì*), which states: "For this particular festival, all formal greetings shall be conducted on the Dharma Hall floor tomorrow; attendance at the Abbot’s quarters is hereby waived. We hope that the assembly will take full note of this. [Signed] "The Mountain Dweller, [Name]. This supplementary notice is posted above the interval in the Sangha Hall.

When the signal bell for the end of the session is struck without sounding the call to prayer, members of each local community shall proceed according to the posted notices to their respective locations to perform collective prostrations; the four seasonal festivals are all conducted in this same manner.
However, at the winter festival, after the ritual soup has been consumed, offerings of rice cakes and fruits are presented.
Just as the medicinal decoctions are being administered,
the Ku-si (Provision Office) will serve one round of hot tonic this evening in the Cloud Hall specifically for the Chief Seat and the assembly.
I briefly set forth the protocols for this particular occasion.
I humbly hope that all compassionate ones will deign to descend and grace us with their presence.

[Official Notice] On the [day] of this month, the bhikṣus of the storehouse office, [Name] and others, respectfully announce: Regarding the ritual procedures for the commencement of the retreat (jie-zhi), on the day of the commencement, at the second watch of the fifth watch of the night, the members of the two orders—both senior and junior, as well as the retired elders—[shall assemble].
Those who have come from the rivers and lakes to attend to affairs, as well as those from the local countryside, lay relatives, and junior disciples,
should all proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and perform prostrations. However,
if one sees the notice posted before the Sangha Hall announcing the exemption from formal greetings, they need not do so.
In that case, he need not go.
The attendant shall inform the abbot’s quarters, and the acolytes shall announce to the assembly to hang up the sign for the morning session.
After the gruel has been consumed.

When the Abbot has finished preaching the Dharma, he shall explain in detail the sequence of the ritual proceedings, stating: "Upon descending from the seat, one first performs a single prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chulil*) to the West Hall Master.
Next, one performs two formal bows with three prostrations (*liangzhan sanli*) to the Administrative Officers."
Next, he exchanges greetings with the Head Seat and the assembly by performing two prostrations with the hands extended and three bows.
Next, he exchanges greetings with the Head Seat and the assembly by performing two prostrations with the hands extended and three bows.
The Karmadāna returns first to the administrative office (kusi).
The Head Seat leads the assembly to the administrative office (kusi).
They perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths as a formal greeting.
The Head Seat then returns to the upper section of the Sangha Hall.
The Rear Hall Official leads the assembly back to the lower section of the Sangha Hall.
After performing three prostrations with open hands as a greeting to the Head Seat,
they stand according to the diagram for chanting.
The Head Seat leads the assembly into the hall and stands in their places.
The Head Seat leaves his position, burns incense before the Sacred Monk, performs three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*),
circumambulates the hall once, and returns to his station.
The practitioner calls out,
and the Head Seat bows in thanks to the assembly with three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths.
Next, the administrative officers enter the hall to burn incense and perform three full prostrations with opened sitting cloths.
Having circumambulated the hall once,
they stand in a row at the head of the seat for the Holy Monk.
The attendant (xingzhe) then calls out:
The administrative official performs a prostration with touching of the ground (litu) before the assembly and three prostrations with touching (sanbai), then does not exit the hall.
The abbot enters the hall, burns incense, performs three full prostrations with the robes spread out (dazhan sanbai),
circumambulates the hall once, and returns to his seat.
The ritual master shouts, "The Abbot and the assembly shall perform a general prostration with full contact for greetings; three bows.
He shouts again.
The assembly collectively performs prostrations, touching the ground with their foreheads in three bows.

They then proceed in order to visit the various quarters. The attendant who has descended from his seat then advances with the incense burner, candle stand, table, and ritual vessels, arranging them in a single straight line.
Once this is completed, [the ceremony continues].
The West Hall Master steps forward for the formal greeting;
next, the Administrative Head (Zhishi) steps forward to offer incense.
Opening the outer robe, he says: "At this time of the summer retreat, I am honored to serve you with the water pitcher and towel."
Relying solely upon the sustaining power of the Dharma, may there be no obstacles to my vows.

Once again, on this day at the beginning of summer, during these auspicious times, I respectfully wish that the Venerable Abbot enjoys many blessings in his daily life. I prostrate three times in humble salutation.
The abbot replies with a single bow.
Next, the head seat leads the assembly in offering incense;
the retired officials and all the various quarters follow in succession.
The incense is offered in succession.
The prostrations and the formal address are the same as before.
When the assembly has withdrawn, the abbot sits in the lotus posture, and the attendant and junior disciples offer incense and perform prostrations.
Next, the head official leads the assembly of attendants in offering incense, prostrating, and bowing. Following this,
the head official leads the senior attendants, the various hall stewards, palanquin carriers, and servants in their salutations.
The Head Seat leads the assembly to the administrative office (kusi),
where they perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths as a formal greeting.
The Head Seat of the Rear Hall leads the assembly back to the lower section in front of the Sangha Hall and stands there in formation.
The Head Seat of the front hall occupies the upper chamber.
The attendant of the Hall Office calls out, "The assembly shall perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths to greet the Head Seat.
Once this is completed, they stand according to the diagram for chanting.
The Head Seat leads the assembly on a circuit through the hall, returning to their positions to stand.
The Attendant briefly arrives and conducts a circuit through half the hall.
The attendant stands behind the shrine of the Holy Monk.
Those who have arrived for a brief visit stand fixedly before the attendant.
The Head Seat leaves his position and advances before the Holy Monk to burn incense.
Perform three prostrations with fully extended mats.
Circumambulate the hall once.
Return to your position and announce:
The Head Seat bows in thanks to the assembly;
having completed three prostrations with full prostration (*tuchli*),
the administrators (*zhishi*) enter to burn incense and perform prostrations, completing the circuit of the hall, and then stand in a row at the head of the Holy Monk’s seat.

The *he* (the master of ceremonies) says, "The administrative officers prostrate to thank the assembly. Having performed three prostrations with the forehead touching the ground (*duili*), they do not leave the hall.

The Abbot enters the hall, burns incense, performs prostrations, and circumambulates the hall before returning to his seat; the junior disciples must certainly avoid him and exit through the rear gate.
When the Master has finished the lecture on the ritual and returns to his seat for tea, he utters "Hé! and says: "The Abbot and the assembly shall exchange greetings;

perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths. He utters "Hé! again and says: "The assembly shall all together perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths. This is recorded in the ancient regulations.
After the administrative official (jishi) has exited the hall, he proceeds to enter it;
however, he does not respond to the official’s salutation.
This is because there is no instance where a salutation is not answered.
Recently, Master Xishi and Master Yishan both taught and practiced in this manner:
those who recognized [the signal] approved of it; the administrative officers withdrew their bodies and exited the hall, and the attendants arrived briefly and followed them out immediately after.
The assembly takes their seats.
The attendant returns to the center to inquire after them and bow them into their places.
He then proceeds to the central incense burner, moving between the upper and lower sections, and goes to the outer hall to burn incense.
Place the incense case back in its original position.
Withdraw to the center of the hall and exchange greetings.
Having finished exchanging greetings with those in the upper and lower sections and outside the hall, return to stand in the middle.
Strike the bell twice.
Distribute tea until the vessel is empty, then exit as before and stand in the position of inquiry.
Strike the bell once to collect the cups.
The bell is struck three times;
the assembly leaves the hall and disperses,
and the abbot proceeds in order to visit the various quarters.
Each quarters shall be solemnly furnished with chairs and incense tables;
the abbot shall wait outside the gate and proceed from the first quarters along the eastern corridor.
Rising, they proceed before the incense table in their respective quarters.
The head of the quarter, together with the assembly, offers incense and says:

"On this day, we ought to offer our congratulations; we are deeply honored that you have deigned to return our courtesy with this incense. In response, the guest offers incense and says: "I have just received your gracious congratulations; I specifically offer these thanks. He then escorts the abbot for several steps.
Furthermore, standing to the right of the incense table with palms joined in greeting, he waits until the assembly has passed; then,
following at their tail, he proceeds to circumambulate them in order.
The attendants of each quarters follow in succession to perform the circumambulation.
Upon reaching the Dharma Hall,
the Abbot stands in the center before the incense table.
The assembly proceeds past, with three individuals leading the way to inquire after one's well-being.
They circulate until they reach the side of the incense table in their own quarters,
where each stands in their respective order with palms joined.
Distribute [the items] by circling through each one individually;
the four sections are identical in this regard.

During the four occasions when the abbot presides over the *bǐfú* (dharma-lecture), he says at the time of the *xiǎocān* (small informal sermon): "Tomorrow morning, after the midday meal has concluded..."
The Chief Administrator (Kannya), the Steward (Jisha), the Rector (Nin'a),
and the Attendant (Shijō) shall carry the plaque and fly-whisk to the Head Seat (Shuso) and request him for service at each respective location.
On the evening of the following day, he shall preside over the *bǐfú* (the whisk) for the assembly; on the next day, after the midday meal, he shall burn incense.

The attendant shall immediately instruct the guest-head acolyte to carry the master’s staff, plaque, and whisk, while servants carry the tray, cloth, incense burner, and candles, accompanied by approximately the head monk (*dū sì*) and the rector (*wéi ná*).
Together they proceed to the quarters of each of the head officers.
They offer incense and perform one prostration with full obeisance, reporting:
"By the compassionate command of the Abbot, the Venerable Master."
We, [Name] and others, respectfully carry this plaque and whisk to specifically offer our invitation. This evening,
we shall perform the Buddha-recitation for the assembly, having invited each one individually.
The Head Seat (shouzuo) coordinates with the other heads of the community (toushou) who have received the invitation;
accompanied by attendants (xingzhe), they take the plaque, whisk, and staff,
and proceed together to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to offer their formal leave.
The abbot should earnestly exhort him to leave.
The head seat then turns and reports: "Since the Master’s command is solemn, I cannot decline.
May I venture to borrow the Dharma seat?"
I humbly beseech your compassionate grace. In the past,
those who held the whisk (the master of the assembly) were frequently provided with a separate seat.
Now, this practice has become customary.
Later generations have not heard of it. Next, proceed to the place of the incense-burning attendant and borrow the Dharma drum.
The whisk-bearer instructs the tea-head attendant and the ritual practitioner to invite the holy monks, the attendants, and the Zen guests;
once the incense has been burned and the tea offered, he says: "Tonight, there will be the whisk-bearing ceremony."

He immediately requests the attendant to burn incense; when the Zen practitioners have finished their inquiries, he further instructs the acolyte to hang the "Staff-Bearer" (bingfu) plaque before the Sangha Hall.
The Abbot then invites the staff-bearer to partake of medicinal food (yaoshi).
Exempting those who would otherwise have to attend the funeral procession.
The attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi Xingzhe) arranges the Dharma seat by spreading a *fusi* screen to the left of it and establishes the position for the Abbot.
When the evening bell tolls,
the ritual attendant covers the whisk-bearer;
next, the abbot covers [the whisk] as the drum is struck once and the assembly gathers.
The procedure for the minor *sǎn* (small sermon) is the same as for the formal ceremony.
The abbot steps forward and returns directly to his position, standing still.
The chief steward (*dutì*), the ritual master (*wéinà*), and the attendants (*shìzhě*) proceed together to the person presiding over the *bǐngfú* (the ceremonial whisk) and exchange greetings.
The whisk-bearer proceeds to the abbot’s seat to pay his respects,
then to the prior to pay his respects,
and continues the circuit until the end of the assembly row.
Next, he proceeds before his own class to perform a greeting.
He continues this circuit until reaching the end of the row, at which point he raises his hands to perform a universal greeting with the entire assembly.
He then ascends the seat and sits down.
The whisk-bearing attendant (bingfu shizhe) and the attendants of the abbot (fangzhang shizhe) exit from beneath the seat to perform the ritual inquiry (wensun).
The two orders of officials and the West Hall monks inquire in succession.

When the abbot performs the inquiry, the person holding the whisk should rise and then return to their seat, saying: "Attendant, please invite the Abbot to sit cross-legged. The whisk-bearing attendant then approaches the abbot and performs the ritual inquiry.
Turning around, he ascends the seat and burns incense.
Holding his sitting cloth (niṣīdana), he makes inquiries;
then, with palms joined, he stands to one side.
After the person holding the whisk has finished the dialogue of questions and answers,

and the formal presentation of the outline, the expression of gratitude, and the addresses to the Abbot, the two orders of officers, the retired elders, and the assembly of the various quarters are concluded. Then,
the public case for the Abbot’s small-scale sermon is presented.
Having either picked up the whisk or finished the verse, he descends from the seat.
He bows before the abbot and returns to his original position.
Those who follow in succession to hold the whisk perform the same rites as previously described.
When the whisk-holding ceremony is concluded,
the guest master (katō) of the abbot’s quarters shall announce the invitation for hot soup and fruit,
as is done during the small session of instruction (sōsan).
The person holding the whisk then carries incense and,
together with the others, proceeds to the abbot’s quarters to offer thanks.
They take their seats for tea and fruit.
The following day, the Abbot invites [the guest] for tea.
If the Chief Administrator (Dusi) prepares a vegetarian feast, he shall also invite [the guest] for tea and half-feast refreshments.
On another day, he ascends the hall to express his gratitude for the hospitality provided.
Alternatively, if the West Hall is requested to stand in the assembly, they shall preside over the *bǐfú* (the incense-burning sermon) on the second night.
When the Abbot delivers a *xiǎocān* (a brief informal sermon), the West Hall should offer a detailed and earnest exhortation to proclaim the Dharma.
One may freely select and provide verses for public cases (gong'an) to mutually stimulate and exalt this Way; recently, however,
expressions of gratitude have become a mere habit of excessive verbosity.
To cause others to grow weary of listening and to incur the derision of those who possess true knowledge,
is because one who holds the whisk [as the presiding master] takes the Dharma as his gift;
if he merely conforms to temporal etiquette and simply enumerates names, he fails in this duty.
A brief mention of these transgressions will suffice.

Regarding the special tea service for the Head Seat and the assembly during the four seasonal festivals of the Abbot: on the appointed day, after the morning gruel, the guest-inviting attendant shall write out the tea notice, as shown below.
Prepare a tray, a cloth, an incense burner, and candles; proceed to the quarters and light incense.
Prostrate and request: "Venerable Abbot, this morning after the midday meal, you shall partake of tea in the Cloud Hall."
I specifically request that you grant me the honor of posting this notice on the upper section in front of the Sangha Hall.
The guest master (kètóu) and his attendants shall then invite the successive head officers of the various quarters,
as well as the administrative officers (zhīshì).
The attendant for lighting incense hangs up the tea signboard.
The long board resonates.
The guest-inviting attendant enters the hall and burns one stick of incense before the Sacred Monk.
Perform three full prostrations with the robes spread wide.
Circumambulate the hall once.
Upon reaching the center, perform a formal inquiry and withdraw.
This is called "Circumambulating the Hall to Request Tea.
A special signboard is set up in front of the hall;
the Head Seat (shouzuo) sits facing the Abbot (zhuchi).
The chief administrator (shangshou zhishi) shares a seating position with the abbot;
the rector (weina) follows next.
The subordinate administrators (yici zhishi) share seating positions with those who have received special invitations.
The drums are beaten to assemble the congregation.

The incense-burning attendant performs the rites together with the steward’s office for the special offering of hot water; then, together with the Head Seat, they proceed before the Abbot to express gratitude for the tea.
They perform two prostrations with the robes fully spread and three full prostrations.
First folding: "On this occasion, we have been specially graced with the offering of tea;
our humble hearts are filled with the utmost gratitude. Second folding: "At this very time of year, we respectfully wish you all well."
When the Abbot is receiving guests, the Resident Preceptor (Zhuzhi) should prostrate three times with the hands touching the ground;
at each full prostration, the Abbot should signal him to stop.
Upon the final prostration with hands touching the ground, the Abbot shall respond with one prostration.
The Head Seat turns around and exits to the right from behind the Holy Monk;
the Abbot briefly sees him off and returns to his position,
while the Attendant burns the "light-companion" incense.
The bell is struck to collect the bowls, and the drum is beaten to dismiss the assembly,
as before. The Head Seat first proceeds to the Dharma Hall.
The Abbot awaits [the arrival of] the assembly to offer thanks;
if they are excused, he performs a *wenshen* (inquiry).

**Notice:** This morning, following the midday meal, the Head Monk (Tangtou Wuheshang) will serve one round of tea in the Cloud Hall (*yuntang*) specifically for the Chief Seat (*shouzuo*) and the assembly, as a modest mark of respect for the seasonal observance. We also respectfully invite all the administrative officers (*zhishi*) to grace the occasion with their presence. On the ______ day of this month, respectfully submitted by the attendant official, [Name]. **Tea Service for the Four Seasons for the Chief Seat and Assembly at the Storehouse Office (*kusì*):** Following the morning gruel on the second day of each of the four seasonal festivals, tea is served for the Chief Seat and the assembly at the Storehouse Office.
The administrative office prepares a tea notice; the tea is invited along with the soup, the announcement is made to the assembly, and the signboard is hung.
When the long board gong sounds, one enters for the regular tea service, which is conducted in the same manner as the serving of attendants.
Upon retiring from the fast, remove the name tablets. Arrange the seats,
strike the drum to assemble the assembly,
bow for seating, bow for incense, and bow for tea, then perform the ritual salutation while circumambulating the hall.
The Abbot goes forward to perform prostrations and deliver a formal address;
this is conducted in the same manner as the ritual for the hot tonic.

On the third day of each of the four seasonal festivals, the Prior’s Hall (Qiantang) specially prepares tea for the assembly of the Rear Hall (Houtang). On the third day of each of the four seasonal festivals, the Prior’s Hall specially prepares tea for the assembly of the Rear Hall.

The Head Seat prepares a formal tea invitation (chazhuang) as seen below; he then proceeds to the Rear Hall, the Head Seat’s quarters, and the Abbot’s quarters to request the tea service and perform the prescribed rituals.
The sequence of these proceedings is identical to that of the administrative office (kusō).
Special Tea Service for the Office Holders. [Name], Chief Seat of the Rear Hall, respectfully informs [Name], Chief Seat of the Front Hall:

Having retired from the morning meal, we shall now attend the tea service. A single session of tea will be served in the Cloud Hall specifically for the office holders. To briefly commemorate the observance of [Name]'s festival day, we further invite all the office holders to graciously join us as honored guests. On this day of the month, [Name], of humble station, respectfully submits this document. [Seal] Formal Request to the Chief Seat of the Rear Hall and the Assembly: [Name], of humble station, respectfully seals this. Morning and Evening Hall Rounds of Tea. After the Abbot has finished his discourse upon ascending the hall, [the following occurs]: Morning and Evening Hall Rounds of Tea. The Abbot ascends the hall to preach the Dharma; having concluded, [the rounds of tea follow].

Baoyun descended from his seat and conducted the tea service while circulating through the hall. When the assembly reached the front of the Sangha Hall, they stood according to the *nian-song tu* (recitation diagram).
They entered the hall in succession;
those who had arrived temporarily and the attendants (*shizhe*) followed the assembly in their circuit.
Upon reaching the rear of the Sage’s shrine,
he briefly enters and stands facing the attendant.
Once the assembly has completed their circuit and is standing still, the hall bell is struck seven times.
The abbot enters the hall, burns incense, and performs one circuit of the hall before returning to his position.
The administrators line up before the Sacred Monk and perform a bow;
they then turn and bow before the abbot.
Starting from the head seat, the incense-bearer circles the hall once.
Those who have arrived temporarily and the attendants follow after the administrative affairs are concluded.
The incense-bearer then takes his place in the center, bows in greeting, and invites the assembly to be seated.
Waiting for the assembly to be seated,
he steps forward to burn incense and proceeds through the upper and lower halls and the outer hall,
first entering the lower section.
Next, having placed the incense censer at its original position before the burner and performed the ritual salutations and bows for each incense offering in turn,
return to the original seat.
Strike the bell twice.
The tea pitcher-bearer exits and again performs the inquiry as before;
they bow for the tea and withdraw.
One stroke of the bell signals the collection of the cups.
The bell is struck three times;
the abbot exits the hall,
followed by the head seat and the assembly in succession.
If one is constrained by external circumstances,
or if one remains in residence and does not attend the assembly for a short time, then once the gruel has been finished,
one proceeds to one's seat to drink tea.
The attendant performs the ritual as before.
When the Abbot serves tea in the Hall for the monks on their seasonal anniversaries (*jielüe*), after the tea service in the Sangha Hall has concluded,
the attendant, together with the Guest Master, goes to the Hall to serve tea.
The guest master announces the arrival of the visiting head; the attendant hangs the tea signboard and notifies the assembly.
Hot water is prepared and cups are brought out; the guest is invited to join the director of the kitchen (Dianzuo) for the ceremony.
The abbot sends tea in advance.
The attendant arrives at the administrative office (kusi).
The head cook (dianzuo) receives him inside.
The head of the assembly (candou) and the hall master (tangzhu), leading the various attendants (xingzhe), welcome him at the gate.
The attendant occupies the position of the master, acting on behalf of the abbot.

The registrar takes the seat to the right; the attendant steps forward from the center to burn a single incense stick, returns to his position, and bows with his hands to the assembly as they take their seats.
When the tea ceremony is concluded, the *jizō* (kitchen steward) escorts [the guests] out;
the *santō* (head of the assembly) and the *dōju* (abbot’s assistant) see them off at the gate.
They then proceed immediately to the *bōzō* (abbot’s quarters) to express their gratitude for the tea.
After the Head of the Abbot’s Office has finished serving tea in the Hall of Practice,
the administrative officials proceed to the Hall of Practice.
The *chajishi* (tea-offering administrator) occupies the seat of honor.
The *dianzuo* (head cook) distributes the tea and performs the ritual salutations in the same manner as the abbot’s attendants.

Upon escorting them out the door, he cries out, "The head of the assembly and the great congregation proceed to the *kusisi* (storehouse office) to express gratitude for the tea. The *ketou* (guest master) of the *kusisi* reports back, saying, "The *chajishi* has conveyed word that the tea is excused. The *tou-shou* (heads of the monastic order) wait until the tea for the Sangha Hall is served and the two orders of officials have finished their rounds.
The attendant of the Hall Office shall inform the head of the retreat group to hang the signboard and notify the assembly.

He shall then invite the Chief Cook to accompany him in performing the rites; the departure from the administrative office (kusi) and the formal expressions of thanks and dismissal shall be identical to those performed with the administrative office.
Monthly Schedule: What Must Be Known Regarding the Monthly Schedule.
In the first month, on the first day, at certain locations, the assembly performs circumambulation and recites sutras to pray for protection.
Following this, they prepare a formal petition.
Officials, patrons, and abbots of various mountains offer New Year’s greetings.
On the seventeenth day is the anniversary of Baizhang’s passing.
In the second month, on the first day, the hearth is closed within the Sangha Hall.
Alternatively, at mountain temples where it is high and cold, one may not be restricted [by these dates].
On the fifteenth day, the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*.
On the first day of the third month, the Hall Administrator issues the draft roster.
On the Qingming Festival, the Patriarchs’ Hall, the various ancestral pagodas, the lay patrons, the shrine,
and the storehouse office shall notify in advance that they will sweep the grounds and prepare offerings;
the assembly shall gather to chant sutras.
This month, a notice was posted prohibiting the gathering of tea and bamboo shoots from the mountain forests.
On the first day of the fourth month, the *danguo* (guest quarters) were locked.
Between the fourth and fifth days, there was the incense offering and the general discourse (*pushe*). On the eighth day, the Buddha’s birthday, the Buddha was bathed.
The administrative office prepares black rice in advance;
the Abbot invites the assembly for a light meal before the summer retreat.
On the thirteenth day, the Śūraṅgama Assembly is established.
On the fifteenth day, the retreat begins; as the weather permits, warm curtains are hung inside the Sangha Hall and cooling screens are placed above.
On the fifth month, the Double Fifth Festival, at dawn, the administrative officers burn incense and serve calamus tea within the Sangha Hall.
When the Abbot ascends the hall in the prescribed order to establish a Green Sprout Assembly (*qingmiao hui*),
the Hall Administration (*tangsi*) shall issue in advance attendance lists for the various quarters for the purpose of reading and chanting the scriptures.
The Quarter-Master (*zhisui*) shall inspect all locations to ensure that leaks are repaired and the facilities are in order.
The drainage ditches and canals were dredged.
The Abbot visited the various quarters, hermitages, and pagodas,
providing a day of tea service at each to express his warm regards.
A canopy is hung within the Sangha Hall.
On the first day of the sixth month, due to the onset of the intense summer heat, the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) is exempted from sounding the board for seated meditation.
Upon the commencement of the "Fǔ" period, the Hall Attendant (Tángsī) shall supervise the drying of the meditation mats.
The charcoal master or the administrative office prepares the charcoal cakes.

During the first ten days of the seventh month, the Hall Master (Tangsi) issues in advance the seating lists for the various quarters to attend the *Yulanpen* assembly for the recitation of scriptures.
He also preempts the collection of communal funds.
Preparations were made for the offering of *bali* food;
on the thirteenth day, the *Śūraṅgama* assembly was dispersed,
and on the fifteenth day, the retreat (*zhi*) was concluded.
That evening, the Ullambana Assembly was held;
sutras were chanted and food offerings were made.
On the first day of the eighth month, the guest quarters were opened for the morning.
The guest prefect pre-spreads the mats and cushions within the quarters.
During this month, the resident monks repair their own robes and do not yet hastily pack their bedding;
the curtains of the Sangha Hall are rolled up.
The first day of the ninth month: the Head Seat again strikes the board for seated meditation.
The Hall Superintendent oversees the plastering of the windows of the Sangha Hall and the hanging of the summer screens below and the winter curtains above.
On the morning of the Double Ninth Festival, the administrative officers burn incense and serve *ju-yu* tea.
The Abbot ascends the hall and permits visitors to come and pay their respects.

On the first day of the tenth month, the furnace is opened; there is a formal "Great Inspection" (*dà xiāngkàn*) at the Abbot’s quarters. On the fifth day, it is the anniversary of Bodhidharma’s passing.
The twenty-second day of the eleventh month: the anniversary of the Imperial Preceptor’s passing.
On the winter solstice, the administrative office prepares glutinous rice cakes and fruits in advance.
During this month, matters concerning promotions or resignations may be submitted.
Or, on certain seasonal festivals, the Abbot invites the assembly for a winter snack prior to the winter solstice.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, the Buddha attained enlightenment; the administrative office (Kusi) prepares red fermented grain (hong-zao) in advance.
At the end of the year, all various registers and books are compiled and presented.
The chapter on Festivals and Ancestral Sacrifices concludes. *Imperially Commissioned Baizhang Qinggui*, Scroll Seven.
*Imperially Commissioned Baizhang Qinggui*, Scroll Eight.
The Subject Monk Dehui, Abbot of Dazhi Shousheng Chan Monastery, respectfully presents this revised compilation under imperial decree.

The Subject Monk Dasu, Abbot of Daxiang Jiqing Monastery, respectfully presents this corrected edition under imperial decree. Chapter Nine: On Ritual Implements. In the ancient age, there was transformation without formal teaching.
When transformation was insufficient, ritual and music were instituted.
The song of those who beat the ram-earth blocks was not equal to the performance of the ninefold music;
the drinking from the hollowed-out gourds was not as refined as the five grades of grain wine.
However, as expression arises from substance, the fundamental essence is what is valued.
When our Sage of India first manifested his transformation in the world,
he taught that every person possesses wondrous enlightenment, fundamentally devoid of the distinction between ordinary and sage.
Since every single thing is entirely true, how could there be purity or defilement?
Being without artificial cultivation or realization, it does not involve effortful application;
yet those who are ignorant remain bewildered and lose themselves.
If one were deaf and blind,
[the Buddha] would accordingly establish teachings by striking the *ghanṭā* to assemble the assembly and expound them; these were compiled as the Tripiṭaka.
He cultivated these practices as meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
This continued until the forty-ninth year, at which point his transformative ministry came to an end.
In the Sanskrit language, *ghanṭā* refers generally to any object made of clay, wood, copper, or iron that produces sound.
As for the bells, stone chimes, hand-cymbals, drums, mallets, wooden boards, conchs, and chanting,
the monastic communities have followed their design and employed them to this day,
thereby serving to awaken those who are drowsy or indolent.
It solemnizes the teachings and commands to guide those who are obscure and stagnant, thereby harmonizing spirits and humans.
As for the Great Stability that constantly responds and the Great Function that is eternally quiescent:
hearing is not hearing, and awareness is likewise not awareness.
By examining and by striking [the truth], the profound wind is further propagated;
through non-thought and non-action, the days of transformation naturally lengthen.
How harmonious is this realm of benevolence and longevity!
This is the capital of pure tranquility.
The great bells toll; these great bells are the source from which the commands of the monastic community originate.
When struck at dawn, they shatter the long night and awaken those who sleep.
When striking with longing, one awakens the darkness of the path and clears away the obscurity;
when drawing the pestle, it should be done slowly, and the sound raised should be sustained.
There are three rounds in total, each consisting of thirty-six strokes.
In total, there are one hundred and eight strikes;
at the beginning and end, three strikes each are slightly tighter.
As the bell-ringer rings the bell, they recite this verse of visualization: "May the sound of this bell transcend the Dharma-realm."
Throughout the dark reaches of the Iron Ring Mountains, all hear [this sound].
Hearing the objects of the senses purified, they realize perfect penetration.
All sentient beings attain true awakening while still reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The benefits of responding to the invocation of his name by striking [the bell] are exceedingly great.
On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, when the scriptures are being read, whether the Emperor is ascending or descending from the throne, [one should do so].
On the eighth day of the third month, during the recitation services for the Buddha’s birth, enlightenment, and parinirvāṇa,
and when holding the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi* assembly, chanting scriptures, or serving morning and evening meals,
there shall be eighteen strikes of the bell at the hour of night-cessation (*niyama*).
Regarding the reception and escorting of officials, abbots, and venerable elders,
there shall be no fixed limit on their number;
the administrative office (kusi) shall take charge of this matter.
The Sangha Hall Bell: This is struck whenever the assembly is to be convened.
Whenever the Abbot goes to join the assembly and enters the hall, it is struck seven times.
It is also struck when the meal or gruel service concludes and when the session is dismissed.
At dawn and at the full moon, when the abbot circulates through the hall to drink tea and descends from his seat, he strikes the board three times for each instance.
If the abbot does not attend the hall or is on leave, it is not struck. When reciting the Buddha’s name before the hall, one recites "Namo Amitābha" once.
Ring the light bell once.
Fold the mat once.
The Hall Official presides over this.
The Hall Bell: When the Abbot performs the morning incense offering, this bell is struck seven times.
Whenever the assembly gathers in the hall, it must be struck in coordination with the Sangha Hall bell.
The *Gantong zhuan* (Biographies of Resonant Responses) states that Krakucchanda Buddha was at the Sūtra Hall in Gandhāra.
He cast a bell of blue stone.
At the time of sunrise, various transformation Buddhas emerged together with the sun,
secretly expounding and clearly manifesting the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Those who hear the Dharma and realize the state of sainthood are beyond counting.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"When the bell is struck, all sufferings of the various evil realms are simultaneously suspended."
Furthermore, the *Jinling Zhi* states:
A commoner died suddenly and entered the underworld,
where he saw those bound with the five wooden stocks and fetters.
He told him,
"I am the former sovereign of Southern Tang.
I have come to this state because Song Qiqiu mistakenly killed the surrendered people of Hezhou."
"Whenever I hear the sound of the bell, my suffering ceases for a moment.
Entrust yourself to the successor of the throne and request him on my behalf to have a bell cast."
The people returned and reported everything to the Later Sovereign,
who consequently had a great bell cast at Qingliang Temple,
upon which was inscribed: "Dedicated to the late Emperor Xiaogao, that he might be delivered from obscurity and released from peril."
For the large wooden board used during the two periods of the midday meal and the morning gruel, one strikes it three times for a long duration.
Following the wooden fish, one strikes it three times in rapid succession;
this is called the "long board."
During the *Śūraṅgama* recitation assembly, bells are struck three times each as a warning regarding fire and candles.
When reporting the watches of the night, they are struck in succession according to the respective watch.
The Abbot’s quarters, the treasury office, the head seat’s quarters,
and all other quarters each have a small wooden board;
these are all struck long when the period of silence is opened.
When notifying the assembly, strike twice for each announcement.
Each of the inner and outer sections of the communal quarters has its own wooden board;
the outer board is struck three times daily when the assembly performs the ritual of mutual greeting (*wenshen*).
When sitting in meditation or entering for formal inquiry (zazen and zazensan), strike three times each;
wait until the assembly has returned to the hall and then ring them in succession.
When serving tea or medicinal soup, strike them long and sustained.
When entering the quarters after being assigned to a room, strike the board three times.
When serving tea or soup with cups, strike it twice;
when collecting the cups, strike it once.
When descending from the seat, strike the board three times.
For the small-seat soup, the head monk strikes it long.
For the wooden fish, during the two periods of midday and evening meals, strike it long for two rounds.
For the general labor of the monastic community, strike one long toll;
for the invitation of the practitioners, strike two.
Thus it is traditionally transmitted.
Fish are always awake day and night;
therefore, one carves wooden figures in their likeness and strikes them to warn against dullness and indolence.
At the time for the *zhizhai* (vegetarian) rice gruel,
the monks open their alms bowls within the Sangha Hall;
they chant the Buddha’s name and partake of the food as it is distributed.
When the assembly is offered material gifts, everyone rings [the bell];
the Rector (Karmadāna) presides over this.
When descending from the hall, the attendant of the Holy Sangha (Śrāvaka-saṃgha) rings it.
When the administrative official (kaji) announces his retirement,
the bell is also struck when requesting him to serve.
It is likewise struck when the abbot enters the monastery and prepares to ascend the hall to preach the Dharma.
The foremost among the assembly struck it;
this is called "striking the gavel.
One day, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and the great assembly had gathered in order, [the gavel was struck].
Mañjuśrī strikes the gavel and says:
"Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma King;
such is the Dharma of the Dharma King."
The World-Honored One then descended from his seat.
When the great hall bell tolls early for the abbot and the administrative officers to offer incense,
and when the assembly gathers to observe the recitation of sutras and dharanis.
The attendant of the inner chamber sounds it when the robes are being chanted for;
the *karmadāna* sounds it when the robes are being measured;
and the *upādhyāya* sounds it when the practitioner undergoes tonsure.
A small hand-bell (*keng*) is kept by the attendant of the Hall Office (*tangsi xingzhe*) at all times;
it is struck whenever the assembly recites sutras to mark the intervals for beginning and ending.
*Naobo naobo*. Whenever the *vīnā* (chant leader) bows to the Abbot and the two orders of officers,
when they step forward from the platform to offer incense,
and during the prayers and praises at the Sutra Repository Hall for the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
The practitioner strikes it.
When encountering the rites of welcoming, leading, or escorting the deceased,
the practitioner shaves their head.
When the great assembly performs ritual processions or when welcoming a new abbot into the monastery,
this [instrument] is sounded on all such occasions.
Regarding the striking of the Dharma drum: whenever the Abbot ascends the hall for a formal sermon,
a small discourse (*xiaocan*), a general exposition (*pushe*), or a private interview (*rushi*),
the drum is struck in each case.
Regarding the method for striking the drum when ascending the hall: first, strike the drum base lightly twice;
then, strike it heavily and slowly, ensuring that the tension and slackness alternate.
The tones were balanced in weight,
the sounds harmonious and flowing;
their rising and falling were linked like a chain, deep and resonant, like the roar of spring thunder striking the earth.
First, extend the sound and strike it for a long duration;
after a brief pause, proceed to the second stroke;
then, with the sounds joined and slightly more rapid, continue without further pausing.
Then, while turning the third signal, he strikes with a continuous roll of the sounding block;
once the Abbot has finished ascending the seat, the sound ceases,
and he strikes the double-headed mallet three times in succession for the morning small lecture.
For the general announcement of the five [periods],
the three strikes for entering the room, and all other instances, one should strike slowly.
For the tea drum, strike it once for a long duration.
The attendants take charge of this.
The signal drums for the meal are struck three times,
as when ascending to the hall.
It is merely that the intervals between the services are somewhat shorter.
For the *fushō-kō* (general labor drum), strike it once with a long roll.
For the *kōkō* (watch drum), strike it three times levelly at both morning and evening.
The others follow in sequence as they strike.
The storehouse master oversees this.
As for the bath drum, it is struck four times; the sequence for waiting upon the assembly to strike it is detailed in the "Chapter on Bathing" and overseen by the bath master.
The items listed above should each have their established standard measures;
do not allow them to deviate from these norms.
This applies particularly when a new abbot enters his residence.
All the musical instruments for the Dharma sounded together.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa dreamed of a golden drum one night.
Its form was magnificent and its radiance shone universally,
like the light of the sun.
Within that light, one could see the Buddhas of the ten directions seated upon lapis lazuli thrones beneath trees made of various jewels.
Surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands, he preached the Dharma.
One person, appearing like a brahmin,
struck a drum with a mallet, producing a great sound.
A voice proclaimed verses of repentance.
Having awakened from his dream, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa went to where the Buddha was.
He related to the Tathāgata the golden drum he had seen in his dream as well as the verses of repentance.
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
Ānanda, listen further to this: in this Jeta Grove, when the meal is prepared, the drum is struck for the assembly to gather, and the bell is tolled;
the sounds of the bell and drum continue one after another in succession.
What do you think?
Do these sounds come to the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sounds are?

The Chapter on the Vessels of the Dharma concludes. Epitaph and Preface for the Late Chan Master Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou, Tang China, composed by Chen Xu, Acting Court Attendant Censor, Rank of Willing-to-Serve Official; calligraphed by Wu Yi, Acting Assistant Magistrate of Xin Prefecture, with the status of a Provisional Regular Official. The celestial sphere entwines the Dipper’s position; the mountain’s form stands like a vulture.
The foremost among the śramaṇas was Chan Master Huaihai;
it was here that his chamber stood, it was here that he resided,
